sections.Parameterization and Experimental Design:
The experiments presented in this article are primarily theoretical. In contrast to empirical ABMs, which are calibrated and validated using real-world data, processes, and patterns, theoretical ABMs are usually verified using standard software testing routines and well-understood theoretical cases (Manson 2003; Manson, Sun, and Bonsal 2012). We also followed such methods. In particular, we calibrated model parameters with a combination of mathematical reasoning and parameter sweeping and verified every unit or module with testing, including ensuring that a version of the model could replicate results from ALMA, written in

Netlogo (Filatova, Parker, and van der Veen 2009). Finally, we structurally validated LUXE as it produced the exact same land change patterns as the analytical von Th¨ unen model in the case of homogenous buyers without spatial externalities.

Three categories of parameters were used to initialize LUXE: a set that is constant for all model runs (Group I in Table 3); a set that controls variation in the agents' characteristics, the economic environment, and the spatial environment (Group II.a); and a set that varies in ways that define the four levels of market representation (Group II.b). Although the constant parameters can significantly alter the outcomes of LUXE, their impacts can be shown either theoretically or analytically to be largely predictable. By contrast, the other two groups of parameters are tightly linked to market behaviors and interact with each other, exhibiting typical characteristics of nonlinear complex systems. We therefore conducted multiple model runs that incrementally varied the values of the nonconstant parameter groups to examine their influence on the model outcomes. Chosen parameter values were selected to balance the breadth and the representativeness of all experimental cases, with the goal of drawing concrete and robust conclusions (see the Appendix for Group I and Group II.a parameter values).

The parameters that were used to represent the four market levels included (1) the number of land parcels that a buyer chooses to evaluate-to allow for utility maximization, (2) the seller's WTA value-to represent absence or presence of the budget constraint ( BC ), and (3) the maximum number of bids allowed on a parcel-to operationalize competitive bidding ( CB ).

Marketlevel 0 (L0) has no BC or CB. In L0, the number of parcels selected by a buyer for evaluation ( Nsp ) is set to all available parcels. The reservation price of agricultural land Pag is set much lower than buyers' minimum budgets so that every buyer can afford any parcel in the landscape. L0 essentially implements sequential allocation of parcels according to buyers' preference ranking.

Market level 0.5 (L0.5) adds CB, but without imposing BC. The maximum number of bids allowed on a parcel (max Nbd ) controls whether CB takes place. In L0.5, max Nbd is higher than one, meaning that a seller will receive multiple offers. The highest bid (i.e., WTP) wins the parcel, if it is above the seller's reservation WTA.

Market level 1 (L1) imposes BC on buyers but with no CB, leading to budget-constrained first-come,

sections.Analysis of Output:
With LUXE, we simulated LUC outcomes for the four market levels (Tables 2 and 3). We then analyzed differences in outcome metrics across these levels by applying statistics, regression, and visualization. Model experiments were replicated fifty times with different random seeds to capture the variability in outcomes associated with heterogeneity in agents' budgets and preferences.

To compare model outputs under different market representation levels, we calculated a series of nonspatial and spatial measures to describe the quantity of LUC ( Q ) and its spatial patterns. Q can be either exogenous or endogenous in LUXE, depending on the market level and model parameters. In some market scenarios, where every buyer acquires a parcel, Q is essentially exogenous and fully determined by the number of buyers. Whenever budget constraints are imposed, a certain proportion of buyers (depending on market conditions) do not participate in the LM, and Q becomes endogenous.

Wechose standard fragmentation measures to depict and compare the spatial patterns of projected LUC. Although the definition and measurement of real-world patterns of fragmentation and sprawl are fiercely contested issues across disciplines (e.g., Galster et al. 2001; Ewing, Pendall, and Chen 2003; Parker and Meretsky 2004; Torrens 2008), we argue that several commonly used metrics effectively depict relevant dimensions of the spatial patterns of our simulated landscapes (Table 4). They are transport cost, landscape shape index, fractal dimension, edge density, and the adjacency, contiguity, and centrality indexes (see Appendix for definitions and Table 5 and Figure 2 for representative cases). To address the issue of comparing landscapes of different sizes across experimental settings (Saura and Martinez-Millan 2001), we also construct and report quantity-controlled version of several of these metrics.

We first used descriptive statistics and linear regression to illustrate the overall impacts of markets on LUC outcomes. Descriptive statistics gave a relatively clear picture of the effects of market representation; however, they were limited to an aggregate picture of the outcome space. As the effects of market representation might vary across model parameters, we applied regression that is normally applied to empirical observations to inductively estimate relationships between model parameters and model outputs (Axelrod 1997; Parker forthcoming). To examine and compare outputs from individual runs with different parameter settings, we also applied a visualization technique we termed comprehensive plotting to assemble results from multiple sets of parameters into a single plot to illustrate the impacts of four market levels on a single output metric, averaged across fifty runs per each set of parameters. Comprehensive plotting not only verified conclusions drawn from statis- tics and regression but visualized model sensitivity and helped identify conditions that produced anomalies.
sections.Results: The presentation of our results focuses on how LUC quantity and spatial patterns vary across the four levels of market representation. Our chosen spatial metrics were organized into three groups-overall spread, local fragmentation, and quantity-controlled metrics-that depict different aspects of the simulated LUC patterns. The effects of market representation levels, through the presence of budget constraints ( BC ) and competitive bidding ( CB ), were examined separately for each of these grouped spatial metrics.

Spatial Patterns of Change. Compared with Q, spatial outcome measures produced less consistent results and revealed the multidimensional spatial complexity widely understood to characterize sprawl (Table 6). Based on consistencies in the same qualitative changes in metric values (i.e., increase or decrease) across market levels, we identified three groups of metric values that represent three dimensions of the simulated landscape patterns (Figure 4).

The first dimension (T1) includes the metrics of average and maximum transport costs ( Ctran and C max tran ), as well as landscape shape index ( LSI ). We interpret this dimension as the overall spread of the simulated landscapes, which is generally related to the development density and the overall spatial coverage of the LUC. The second dimension, which includes edge density ( ρ e ), fractal dimension ( d f ), aggregation index ( AI ), centrality index ( CI ), and contiguity index ( CTI ), describes the local pattern of fragmentation (T2 in Figure 4). The quantity-controlled metrics show yet a separate dimension (T3) from the noncontrolled metrics. We separately examine how market levels and their defining elements generate these dynamics.

Overall Spread. The L2 LM, with both BC and CB, led to a statistically significant decrease (compared to L0) in the overall spread as measured by Ctran , C max tran , and LSI (Table 6) and visualized by T1 (Figure 4).

Intuitively, buyers who were not able to obtain their first choice parcel, but were not budget-constrained, located farther away from the urban center, trading off the value of proximity for increased OSAs.

The quantity-controlled metrics include one metric from T1 measuring spread ( LSI q ) and three metrics from T2 measuring fragmentation ( ρ q e , AI q , and CI q ). Both CB and BC independently decreased sprawl, and the net effects of an introduction of both market elements (L0 to L2) was a decrease in fragmentation: a 26 percent and 52 percent decrease in LSI q and ρ q e , and a 199 percent and 217 percent increase in the AI q and CI q , respectively.

sections.Linear Regression Analysis:
We ran four ordinary least square (OLS) regressions of main input parameters on Q, Ctran , ρ e , and ρ q e to examine how the influence of market levels varies with other factors. The dependent variables for the OLS were chosen from the four groups that represent different aspects of the simulated landscape. Independent variables included the radius of the circular neighborhood used to evaluate OSA ( rN ), RHAs' mean budget levels ( ¯ B ), and their mean preferences for PUC ( β u ). The two market elements, BC and CB, were added as two dummy variables BCdv (1 for with budget constraints, 0 for without) and CBdv (1 for with competitive bidding and 0 for without). Their interaction term ( BCCBdv ) was also added as a dummy variable. The three dummy variables, therefore, can effectively differentiate the four market levels that the model implemented. Quantity of Change. As noted before, CB alone (L0 to L0.5) did not reduce Q. Again, the comprehensive plot illustrated that BC (L1) reduced Q, and the addition of CB (L2) generally led to further, but smaller, reductions (Figure 5). The latter result did not always hold, however, and the anomalous outcomes represent a variety of specific situations (Figure 5). When buyers prefer OSA much more than PUC ( ¯ β u = 0 . 2) and they use a relatively large neighborhood ( rN = 3), which incorporates the open-space value of more remote parcels, the addition of competition increased the amount of land conversion. One can observe this on three occasions, which are highlighted in green circles in Figure 5, where the line of market level L2 is above line L1.

At the same time, it is clear that neighborhood size had an interesting interaction with buyers' preference for proximity. In the L2 market, if average agent preference for OSA was high (i.e., low preference for PUC ¯ β u = 0 . 2), an increase in the neighborhood size would increase Q (Figure 5, follow the green upward arrow where the L2 curve goes up as the neighborhood size increases from 1 to 3). When average agent preference for PUC was high ( ¯ β u = 0 . 8), its impacts became negative (e.g., downward green arrow in Figure 5). In other words, when people prefer living close to the urban center and also consider open space over a broad radius to calculate utility, less land would be developed if they are financially constrained and compete with each other. This implies that fewer people buy-primarily because land that is both close to an urban center and has a high proportion of open space in the neighborhood will be relatively scarce. As a result, many buyer agents simply were not motivated to participate in the market. We characterize those with a strong preference for OSA over a larger neighborhood as 'suburb lovers,' and those with a relatively high preference for PUA and close-in open space as 'city lovers.' In general, a market representation with CB and BC is likely to increase projected sprawl for suburb lovers but decrease it for city lovers.

sections.Discussion and Conclusion:
LMs are made up of a number of mechanisms that give rise to complex interactions among buyers, sellers, and other actors involved in land exchanges. Researchers have attempted to represent markets to understand aspects of the complex land system. The most frequently implemented market elements in land-use models (as determined through literature review) include budget constraints and competitive bidding. We presented LUXE, a new, stylized ABM of LUC that was used to systematically alter the combination of these two market elements to evaluate their effects on the quantity and patterns of LUC in simulated landscapes. Our results revealed the significant yet complex effects of LMs on LUC patterns, illustrating the relationships between market representation and model outcomes under different assumptions of the agents' heterogeneity in preferences and budgets, and the neighborhood size as well.

We used and compared three complementary methods-descriptive statistics, OLS regression, and comprehensive plotting-to analyze our data. These methods generally tell similar stories, but each provided a unique and useful view. Results from descriptive statistics and regressions were largely consistent, but some small differences emerged. The regression approach allowed us to not only control for but also formally examine the influence of other explanatory variables. For example, our estimated models showed that open-space preferences and neighborhood size remained important determinants of spatial outcomes, independent of the market representation. The use of comprehensive plots allowed us to examine the context-dependent cases, helped reveal how and under which conditions differences emerged, and provided an understanding of where exceptions to generalizations occurred, what role they played, and to what real-world circumstances they might be analogous.

Market elements in LUC models, particularly budget constraints and competitive bidding, can alter projected land-use patterns; their impacts on both quantity and spatial metrics were statistically significant under most conditions. Our results demonstrated that if

market elements were excluded from an LUC model, one might overproject the extent of LUC and the degree of sprawl in many circumstances. In general, we found that the endogenously generated quantity of LUC decreased with an increase in the level of market representation. Budget constraints played a dominant role in this process, and competitive bidding played a strong secondary role when budget constraints were present. Competitive bidding in the absence of budget constraints, however, might increase overall spread of simulated LUC. Thus, the direction of the impact of competitive bidding depended on whether buyer agents were financially constrained. Although the case of a completely budget-constraint-free for all is impossible in the real world, subprime mortgages through ill-regulated financial markets might be able to lift budget constraints for some in the short term.

The decreasing amount of land development resulting from increased representation of the market, however, did not guarantee a less fragmented landscape pattern. In contrast to what might be expected, increasing market representation, on average, actually produced more locally measured fragmentation. The introduction of budget constraints was responsible for 74 to 83 percent of change across four fragmentation metrics, with the activation of competitive bidding contributing the rest. When we controlled for the quantity of change, however, both budget constraints and competitive bidding reduced projected sprawl. Our experiments also showed that exceptions might occur when the neighborhood size is large and buyer agents have a high preference for open space, which is not uncommon in the cultural context of North America. In this case, the stronger market representation led to a higher degree of projected spread and fragmentation. In other words, market competition among buyers with a high preference for open space drove sprawl when they also used large neighborhoods to assess land quality. This is consistent with the expected interplay between high preferences for OSAs, the sorting that results from

competitive bidding, and the land scarcity that results from budget constraints.

The implications of our results for LUC research are twofold. First, the explicit representation of market elements in LUC models can alter our projection of LUCandcharacterization of the complexity inherent in coupled human-environment systems. Omitting LMs is likely to generate biased outputs in both the quantity of LUCandits spatial patterns. Second, the effects of LMs interact with many factors that are related to actors' (and their virtual representation as agents) preferences and spatial configurations like neighborhood size. Researchers should be cautious to draw universal conclusions as they might overlook some critical dynamics and complex interactions in LMs and heterogeneous agents. Our experiments suggest that mechanisms at the core of a market institution and their pertinent market conditions should be examined individually and as a whole to understand the functioning of LMs and their impacts on LUC.

Although our developed model is deliberately abstract, we anticipate that these conclusions will also apply to empirically parameterized models used for planning and policy analysis. Our results suggest that projections of LUC or land values that do not incorporate market elements such as budget constraints and competitive bidding might produce incorrect policy recommendations. For example, an econometric hedonic value of open space, derived using only spatial and transaction data, might provide a biased estimate of the market values of open space. Policy recommendations based on decision-support tools might also fail to achieve intended goals should they neglect regional and local market and geographic conditions such as residents' preference for OSA versus PUC and their perception of neighborhoods for land quality evaluation. For a hypothetical and homogeneous landscape, LUXE can trace the rate and location of land development over time under different market situations characterized by market levels. This tracing capability could be presented to decision makers for a better understanding of LUC pattern with given economic dynamics. Additionally, an extension of LUXE currently under development is able to explore the combined effects of LMs, landscape heterogeneity, and policies of environmental taxes and subsidies on the spatial patterns and extent of LUC, land rent, and ecological services.

The robustness of such assertions depends, of course, on the extent to which our results, derived using a simple, stylized model, are robust to alternative and more detailed model specifications. In that light, we acknowledge again several limitations of our model and suggest possible extension for further exploration. First, the model could be expanded to explore polycentric landscapes, docking to baseline analytical models such as Filatova, van der Veen, and Parker (2009). Second, alternatives to the CD utility function could be explored to evaluate sensitivity to the land decision-making algorithm. Different neighborhood definitions, including multiscalar neighborhood perceptions and interactions, could also be added. LUXE currently has no mesoscale agent perceptions or cross-scale neighborhood interactions. Neighborhood amenities are perceived at a local scale, and market conditions are essentially perceived at a city scale, as agents are assumed to sample the entire landscape. The model could be extended to contain multiscalar neighborhood definitions and agent perceptions, with feedbacks between neighborhoods (Torrens and Benenson 2005; Torrens 2006).

In additional to relaxing these simplifying assumptions, future research could develop in several directions. First, additional components like land investment and speculation, resale, and credit availability could be added to the market model. Second, empirically informed strategies on location and price decision making are required to accurately represent the real-world LMs and to be able to support policymakers. Third, as an example of an ABM of LUC, our model does not yet represent the whole process of converting agricultural land to inhabited homes. Incorporating developers and homebuilders is a work in progress. Finally, although our methods of analysis have revealed many salient patterns in the simulated data, more advanced methods of analysis and visualization could further enhance our understanding of the effects of various market representations on the LUC projections.

sections.Constant and Household Level Parameters:
Six constant parameters (Group I) are tightly related to the modeled land markets. To make a symmetric landscape and avoid geometric artifacts, we set the landscape size as 49 by 49 and the number of RHAs as 400. The number of 400 was large enough to generate outputs that support statistical examination. It was also small relative to landscape size and therefore prevented edge effects in spatial pattern measures. The proximity preference parameter was bounded by a range of 0.2 to avoid anomalies. Budget splitting factor was set as 0.6 and can allocate about 30 percent to 70 percent of budget to housing in most cases (values depends on land utility). Transport cost was set as one per cell unit.

We bounded the values of Group II.a parameter to only include what we determined were economically or spatially relevant cases. Mean budget levels were 120, 140, 160, 180, and 200. With a standard deviation of 50 and budget splitting factor of 0.6, these budget levels created a diverse population of RHAs that had WTP above and below sellers' WTA (100 in the case of budget constraints). Similarly, we implemented preference levels of 0.2, 0.5, and 0.8 to represent RHAs who, on average, favored OSAs over PUC, the two equally, and PUC over OSAs. These variations in budget and preference values well characterized agent heterogeneity. The identification and delineation of neighborhood is central to spatially explicit land-use land-cover ABMs (Torrens and Benenson 2005). Neighborhoods can be defined using fixed, preexisting boundaries like census tracts, postal zones, or administrative units. They can also be dynamic, focal neighborhoods defined using Euclidean or network distances. By using contiguity and other topological relations, neighborhoods can be multiscalar and hierarchical (Sun and Manson 2012). Previous studies show that the size of neighborhoods has greater impacts than their shapes and forms in ABMs (Fossett and Dietrich 2009). In our model, we varied the radius of circular focal neighborhood from 1, 2, to 3, which contained five, thirteen, and twenty-five cells, respectively, and helped capture the effects of various neighborhood sizes.
sections.Spatial Outcome Metrics:
First, we used the maximum and average transport cost ( Ctrans ) as two simple indicators of the overall size and distribution of the developed area. The transport cost is proportional to the Euclidean distance to the urban center. The maximum of transport cost is an approximate measure of the extent of the simulated monocentric, near-symmetric land development pattern. Average transport cost, taking both the quantity of LUC and their relative distances to the urban center into consideration, roughly measures the overall intensity of spread of the developed landscape.

Second, six standard spatial pattern measures were used to describe different aspects of the simulated landscape patterns.

1. Landscape shape index ( LSI ) is calculated as the ratio of total length of edges ( E ) to the minimum length of edges when the developed parcels are hypothetically rearranged to be the most compact (McGarigal et al. 2002). LSI is positively correlated with sprawl and fragmentation.

<!-- formula-not-decoded -->

2. Fractal dimension ( d f ), a metric that is empirically demonstrated to describe important differences in human-related landscape features (Batty and Longley 1986; O'Neill et al. 1988; White and Engelen 1993; Torrens 2008), is used to measure how self-similar development patterns fill the space.

<!-- formula-not-decoded -->

3. Edge density ( ρ e ) is the average linear distance of edges ( e i ) for all cells of the converted land (McGarigal et al. 2002; Parker and Meretsky 2004). It generally rises with increasing fragmentation.

<!-- formula-not-decoded -->

4. Aggregation index ( AI ) is calculated as the ratio of total number of adjacencies among developed land parcels to the maximum number of possible adjacencies (He, DeZonia, and Mladenoff 2000).

<!-- formula-not-decoded -->

5. Contiguity index ( CI ) examines the spatial connectedness between developed land parcels using a moving window (Ripple, Bradshaw, and Spies

1991). A parcel that is more connected to its neighbors defined by this moving window has a higher contiguity measure. Aggregation and contiguity indexes are positively correlated with compactness and negatively correlated with fragmentation.

<!-- formula-not-decoded -->

6. Centrality index ( CTI ) depicts the concentration of developed land uses around the landscape center (Galster et al. 2001). If CTI is relatively large, it means that most developed land parcels are around the urban center, implying a relatively dense development pattern. It is defined as follows, where R is the radius of the landscape and min (R) is the minimum radius possible given the amount of development.

<!-- formula-not-decoded -->

Although these standard global fragmentation measures are able to quantitatively measure different aspects of the pattern of sprawl and fragmentation, one drawback of these global metrics is that the complex effects of landscape size and quantity of LUC are not accounted for (Saura and Martinez-Millan 2001; Wu 2004). This issue is particularly problematic for some metrics, including LSI, AI, and CTI. To help mitigate such problems, we normalized the quantity of change among experimental cases by halting the simulation once a minimum amount of LUC occurs, which is the minimum amount that occurs under each of the four market-level parameter settings. For example, if L2 produced the minimum number, say 150, of land-use conversions under a specific set of parameters, all other three levels of simulations were halted once 150 cells are converted. At this point we calculated quantitycontrolled landscape metrics AI q , LSI q , and CI q .

Additionally, we revised the standard edge density by considering both quantity of LUC and distances to the urban center, creating a quantity-controlled and distance-weighted edge density ( ρ q e ):

<!-- formula-not-decoded -->

These quantity-controlled metrics not only excluded the confounding impacts of landscape size and land change quantity, allowing us to compare the spatial pattern holding Q constant, but also shed light on the path of the modeled land-use changes, as they allowed us to compare development between experiments at the same stage of LUC.

To intuitively illustrate how these measures map to landscape patterns, we calculated measures for six representative landscapes (A-F) from our simulation (Table 5 and Figure 2). These representative cases show several characteristics. First, some of these measures have the exact same trend between cases. For example, both maximum and average transport cost sort the six cases in the order of C < D < A < B < E < F and fractal dimension and edge density in the order C < D < E < B < F < A . As a result, we can group different metrics that produce the same orders into a single category to simplify our presentation. Second, these groups of metrics reveal different aspects or dimensions of the spatial pattern of the simulated landscapes. In other words, the complexity of spatial patterns cannot be simply depicted by a single metric or a single group of metrics; instead, it has to be examined from multiple angles. Nevertheless, taken together, these metrics provide a rich and comprehensive set of benchmarks to compare spatial patterns generated by LUXE with different market representations.

records.title: Unintended Developments: Gender, Environment, and Collective Governance in a Mexican Ejido
records.abstract: This article examines the unintended outcomes of a neoliberal program designed to privatize Mexico's communal lands. Although postrevolutionary agrarian law excluded women from official landholding and leadership positions, steps toward land privatization inadvertently increased women's access to land, government resources, and political power. Using ethnographic and survey data collected in a Veracruz ejido, I demonstrate how Mexico's agrarian counterreforms triggered novel subjectivities and practices. While men acted as self-imagined private property owners and decreased participation in traditional governance institutions, women became registered land managers and leaders for the first time in the ejido's history. These interlocking processes stopped the land-titling program in its tracks and reinvigorated collective governance. Even state actors charged with carrying out ejido privatization were implicated in the empowerment of rural women and failure to fully privatize land. This research contributes to nature-society debates by arguing neoliberalism does not always end economic self-determination and communal governance in agrarian contexts. Rather, I demonstrate the ways in which processual policy, subjectivity, authority formation, objects, and environmental narratives combine to produce new political trajectories with positive implications for rural women and the environment.

Heidi E. Hausermann

Department of Human Ecology, Rutgers University

This article examines the unintended outcomes of a neoliberal program designed to privatize Mexico's communal lands. Although postrevolutionary agrarian law excluded women from official landholding and leadership positions, steps toward land privatization inadvertently increased women's access to land, government resources, and political power. Using ethnographic and survey data collected in a Veracruz ejido, I demonstrate how Mexico's agrarian counterreforms triggered novel subjectivities and practices. While men acted as self-imagined private property owners and decreased participation in traditional governance institutions, women became registered land managers and leaders for the first time in the ejido's history. These interlocking processes stopped the land-titling program in its tracks and reinvigorated collective governance. Even state actors charged with carrying out ejido privatization were implicated in the empowerment of rural women and failure to fully privatize land. Rather, I demonstrate the ways in which processual policy, subjectivity, authority formation, objects, and environmental narratives combine to produce new political trajectories with positive implications for rural women and the environment. O n a September morning in 2008, Adela 1 waited in the lobby of Registro Agrario Nacional (RAN) 2 in Xalapa, capital city of Mexico's Veracruz state. Adela took over all aspects of coffee production when her husband died in 1999. Nine years and many bureaucratic procedures later, she was finally reregistering a two-hectare plot from her deceased husband's name to her own. The individuals gathered that morning reflected Veracruz's diverse agrarian landscapes and included lowland sugarcane growers, a Totonac leader from a vanilla-producing community, and several coffee producers. The crowd also represented Mexico's long history of gendered agrarian policies: Of fifty-four people waiting to speak with officials, only three were women.

Adela's presence at RAN was an unforeseen outcome of constitutional amendments designed to privatize Mexico's communal landholding system, the ejido. Adela's ejido entered the privatization program in 1997. Following initial steps toward privatization, women gained access to land and leadership positions and helped reassert collective governance. In other words, a policy designed to privatize communal lands not only played out differently than technocrats intended; it helped produce new subjectivities and authorities, ultimately stopping the land-titling process in its tracks.

I do not advocate for top-down development interventions, but I am interested in the unintended outcomes of such impositions and how they might help create new spaces for political change. More often than not, nature-society scholarship focuses on the damaging outcomes of capitalist development for people and environments: new forms of dispossession, gendered and raced exclusions, increased environmental contamination, and so forth. As Heynen and colleagues (2007) put it, 'While neoliberal policies are of course varied and unpredictable in their outcomes . . . we believe it is still reasonable to anticipate that they are more likely to produce negative than positive outcomes' (289). Researchers have demonstrated neoliberalism is anything but an ideal type; instead, policies possess unpredictable and variegated implications in different socioecological contexts (Bakker 2010; see also Larner 2003; Radcliffe 2005; Fisher 2009). This research contributes to this body of scholarship by demonstrating how state-led efforts to privatize communal land helped undo historic exclusions of women from leadership and landholding positions.

This research is based on twenty months of fieldwork in Veracruz. In contrast to the intent of Mexico's agrarian counterreforms, I discovered the national ejido privatization program helped produce unexpected subjectivities and commons-oriented practices within one rural community. I situate this work within Mexico's long history of masculinist agrarian law to demonstrate how steps toward ejido privatization triggered new positions for women as political leaders and registered ejido members. These unfoldings also inspired new tactics to reassert collective governance. I thus make empirical links between steps toward ejido privatization, production of new gendered subjectivities and authorities, and reinvigoration of collective governance. I then illustrate how these interlocking processes shortcircuited the original intent of Mexico's neoliberal counterreforms (i.e., full title privatization of communally managed land). The next section places this research within recent scholarship on nature-society dynamics in the context of neoliberalism.

sections.Nature-Society Dynamics in the Neolibera:
In the last thirty years, neoliberal economic development-led by governments, lending institutions, and other powerful organizations-became aligned with fiscal restraint, free trade, and privatization. Worldwide, agrarian livelihoods were deeply implicated in these efforts as diverse people and agroecosystems were labeled 'inefficient' and 'unviable' in terms of their ability to compete in liberalized markets. Property rights became the focus of attempts to make natural resource management, and human subjects, 'modern,' 'efficient,' and 'competitive' through privatization and enclosure measures.

The outcomes of neoliberal development policies became a major focus of nature-society geographers (e.g., Mansfield 2004; McCarthy 2005; Perreault 2009; Bakker 2010; Robertson 2011; Lave 2012; Radcliffe forthcoming). Many researchers revealed unexpected consequences of privatization and enclosure efforts. For instance, as property regimes in Mexico became messier despite state attempts to privatize resources (Perramond 2008), water and other nonhuman natures resisted commodification and control (e.g., Bakker 2005; Robbins and Luginbuhl 2007). Researchers have also identified the need to better understand the variegated outcomes of neoliberal projects in terms of gender (Harris 2009), nonbinary understandings of agency and power (Bakker 2010), and state practice (Ferguson and Gupta 2002). Thisresearch builds from these calls to demonstrate how attempts to privatize communal lands unexpectedly

yielded political power and resource access for women. Women, moreover, used their new positions to reinvigorate communal practices around shared understandings of the environment, particularly water catchment and quality. The formation of new, ejido-level authorities was critical to these processes.

Local authority formation is particularly complex in postcolonial contexts wherein multiple institutions and understandings-ranging from contemporary land use policies to customary rights-coexist to sanction land claims (Sikor and Lund 2009; see also Hagberg 2006; Lund 2006b). In Latin America and beyond, even the mundane practices of ordinary people shape new authorities mediating land use and access (Lund 2006a, 674; see also Hausermann 2012). For instance, Ghanaian landholders reproduced the government's understanding of private property to reinforce resource claims and build local authority (Lund 2009). In contrast, religious cults in Benin used customary land rights to develop political power among disparate frontier communities (Le Meur 2006). The relationships between authority formation and land tenure are key to understanding property arrangements and access in the neoliberal era. To understand how authority is formed and wielded in everyday social encounters, and the broader implications for property and governance, the processual aspects of authority formation require examination (Lund 2006a; see also Rose 1999). I follow this tack here, linking neoliberal counterreforms to new forms of authority, subjectivities, and reclamation of communal arrangements. To do so, I build from scholarship on subject formation under neoliberalism.

Nature-society scholars have examined how people internalize elements of neoliberal capitalism. While capitalist subjects emerged with exclusive fishing rights in Alaska (Mansfield 2007), migrants self-disciplined in heteronormative ways to access resources enclosed in Indonesian forests (Elmhirst 2011). And based on fieldwork in Nepal, Nightingale (2005) detailed how community members appropriated and resisted neoliberal expertise and market relations along lines of gender, education, and caste, producing new subjectivities in the process. Sundberg (2003, 2004), moreover, showed how a conservation organization intervened in rural Guatemala with preconceived ideas about the Maya, prompting indigenous conservation subjects to perform in ways that met those expectations. Existing research thus suggests that individuals and communities come to self-govern in insidiously subversive ways, privileging the interests of neoliberal development, government, and environmental conservation.

This research has greatly furthered our understandings of neoliberalism's complex implications. Yet, the tendency exists in nature-society scholarship to treat neoliberal development discourse and practice as having colonized entire economic landscapes, leading to the end of economic self-determination and traditional governance. As St. Martin (2009) has argued, noncapitalist processes are almost always represented as threatened or disappearing as the 'logics' of capitalism conquer and expand. Although neoliberal reforms clearly catalyzed dramatic changes in many settings, such 'crisis' situations often inspire novel and creative action, transforming the world in the process (Deleuze and Guattari 1987). New political configurations can indeed emerge from moments of profound change.

Marston, Jones, and Woodward (2005) are helpful here, positing that things in the world are material actualizations resolved through heterogeneous interactions of different objects-ranging from coffee plants to human bodies and government policies. By examining interactions of differential combinations we can see repetitiveness and capacity for newness. These complex potentialities help us understand how diverse relations (both actual and potential) produce different sites and orders, with politically productive unfoldings (Marston, Jones, and Woodward 2005, 425). Following this line of thought, capitalist processes, such as a national land privatization program, might indeed possess diverse implications for peoples and places and create politically differentiated trajectories. It is thus important to examine how policies interact with gender, historic institutions, subject formation, and authority without a priori understanding of one element possessing greater spatial reach than others. Indeed, in the 'illimitable et cetera' of actually existing difference, we find new departures for politics (Butler 1990, 196). Such a view allows researchers to carefully examine interplays to understand outcomesandpossibilities, most of which, given the vast socioecological difference that makes up the world, are unpredictable.

I found Mexico's neoliberal agrarian counter reforms unexpectedly triggered an undoing of women's historic exclusion from local leadership and landholding positions. Following the ejido's entrance in a land privatization program, men identified as private property owners and became apathetic toward traditional governance while women developed political authority and helped reinvigorate collective practices. These processes, moreover, kept the ejido from being fully privatized. In other words, new interlocking subjectivities and forms of authority undermined the land-titling

process itself and communal practices were reclaimed in new contexts. Before describing these findings in greater detail, I provide background on Mexican agrarian reform and its undoing.
sections.Agrarian Reform and Gender in Mexico (19:
Between 1917 and 1992, the Mexican government expropriated large landholdings throughout the nation, redistributing resources to small-scale farmers, pastoralists, and fisherfolk in the form of communally managed ejidos. 3 Ejidos are often a combination of solares (urban plots), parcelas (farm plots), and a preagreed percentage of tierras de uso com´ un (commonsland and resources). In the decades following the Mexican Revolution, 28,000 ejidos and agrarian communities were created, occupying more than half of Mexico's arable land surface (Instituto Nacional de Estad´ ıstica y Geograf´ ıa [INEGI] 1990). By 1992, when constitutional amendments brought an end to Mexican land reform, millions of ejido members (hereafter ejidatarios ) were registered in these communities.

Postrevolutionary agrarian laws were designed to create and protect ejido land from concentration. Ejidatarios never legally possessed fee-simple titles to land. Instead, the state granted usufruct access, the right to use property belonging to someone else, in this case federal land and water. Even in ejidos where members work individual parcels, producers possess land exploitation rights in usufruct form (Procuradur´ ıa Agraria 2007). Put differently, whereas ejidatarios could pass land to others through inheritance, they could not legally lease or sell land, although many did through de facto practices (e.g., Sheridan 1988; Nu˜ nez-Madrazo 2005; LastarriaCornhiel 2011).

Agrarian laws also mandated collective decision making,requiring ejidos possess a general assembly comprised of all registered members. 4 This regularly convened assembly is the venue for collective decision making: establishing rules, elections, solving disputes, and so on. Within the assembly, elected leaders serve three-year terms. 5 While promoting collectivity in land management and local governance, Mexican agrarian laws systematically excluded women from official entitlement and political participation.

Women could only become registered ejidatarias as widows or a household's sole economic provider, the latter being difficult to prove. Until 1971 a woman was required to forfeit land rights and official status if she married an ejidatario. Constitutional amendments in 1971 reworked the status of women; women would no longer lose ejido membership upon marriage. Inheritance rights were also created, meaning that land could be willed to individuals irrespective of sex. Deere and Le´ on (2001b, 71), however, argued that the 1971 amendmentsdidlittle to promote women's roles in ejido decision making. Brunt (1992, 82) demonstrated that when women did gain access to ejidataria status, men rarely allowed them to serve as leaders (see also De Walt and Rees 1994; Esparza Salinas, Su´ arez, and Bonfil 1996). Despite significant roles in agricultural and social (re)production, women account for under 18 percent of registered ejido members (V´ azquez-Garc´ ıa 1997; Radel 2011). By extension, local leadership positions requiring ejidatario status are dominated by men. Women are also often excluded from government programs tied to official standing, such as credit and agricultural extension services.

While fostering male dominance in resource access and politics, the ejidal sector became an important site of state formation, ecological transformation, and cultural symbolism in postrevolutionary Mexico. By the end of 1987, though, largely due to the 1982 oil crisis and massive borrowing, the Mexican government had accumulated US $ 107.6 billion of foreign debt (Hern´ andez-Estrada, Villa-Issa, and Quintana Loya 1989). Foreign lending institutions began to mandate austerity measures, including privatization and government cutbacks. During this period, the World Bank began discussing agricultural reform with Mexican technocrats, including changes to the ejido sector (Teichman 2004). Land-titling in ejidos, the bank argued, would create incentives for farmers to enhance productivity and provide collateral for further investment (Deininger and Binswanger 1999, 249).

The 1992 constitutional amendments (to Article 27 in particular) were designed to open ejidos to privatization. Land previously held in usufruct could now be transformed into private property and leased or sold to firms or individuals (both foreign and national). At the time, President Carlos Salinas de Gortari (1988-1994) argued that the changes would result in government withdrawal from the agrarian sector and empower peasants to make decisions as 'legitimate owners of the land' (Craib 2004, 256). Federal legislation created Programa de Certificaci´ on de Derechos Ejidales y Titulaci´ on de Solares (PROCEDE) 6 to facilitate the process. Through this ongoing program, ejidos can opt to transform 'usufruct fields' into official 'parcels,' via a bewildering array of bureaucratic tr´ amites (procedures), involving cartography, notaries, and other forms of certification. 7 If an

ejido's general assembly votes to enter PROCEDE, ejidatarios can obtain land titles to urban plots, farm plots, and a preagreed percentage of the ejidal commons (Nuijten 2003). Ejidatarios can choose to title any or all of these land uses. For example, some ejidos pursued ownership of individual parcels while retaining communal control of resources such as forests and grazing lands (Perramond 2008).

By entering PROCEDE, ejidatarios must allow INEGI, 8 Mexico's cartographic agency, to measure and map urban and agricultural plots. Once parcels are mapped, ejidatarios receive a certificate verifying boundaries. Yet, even after this laborious mapping strategy, individual parcels are not considered private property by the state. Before land is officially privatized-thereby legalizing land sales, rentals, and so on-the ejido's general assembly must vote to proceed with privatization and disband the ejido. If 20 percent or more of ejidatarios abstain or vote to discontinue PROCEDE, the entire community's privatization progress is stalled. Put differently, no land is legally considered private property until 80 percent of ejidatarios agree, in vote, to finalize PROCEDE, achieving dominio pleno (fee-simple ownership). Until dominio pleno is reached and the ejido disbanded, ejidatarios are technically subject to ejido rules and regulations. I argue that the processual nature of PROCEDE combined with new subjectivities and practices to derail steps toward full privatization.

The 1992 amendments and creation of PROCEDE inspired significant criticism. Critics warned that the changeswouldresult in further dispossession of the peasantry, resource consolidation, and monopolies (e.g., Foley 1995; Harvey 2003). There was also speculation the amendments would further alienate women from resources and decision making (Stephen 1993, 1996; Zapata 1995; Bonfil S´ anchez 1996; Esparza Salinas, Su´ arez, and Bonfil 1996; Appendini 2001; Hamilton 2001; De Ita 2007). Deere and Le´ on (2001a) projected that PROCEDE would negatively affect women, as ejido parcels, held largely in men's names, transitioned into maleowned private property. So far, however, the policy shifts have not produced the sweeping effects proponents desired and critics feared.

Two decades have passed since constitutional reforms allowed for ejido privatization. By 2006, 97 percent of Mexico's ejidos had entered PROCEDE (Perramond 2008; Kelly et al. 2010). Yet, despite widespread steps toward privatization, the ejido sector has experienced little private investment (Cornelius and Myhre 1998; Perramond 2010). Very few communities have achieved dominio pleno. Scholars suggested that farmers are reluctant to finish PROCEDE because of fees associated with dominio pleno (201 pesos/title; currently about US $ 16) or in avoidance of property taxes (e.g., Deere and Le´ on 2001b; Wilshusen 2010). Researchers demonstrated that land tenure is more complex now than before PROCEDE (e.g., Nuijten 2003; Haenn 2006; Kelly et al. 2010; Perramond 2010; Wilshusen 2010). Yet, we know little about the relationships among privatization efforts, gender, subjectivities, and commons-oriented practices. Before I turn to empirics to untangle these relationships, I discuss the study site and methods used to conduct this research.
sections.Study Site and Methods:
This article is the result of fieldwork carried out in an ejido called La Grullita located in central Veracruz, on the eastern flanks of shield volcano Cofre de Perote, near Coatepec (Figure 1). The community has a population of approximately 1,529 inhabitants, 156 of whom are registered ejidatarios (INEGI 2005). Except the urban area and a scattering of pasture plots, shadegrown coffee dominates land use in polyculture fi ncas (coffee orchards). Ecologists have shown that central Veracruz coffee systems provide several environmental benefits, including water catchment, nutrient cycling, and carbon sequestration (e.g., Greenberg, Bichier, and Sterling 1997; Moguel and Toledo 1999; Manson, Contreras Hern´ andez, and L´ opez-Barrera 2008). Veracruz plantations also possess levels of biodiversity similar to less altered forests in the region and serve as habitat corridors for migratory bird populations.

Between June 2003 and November 2008 I conducted twenty months of fieldwork in Veracruz. I was introduced to La Grullita in June 2006 during predissertation fieldwork and the ejido was one of two case study communities selected for my doctoral research. It quickly became clear that PROCEDE, women leaders, and collective tree-planting efforts were important ongoing topics of discussion within the ejido. To understand these dynamics in greater detail, I employed an ethnographic approach. Within La Grullita, I conducted twenty-four semistructured interviews with local leaders, male and female ejidatarios, and other individuals. 9 Twenty-one additional interviews were carried out with state actors, including officials from agrarian reform, agricultural, and development agencies. All interviews were transcribed and coded during the fieldwork period.

Participant observation was another important method for this study and allowed observation of

I conducted thirty-five surveys in October 2008, surveying nearly one quarter of registered ejidatarios. Respondents were randomly selected from an official roster of ejido members. The survey was divided into four sections to query: (1) agricultural production, (2) participation in state programs, (3) land use change, and (4) local institutions. Descriptive analysis of the data allowed me to observe patterns, variations, and anomalies in people's experiences and perceptions. The following pages reveal post-PROCEDE dynamics in La Grullita.
sections.Breaking the Rules: Self-Imagined Privat:
La Grullita was declared an ejido in 1936 and since possessed various rules about local governance and land use (Table 1). Until 1997, when the assembly voted to enter PROCEDE, the ejido largely functioned in accordance with these internal rules and agrarian laws. La Grullita initiated the privatization process for 472 hectares, already divided into individual parcels, yet subject to usufruct rights under agrarian law. The ejido elected to keep its sixty acres of commons land out of PROCEDE and in collective control. RAN officials were quick to visit the community to discuss the transition. INEGI surveyors followed to measure and map. According to former community leaders, INEGI t´ ecnicos were impressed by the ejido's quantity of water, both surface and underground. Ricardo, ejido president at the time, remembered an INEGI surveyor pulling him aside:

He told me, 'We traveled over the entire country and have never seen an ejido with as much water as this one. Be very careful selling the land . . . and if you sell, sell for a good price.'

Others remembered similar reactions from the INEGIt´ ecnicos. One fifty-two-year-old ejidatario recalled:

We walked the boundaries of my parcel and that of my brother. They had their equipment and wrote everything in notebooks. . . . They commented a lot about the water . . . how much there was, how clean it was . . . they asked me a lot of questions about water.

INEGI bureaucrats worked as double agents in neoliberal policy implementation. On one hand, they enacted the first steps toward ejido privatization: boundary delineation and mapping. On the other hand, these state actors cautioned ejidatarios on potential exploitation resulting from PROCEDE and educated people on potential land values. And as we will see in the following pages, the t´ ecnicos' perceptions of the ejido's prolific water resources triggered an environmental narrative around which women later worked to reinvigorate commons-oriented practices.

Following INEGI's mapping efforts, farmers were provided with certificates indicating parcel size and perimeters. If the ejido voted to continue through PROCEDE's hoops, these certificates would be used to apply for individual titles. Yet-and this is an important point-the assembly did not vote to continue the privatization process and La Grullita has not passed through PROCEDE's

Lund (2006a) argued that although development interventions claim to be technical and discrete, they are often political and engender structural change (see also Craib 2004; Mitchell 2002). INEGI's mapping efforts catalyzed important political reshufflings within the ejido. Ejidatarios should follow regulations until achievement of dominio pleno, but many behaved as if they already possessed titles, marking a clear shift from how transactions unfolded in the ejido's past. Although not legally permitted by agrarian law, community members agreed that intra-ejido land sales and rentals occurred prior to 1997. But ejidatarios followed local protocol for such exchanges, obtaining permission from the Executive Committee prior to land sales. Entrance into PROCEDE altered these de facto procedures.

Male ejidatarios acted as self-imagined private property owners following certificate dispersal. Mario, who sold a large portion of his farm to a cousin in 2001, explained his decision:

I sold land to my cousin . . . he wanted to build a trout farm and my parcel is in a good location, close to the road and stream. . . . I sold the land for a good price, although I didn't charge too much. I built a new room [on the house] and put the other part [of the money] in the bank.

Indeed, many community members noted increased land sales following PROCEDE. Respondents estimated that 25 percent of ejidatarios sold portions of land since PROCEDE, mostly to family and community members. People largely believed that these transactions did not pass before the ejido assembly. Many men admitted that they did not seek permission to divide or sell land. This contrasts with people's pre-PROCEDE recollections: Although land sales did occur occasionally, individuals always presented transactions to the assembly for approval. Now, however, with certificates in hand, many men acted in their own self-interest, bypassing customary channels. Ejidatarios used certificates to back up their desire to act autonomously with regard to land use decisions. The certificates, in other words, became objects for making claims and justifying particular behaviors.

Postcertificate land sales in La Grullita reflect the emergenceof rational, profit-seeking individuals following land-titling projects (Mansfield 2007, 396; Wolford 2007). Kelly et al. (2010) noted similar dynamics as ejidatarios in San Luis Potosi assumed that parcels would eventually convert to dominio pleno. The production of identities and practices linked to private property, in other words, prelude land privatization itself. Because postrevolutionary agrarian laws ensured that most ejidatarios were men, certificate dispersal, and subsequent land use practices, largely influenced male subjectivities.

Yet, although men fancied themselves private property owners and used elements of the neoliberal state to

back up their actions, many found that they still needed ejido institutions, particularly when autonomous control of private property did not work out as planned. As Mario explained:

The trout farm didn't happen. My cousin didn't have all the money . . . he wanted me to buy [back] the land. It turned ugly. . . . I went to Enrique [ejido president] so he could support me.

Mario was not alone: There were several conflicts following land sales, mostly disputes about payment. But now, if the assembly was not consulted prior to the transaction's initiation, quarrelling parties must resolve their own conflicts. Enrique, the ejido president, explained:

They [ejidatarios] sell land without the assembly's permission. Maybe later they have a problem . . . they want more money or their land back. Then they come to me for help . . . but if they didn't come to the assembly to begin with, my hands are clean.

Men liked the convenience and autonomy corresponding with their status as private property owners. Treating certificates as titles, many men engaged in land sales, including those based on future speculations like trout farming profit. Yet, such practices put informal sellers in a bind when people, like Mario's cousin, could not pay or wanted to renegotiate initial terms. Men also wanted to continue participating in traditional governance as they saw fit, and according to their needs. The production of male subjects as self-imagined private landowners, moreover, coemerged with apathy and decreased participation among male ejidatarios toward traditional institutions.
sections.Breaking the Rules: Decreased Participat:
The initial meeting with PROCEDE officials, sixteen years ago, was the last assembly attended by all ejidatarios. Shortly after parcels were mapped and certificates received, assembly attendance waned. Survey respondents noted declining participation in communal works projects, assembly attendance, and elections, including a decrease in their own involvement (Table 2). Decreased participation in local governance was partially due to livelihood diversification.

In the last fifteen years, many men in La Grullita diversified their livelihoods through off-farm labor. Although scholars have found that long-distance male migration alters local gender and agricultural dynamics

(e.g., Herrera 2009; Aguilar-Støen, Angelsen, and Moe 2010; Radel 2011), men in La Grullita commuted daily to Xalapa and Coatepec. Involvement in offfarm labor, moreover, was part time, temporary, or both. Of the thirty-five ejidatarios surveyed, eleven-all men-reported working in construction, service, or as drivers at least once in recent years. All but one said that they engaged in off-farm labor due to low coffee prices. Yet, most continued coffee production despite urban employment. As a result, these men were busier than ever, maintaining coffee crops and working as wage laborers. 10 This contributed to men's apathetic attitudes toward governance practices (e.g., assemblies) and communal works projects. Rodrigo, a forty-year-old coffee producer and weekend bus driver, confessed:

Saturday is for the assembly. I know I should go . . . I would like to go, but I would have to rearrange my driving schedule and take a weekday shift. I like driving on weekends because there is less traffic.

For Rodrigo, livelihood diversification meant sacrificing participation in local institutions.

More than conflicting commitments, however, respondents linked PROCEDE certificates and new understandings of individual rights to male apathy. One forty-two-year-old ejidatario explained what I heard from many: 'Once we received our certificates, the assemblies weren't necessary.' I spoke with many men who echoed this sentiment: The certificates distributed by PROCEDE meant that they were no longer required to attend official ejido events. As Carlos, who had not attended an assembly since obtaining his certificate in 1998, put it:

The certificate means I am the owner and I can do what I want with my land. I don't have to ask my neighbors or the assembly to make changes.
