1990 and 2000, industry/business was the most important predictor of the permanent migrant versus temporary migrant outcome. For 1990, the next four predictors were, in descending order, college and above, administrative, job transfer/job assignment/joining family, and study/training. For 2000, the second to fifth predictors were study/training, agriculture, college and above, and marriage. These changes suggest the following. First, state-allocated jobs as a pathway toward hukou change have declined in importance. Second, education as a means to change one's hukou has increased in importance. Third, marriage migration is increasingly closely tied to permanent migration.

The overall results for the rural-urban models (Table 7) are similar to the all-migrant models. For the 1990 model and the two 2000 models (ru1 and ru2), industry/business is the most important independent variable, followed by college and above, study/training, and senior secondary. This consistency in ranking, compared with the all-migrant models (Table 6), suggests that the relationship between education and permanent migration is stronger for rural-urban migration than overall migration. The increasing size of the coefficient for study/training, in particular, highlights the strong and increasing connection between higher education and urban hukou. Marriage was not significant in the 1990 model but

had large and significant coefficients in the 2000 models, suggesting that over time the barriers for rural-urban marriage migrants to obtain hukou have become lower. Unlike in the all-migrant models, in the rural-urban models the coefficient for job transfer/job assignment/joining family has increased in size between 1990 and 2000. Jobs in the state sector or sponsored by the state are, therefore, still an important means for obtaining urban hukou.

In the rural-urban models, the coefficient for nonworking is negative and significant for 1990 but positive and significant for both the 2000 models. This suggests that over time, the nonworking migrants are more likely permanent migrants, underscoring the observation that students constitute increasingly large proportions of permanent migrants. Most other occupation dummies have positive and significant coefficients and most coefficients have increased in size between 1990 and 2000. In other words, over time industrial jobs have become an increasingly important predictor of temporary migration and most other occupations are increasingly associated with permanent migration.
sections.Summary and Conclusion:
A legacy of the socialist era of central planning, the hukou system bifurcates Chinese society into a rural group and an urban group and makes it extremely difficult for rural citizens to enjoy the rights and benefits reserved for their urban counterparts. As a result, most rural migrants who have helped China industrialize and urbanize continue to be seen and defined as temporary migrants, despite their having worked and lived in cities for months and years. Migrants who are highly skilled and educated, on the other hand, are welcomed by urban governments to obtain urban hukou and become permanent migrants.

In this article, we ask the question if this twotrack migration system has remained intact over time. We approach this question empirically by examining if the differentials between permanent migrants and temporary migrants have narrowedorwidened.Wehavehighlightedtwo factors that can change the differentials between these two types of migrants. First, hukou reforms that aim at making urban citizenship moreinclusive are expected to have lowered the barriers for rural Chinese to become permanent migrants (and residents) in cities. Under this scenario, the gaps between permanent migrants and temporary migrants would narrow. Yet, if actual implementation of hukou reforms targets only the most competitive migrants and ignores the rest, then the distances between permanent migrants and temporary migrants would remain large. Second, migration theory predicts a negative relationship between maturation of migration streams and migration selectivity. Over time, knowledge, experience, and social networks reduce migration selectivity, and as a result a larger spectrum of the rural population can become migrant workers and would accordingly widen the gaps between permanent migrants and temporary migrants.

Our empirical analysis shows that between 1990 and 2000 the gaps between interprovincial permanent migrants and temporary migrants did not narrow but in most aspects actually widened. The magnitude of temporary migrants increased many fold, whereas the numberofpermanentmigrantsremainedabout the same. Over time, permanent migrants are increasingly represented by young, highly educated individuals and those in prestigious occupations. Selectivity of temporary migrants, on the other hand, has declined. The improvement of educational attainment among temporary migrants is slower than that of the general population and much slower than that of permanent migrants. Over time, increased proportions of temporary migrants work in industrial and commerce sectors, and the proportion of women among temporary migrants has significantly increased, indicating that migrant work as a way of life is increasingly prevalent among rural Chinese. Hukou reforms appear to have made it easier for marriage migrantsincluding rural-urban marriage migrants-to become permanent migrants. Other than marriage migration, however, there is little evidence that the reforms have lowered hukou barriers. At the same time, a larger spectrum of the population, including the less skilled and educated, has joined the temporary migration streams. The net result of these factors is the persistence of a two-track migration system, where permanent migrants increasingly assume the position of social and economic elites and temporary migrants are the disadvantaged and disenfranchised.

Our analysis has two limitations, both pointing to future research and demand for data. First, Chinese society is complex and rapidly changing and thus factors other than hukou reforms and maturation of migration streams might be at work to enlarge the gap between permanent and temporary migrants. For example, expansion of higher education opportunities makes it possible for qualified students to become permanent migrants, opportunities that do not benefit the less well trained. In addition, migrants' intentions to stay influence the propensity of hukou change. Second, our analysis is confined to interprovincial migration and does not address intraprovincial migration. Because the former is increasingly important over time, however, we are confident that our findings reflect the overall trends of mobility in China.

The global financial crisis that began in 2008 is felt also by China's migrant workers. In February 2009, China's Ministry of Agriculture reported that 20 million migrant workers had lost their jobs, with some being forced to return to the countryside and increasing the risk of social unrest ('China's Migrants See Jobless Ranks Soar' 2009). Although this number is disputable, there is no question that as one after another Chinese manufacturers go out of business, migrant workers are the first to suffer. For a quarter of a century, rural migrants have provided the labor for China's rapid industrialization and economic growth. Although urban work helps to improve migrant households' standard of living, rural migrants as a whole continue to lead a precarious and marginal existence institutionally, socially, and economically, and our study suggests that this situation is not likely to change in the foreseeable future. /squaresolid

records.title: A LiDAR-Based Analysis of Stream Channel Cross Section Change Across an Urban-Rural Land-Use Boundary
records.abstract: Little is known about the downstream propagation of stream channel alterations initiated by urban flow regimes. In this study, freely available Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) data were combined with ground survey data to derive information on changes in stream cross sections in a North Carolina watershed, moving downstream across an urban-to-rural land-use boundary. Regression analyses relating LiDAR model and ground survey data exhibit poor relationships for all channel morphometric measurements except reach-average channel capacity. Application of the channel capacity regression reveals a negative power function pattern of downstream decline in channel enlargement. The largest declines occur before streams enter the rural landscape, with more gradual declines afterward. The largest declines in channel size might be attributable to reservoir effects along reaches with wide floodplains. Model results indicate no discernible enlargement once rural land covers and percentage impervious areas of about 60 percent and 16 percent of watershed area, respectively, are reached.

In this study, freely available Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) data were combined with ground survey data to derive information on changes in stream cross sections in a North Carolina watershed, moving downstream across an urban-to-rural land-use boundary. Key Words: channel capacity, channel enlargement, LiDAR, urban stream.

T he morphological characteristics of stream channels coevolve in the short term (10 1 -10 2 years) in accordance with hydrologic regimes and sediment loads (Schumm 1977; Knighton 1998; Brierley and Fryirs 2005; Schumm 2005). These fundamental controls reflect the combined effects of an array of watershed variables including drainage area, relief, bedrock geology, climate, vegetation characteristics, and system history. Land use represents a further major influence that is capable of heavily impacting discharges of water and sediment (Poff, Bledsoe, and Cuhaciyan 2006; Walling 2006). Alteration of land cover changes the rainfall-runoff response of watersheds by changing the capacity of the land surface to absorb rainfall, often leading to greater runoff and increased erosion and sedimentloads (Dunne and Leopold 1978; Gregory 2006). This change is particularly intense in urban environments in which the high impervious surface area greatly magnifies runoff and stream discharge peaks, commonly resulting in channel cross section enlargement and other morphological changes (Booth 1991; Chin 2006).

The mechanisms and results of urban channel enlargement have been well documented in a number of areas within urban environments (Wolman 1967; Hammer 1972; Booth 1991; Chin 2006; Gregory 2006). Most studies have been based on observations of channel morphology as rural streams enter urban environments or of separate rural and urban watersheds (Ebisemiju 1989; Roberts 1989; Gregory, Davis, and Downs 1992). Few studies have evaluated the nature of channel change as streams arising in fully urbanized watersheds flow into rural landscapes. The rate and trajectory of this shift have important implications for rural landowners as well as downstream municipalities whose legal borders might be approaching contact with those of upstream urban areas. In addition, the details of downstream morphological change have implications for understanding the range of natural variability in hydraulic geometry, which is crucial to successful stream rehabilitation (Downs and Gregory 2004).

In this study, Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR)-derived digital topographic models and field survey data are utilized to examine the urban-to-rural transition in channel cross-sectional change for two headwater streams in the North Carolina Piedmont: North and South Buffalo Creeks, in Guilford County (Figure 1). Topographic models constructed from freely available LiDAR data are calibrated using field-surveyed channel cross section measurements, allowing high-density model sampling and tracking of downstream trends. The results are combined with data from independent hydraulic geometry curves and land use mapping to describe and explain the nature of adjustments in channel cross section dimensions for North and South Buffalo creeks as they flow from urban into rural landscapes.
sections.Background:
Urban Stream Syndrome and Downstream Hydraulic Geometry

Urban stream syndrome refers to a set of hydrological, geomorphological, and biological symptoms commonly associated with streams where a significant portion of the contributing upland catchment has been affected by urbanization (Paul and Meyer 2001; Walsh et al. 2005). As urbanization takes place in a watershed, increases in the areal extent and connectedness of impervious surfaces and the concentration of storm flow by physical conduits like sewer systems increase the volume and velocity of flow in channels (Dunne and Leopold 1978; Booth 1991; Schueler 1995). The hydrogeomorphic consequences of this include 'flashier' hydrographs with higher discharge peaks and altered channel morphology (Booth 1991; Paul and Meyer 2001; Walsh et al. 2005). Channel cross section enlargement is the most frequently cited response, with urban channels commonly becoming two to three times and as much as fifteen times larger than nonurban channels of comparable watershed area (Dunne and Leopold 1978;

Figure 1 Buffalo Creek watershed and the city of Greensboro in Guilford County, North Carolina. The ten open circles along North Buffalo Creek indicate stream reaches for which both ground-survey and modelextracted cross-section data were obtained. Filled circles along both North and South Buffalo creeks indicate stream reaches with model-extracted cross sections only. The numbers of ground-surveyed cross sections for each of the ten survey reaches on North Buffalo Creek are Wesley Long (1), Westover (5), Lower Latham (2), Elm St. (3), Church St. (4), Summit (2), White St. (3), Landfill (1), NBCnG (2), and Creekview (2).

<!-- image -->

Booth 1991; Walsh et al. 2005; Chin 2006). Much less enlargement, reductions in size, no clear pattern, and complex patterns of change have also been observed (Gregory, Davis, and Downs 1992; Odemerho 1992; Chin and Gregory 2001; Grable and Harden 2006; Kang, Storm, and Marston 2010).

Although much has been written about urban channel enlargement, little literature exists documenting precise trends in channel cross section adjustment as urban streams flow into rural areas downstream. Knighton (1998) noted that 'the extent to which enlargement is propagated downstream remains unknown' (322). McBride and Booth (2005) found that the general symptoms of urban stream syndrome 'improve' downstream if the riparian zone is substantially forested and devoid of road crossings. Odemerho (1992) found that channel constriction (rather than enlargement) occurred in the urban zone due to large sediment inputs from new construction and that this was rapidly reversed downstream of the urbanized area. Kang and Marston (2006) presented regression results for channel capacity of the predominantly rural Skeleton Creek, flowing out of Enid, Oklahoma. Residuals from their regression line drop sharply to lower capacity following the creek's exit from the municipal boundary, although there are few data points situated across that boundary, and their regression line trends positively overall. In the nearby watershed of Stillwater Creek, urbanization (3.9 percent impervious surface area) was found to have little impact on channel capacities (Kang, Storm, and Marston 2010). The authors cited the importance of geological setting as well as local variations in bank cohesiveness and riparian vegetation characteristics as effective influences resisting erosive urban runoff regimes.
sections.Topographic Measurements from LiDAR: LiDAR technology allows the rapid remote acquisition of highly accurate elevation points at high spatial resolution. Expected horizontal and vertical root mean square errors are frequently less than 1 m and point spacing of refined data sets is commonly less than 4 m (Kraus and Pfeifer 1998; Baltsavias 1999; Hodgson et al. 2003). Several important limitations of LiDAR exist, though. For example, even at 4-m resolution, LiDAR returns might be ill-suited to defining features with precise boundaries such as the tops and bottoms of stream banks, necessitating manual input of breakline data derived from other sources (Maune 2001). Automated methods for filtering buildings from bare-earth surfaces tend to also filter or smooth natural features with similarly sharp topographic breaks (Kraus and Pfeifer 1998; Maune 2001; Bowen and Waltermire 2002; James, Watson, and Hansen 2007). LiDAR returns from water features are generally unreliable, due to the absorption and scattering of pulses (Maune 2001; H¨ ofle et al. 2009). In densely vegetated areas, a nearvertical pulse is needed to effectively penetrate canopy and generate a true bare-earth return (Kraus and Pfeifer 1998; Hodgson et al. 2003). The mean distance to the nearest LiDAR point might be closely tied to land cover class, with the greatest point spacing in deciduous, mixed, and scrub or shrub environments (Hodgson et al. 2003).
sections.Morphometric Analyses with LiDAR:
Despite the limitations, useful geomorphological analyses have been conducted using LiDAR data. An early application of LiDAR technology involved the measurement of channel and gully morphology. Ritchie et al. (1994) made rough estimates of river channel widths and depths by connecting minimum elevation measurements with straight and curvilinear lines using 'best judgment' practices. Bowen and Waltermire (2002) sought to identify the types of river corridor terrain most commonly associated with the largest measurement errors in the Western United States. Large LiDAR elevation overestimations were found to be common in areas with both dense vegetation and steep banks. Charlton, Large, and Fuller (2003) evaluated the abilities of LiDAR to map a gravel-bed wandering stream in the United Kingdom and found that error was introduced by both the presence of vegetation and by deep water, which tended to produce gaps in the point spacing. James, Watson, and Hansen (2007) used LiDAR to map gully networks and headwater streams under forest canopy in South Carolina. Their model captured the location of gully networks accurately but not gully channel dimensions. Overestimation of channel width and underestimation of channel depth were tied to point spacing. The authors recommended the incorporation of ancillary data such as breaklines to explicitly delineate the rims and bottoms of channels.

These studies illustrate that accurate measurements of channel width and depth are difficult to extract from LiDAR data sets. If the limitations of the methods with respect to topography and land cover are consistent or constant, however, then scaled relationships between model and nature might be obtainable. In this study we create and field-calibrate a LiDAR-based model of downstream change in channel dimensions and particularly channel capacities at higher resolution than could be obtained by field studies alone in a similar time frame. We use this model to test the hypothesis that decline in channel enlargement ratio downstream of urban headwaters is directly proportional to the proportion of watershed area that is urbanized, a value that declines exponentially with downstream distance from the municipal boundary.
sections.Field Area:
North and South Buffalo creeks head in Greensboro, North Carolina (population 250,000; Figures 1 and 2), a medium-sized city in the Piedmont physiographic province. The area falls within the humid subtropical climate zone, with an average annual temperature of 14.5 ◦ C and an average annual rainfall of 1,074 mm. Vegetation consists predominantly of mixed deciduous and coniferous trees. Upland soils are formed in residuum from metamorphosed felsic rocks and contain a clay-rich Bt (argillic) horizon. North and South Buffalo creeks (henceforth, NBC and SBC) exit the urban boundary at drainage areas of approximately 65 and 75 km 2 , respectively, and join in

Figure 2 Selected images of North and South Buffalo creeks. Names refer to stream reaches displayed in Figure 1. NBC = North Buffalo Creek; SBC = South Buffalo Creek. (Color figure available online.)

<!-- image -->

rural eastern Guilford County to form Buffalo Creek (total drainage area of 230 km 2 ). Total relief in the watershed is 76 m. The majority of the municipal area within the NBC and SBC

catchments has been fully urbanized since the 1960s and 1970s, respectively; thus, there has been some time for a new quasi-equilibrium state under urban conditions to be achieved.

Data on stream bankfull cross-sectional area (capacity), width, and depth for large numbers of both rural and urban streams in the North Carolina Piedmont demonstrate that urban streams typically exhibit an increase in channel dimensions relative to rural streams of equivalent drainage areas (Doll et al. 2002). Regional hydraulic geometry curves derived from these data display an average channel capacity enlargement ratio (the urban capacity divided by the corresponding rural capacity at the same drainage area) of 2.6. The channels surveyed in this study are partially confined to unconfined and increase in sinuosity downstream, reaching values of 1.4 to 1.8 near the NBC-SBC confluence. Some upper urban reaches have been dredged for flood control as recently as 1986. Elsewhere, deliberate direct modification of channels is uncommon, particularly in areas downstream of the urban boundary. Based on maps of historical land uses in 1895 and 1908, and subsequent 1951 and 1994 U.S. Geological Survey topographic maps, four mill ponds existed on the main stem of NBC and one on SBC at different times prior to 1951. No impoundments on the main stems of either stream were documented for subsequent decades.
sections.Methods:
Field Surveys

Ground surveys using meter tape and leveling (Abney or theodolite) were conducted to acquire data on the dimensions of twenty-six channel cross sections from ten different stream reaches (one to five cross sections per reach, spaced 20-30 m apart) along NBC and one cross section at one reach downstream of the NBC-SBC junction (Figure 1). Surveys were conducted over a period of three years from 2005 to 2008. Sites were chosen to avoid the spatially immediate effects of tributary junctions, bridges, and culverts. Bankfull elevation heights were estimated at each site using morphological criteria, including the top of well-developed point bars and prominent benches (when present) and, more commonly in the absence of such indicators, the elevation of the apparent floodplain (top of lowest bank; Harrelson, Rawlins, and Potyondy 1994). Morphological evidence of bankfull stage was emphasized due to the unreliability of features like temporary scour lines and vegetation zones along eastern streams (Harman 2000; Doll et al. 2002; U.S. Department of Agriculture 2003). Bankfull stages thus identified were judged on the basis of gauging data and postflood field evidence to be reached by flows typically occurring every one to two years, the most common frequency cited for bankfull flows in eastern U.S. streams. Bankfull channel capacity, width, and depth were calculated from the field data for each section.
sections.Channel Model Data Preparation:
LiDAR data acquired in 2000 and 2001, the only years for which these data are available in the study area, were obtained for the Buffalo Creek watershed from the North Carolina Floodplain Mapping Project Web site (http://www.ncfloodmaps.com/ [last accessed 14 November 2011]). Although LiDAR data acquisition predates the field surveys by several years, field observations suggest that rates of channel change along the mainstem drainages of NBC and SBC are sufficiently low to permit useful comparisons. Two data sets, one 'bare-earth' point set with a spatial resolution of roughly 3 m and its associated breaklines and a 6.1-m (20-ft) hydrologically correct raster set, were obtained. Specifics regarding the return information used by the private vendor to create the bare-earth data set for the State of North Carolina are unavailable, although it is likely that the data were processed using a local elevation variance filter applied to all returns. The 3-m data set was cropped to an area within 152.4 m (500 ft) adjacent to stream channels and was used for creating the channel model. The 6.1-m resolution set was collected for a larger area and was used to calculate upstream drainage areas for channel cross sections.

Using ArcGIS (version 9.3; ESRI 2009), the bare-earth 3-m tiles were converted to point shapefiles, projected into NAD83 State Plane Zone 17N (feet) coordinates, the native projection, then converted to SI units. The vector point files were then merged and converted to a triangulated irregular network (TIN) file to create a digital model of the land surface. Breaklines provided with the 3-m data set were insufficiently accurate for determining channel top-of-bank features and thus the top-of-bank breaklines were manually digitized using 2002

orthophotography and verified using contours generated from the 3-m TIN and ground survey data. These breaklines were converted to 3D lines, and a new TIN was generated.

In the 3-m bare-earth data set, automated filtering techniques have resulted in a significant reduction of point density in many areas along the stream channels. To consider these potential omissions, 'raw' unclassified LiDAR point cloud data were obtained from the U.S. Geological Survey Center for LiDAR Information Coordination and Knowledge Web site (http://lidar.cr.usgs.gov/ [last accessed 14 November 2011]). Raw points were selected from in between the top-of-bank breaklines, omitting points redundant within the 3-m set, and then manually filtered to only include points below the breakline elevations. The remaining raw points were then merged with the 3-m data set to create a density-enhanced 'mixed model' point data set. A new TIN surface was derived from this merged set and the breaklines, and manual editing was performed to eliminate obvious non-earth returns (i.e., lone returns more than 1 m higher than surrounding returns) within the channel area.
sections.Model Evaluation, Calibration, and Exten: Channel cross sections were extracted from the LiDAR-derived TIN for the reaches containing ground-surveyed sites. Selection of locations for LiDAR model data extractions were constrained by random variations in LiDAR point densities that produce optimal extraction locations only where points fall near channel margins. As a result, precise correspondence between ground survey and model sample point locations was rarely achievable. Instead, the dimensions from three model cross sections at each field sample location were averaged for comparison with averaged dimensions for field-based cross sections from the same locations. Modeled and field-based average dimensions were regressed to evaluate model accuracy (by coefficients of determination) and determine best practice techniques for subsequent selection of model cross section extraction locations between the ground survey sites. This approach assumes that even in cases where field determinations of bankfull stage place it below the top-of-bank elevation best suited to LiDAR measurement, a substantial degree of proportionality between the two measurements with respect to drainage area will remain. A successful regression model was then used to correct LiDAR-derived cross section measurements from locations in both NBC and SBC without ground surveys to permit higher density sampling of downstream trends in channel size (Figure 1).
sections.Results:
Channel widths were generally overestimated by the LiDAR model and channel depths and capacities were underestimated by it (Figure 3). The fact that LiDAR returns from the bank top rarely occur right at the edges of opposing banks and thus are always set back from the bank edge some distance (less than the LiDAR point-spacing resolution) accounts for width overestimation ( James, Watson, and Hansen 2007). The underestimation of depth might largely be due to returns from the water surface or above-water in-channel features as opposed to the submerged channel bed. Width measurements also appear to be more accurate under lessvegetated conditions, as indicated by the higher regression residuals for Mixed 2 and Forested conditions (Table 1).

Regression lines for modeled and surveyed channel widths and depths have very low ( < 0.1) coefficients of determination ( R 2 ; Figure 3), especially when evaluated on the basis of the individual sample points making up the raw data. R 2 for channel capacity is higher but still low at 0.36. Coefficients of determination for sample reach average values remain poor for

width and depth but are substantially higher ( R 2 = 0.73) for channel capacity (Figure 3). This result is perhaps unexpected, given that poor correlations for width and depth might also be expected to produce poor correlations for channel capacity. The differences between modeled and actual widths (which are overesti- mated by the LiDAR model) and depths (which are underestimated), however, act to offset one another when combined to determine capacity. This effect is proportional; when width is highly overestimated by the LiDAR model, depth is more strongly underestimated (Figure 4). Width is more greatly overestimated for

Figure 4 Scatterplot of variations in model error for width (W) and depth (D) measurements. Model error in depth is inversely proportional to model error in width.

<!-- image -->

narrower channels, possibly because LiDAR point setback from the banks is a greater proportion of total width. That depth is more strongly underestimated in narrower channels might be because there is a smaller area from which to produce accurate LiDAR returns and more of the width is taken up by the exposed bases of banks. Together these decrease the chances for accurate representation of the lowest portions of the channel bed. The resulting systematic offset in model error for width and depth acts to stabilize difference values for channel capacity, resulting in better correlation.

Correcting model-derived channel capacity values using the reach-average regression equation (Figure 3) produces values that largely plot between the Doll et al. (2002) hydraulic geometry curves for urban and rural Piedmont streams (Figure 5). Moving downstream, both ground survey values and model values shift toward the rural curve, with enlargement ratios (ERs) beginning to decline well before the streams exit the urban (municipal) boundary at 65 and 75 km 2 for NBC and SBC, respectively (Figures 5, 6, and 7). The largest declines in enlargement occur at low drainage areas below 35 km 2 , approximately coincident with the first major increase in floodplain widths (Figure 8) and associated gradient reductions.

At SBC, channel capacities attain and even decline below rural dimensions (ER ≤ 1) for several reaches beginning at 90 km 2 (Figure 6), corresponding to 17 percent rural land use and 34 percent impervious area in the watershed (Figure 9A) before enlarging again around 125 km 2 . Although channel capacities at NBC never quite attain ER = 1 (Figure 6), they do occur within the scatter envelope for the rural regression (Figure 5), allowing for the possibility that rural dimensions might still have been achieved above the confluence with SBC. Values within the rural point scatter limits first occur at 88 km 2 drainage area at NBC, corresponding to a 26 percent proportion of rural land use cover in the watershed and 30 percent total impervious area (Figure 9A), and remain within it further downstream (Figure 5). Power functions give better fits than exponentials for downstream changes in enlargement ratios (Figure 6). The power function regressions for NBC and SBC place zero enlargement (ER = 1) at 240 and 143 km 2 , respectively, areas not achieved before the confluence of the two streams. Extrapolated rural area percentages for these drainage areas are 72 percent and 48 percent, respectively; impervious area percentages are 11 percent and 22 percent, respectively.

Although the general downstream trend is toward reduced channel enlargement, there is higher frequency variability displayed in the data plots (Figure 6), some of which is coherent (i.e., apparently nonrandom), particularly at drainage areas greater than 50 km 2 . At NBC, an increase in channel enlargement occurring after the junction with Muddy Creek is followed by a decline to near rural values ( < 1.5) after the junction with Jorden Branch (Figure 6). A similar pattern is also exhibited by SBC beginning around 80 km 2 , with increases in enlargement ratios ranging from 1.5 to 2.3 succeeded downstream by values below 1 before returning to ∼ 1.5 near the NBC junction. Muddy Creek at NBC drains the highly impervious central business district (CBD) of Greensboro and passes through zones of heavy and light industrial development with high impervious cover (Figure 7B).

Enlargement increases at SBC similarly occur downstream of the entrance of drainage from the densely urbanized CBD fringe (Figure 6), which also passes through a long industrial

Figure 5 Channel capacities of North and South Buffalo creeks relative to hydraulic geometry curves for urban and rural watersheds in the North Carolina Piedmont (hydraulic geometry curves based on data from Doll et al. 2002).

<!-- image -->

corridor just upstream of its SBC confluence (Figure 7B). Similar to the NBC case, a rapid decline in enlargement at SBC around 95 km 2 coincides with both reduction in urban area stormwater inputs and the first consistently large expansion of floodplain area (Figures 6, 7, and 8). In the SBC case, the large and sustained reduction in channel capacity does not begin until approximately 4 km downstream of the municipal boundary. An increase in enlargement of SBC near the confluence with NBC (112 km 2 ; Figure 7) coincides in space with a return to greater valley confinement and narrow floodplain conditions (Figure 8).
sections.Discussion:
The free and publicly available LiDAR data we use to construct the channel model are useful but limited by their resolution for purposes of deriving morphometric measurements from headwater channels, as evidenced by the poor correlations between modeled and groundsurveyed channel widths and depths. Even the best regression for channel capacity accounted for only 73 percent of variability in surveyed capacity, and there are several possible factors contributing to this weak result. The resolution issue produced the need to seek cross section locations having optimal LiDAR point

Figure 6 Downstream trends in channel enlargement ratio for North and South Buffalo creeks. Unfilled triangles show the former locations of old mill dams.

<!-- image -->

spacing with returns near the channel edge, and such optimal locations rarely coincide exactly with survey locations. Thus, any random natural variation in channel dimensions over short distances would decrease the strength of individual point correlations. In some locations, error due to local changes in channel morphology taking place between the time of the LiDARflight(2000-2001) and when surveys were conducted (2005-2008) might also weaken the correlation. Judging from observations since 2003, however, change has been localized and minor and in our judgment is of lesser importance than LiDAR model error with respect to accurately defining general downstream trends in channel capacity.

Difficulties in the field identification of bankfull stage, a particularly severe problem in many urban environments (U.S. Department of Agriculture 2003), might contribute error reflected in the point scatter. In our application, LiDAR obtained the best information for top-of-bank locations, which might or might not coincide with bankfull stage as determined from field evidence. Overestimations of bankfull channel capacity in the field at some locations would erroneously increase the Y -intercept of the LiDAR model regression for channel capacity (Figure 3), resulting in exaggeration of both enlargement ratios and projected downstream distances for zero enlargement.

Only through the regression of reachaverage measurements could error be sufficiently equilibrated to produce a useful model of changing channel capacity. The application of this regression model to tracking downstream changes in channel capacity across the urban-rural land use boundary reveals variations in channel enlargement ratio at three scales: (1) the broad negative power function trend in downstream channel enlargement, (2) moderate frequency (e.g., 25 km 2 ) coherent changes embedded in the broader trend, and (3) high-frequency variation between consecutive sites.

Thenegative power function trends that best fit the downstream sequences of enlargement ratios do not parallel the exponential decline of the proportion of watershed area classified as urban as hypothesized. The largest reductions in enlargement occur close to or upstream of the urban-rural landscape boundary (Figure 6). At NBC, the correspondence between this decline, the first major expansion of floodplain width and area, and marked decrease in channel gradient from as high as 0.0023 to 0.0011 suggests that flood-peak attenuation via reservoir effects could be an important constraint on downstream propagation of urban impacts. A similar early enlargement decline and expansion of floodplain width is also evident at SBC (Figures 6, 7, and 8). TurnerGillespie, Smith, and Bates (2003) observed strong flood-peak attenuation in association with wide valley bottoms and low stream gradients in an environmentally similar urbanizing basin near Charlotte, North Carolina. Analyses of hydrographs above and below Latham Park at NBC reveal flood-peak attenuation in eight of the last twelve flow events. Most of these events were below bankfull stage, indicating the importance of both channel and overbank storage at this site.

(A)

Figure 7 Spatial distribution of channel enlargement ratios for North and South Buffalo creeks: (A) relative to municipal boundary and (B) relative to impervious area concentration and tributary inputs.

<!-- image -->

Figure 8 Cumulative floodplain area and floodplain width as functions of drainage area for North and South Buffalo creeks.

<!-- image -->

Turner-Gillespie, Smith, and Bates (2003) noted that flood-wave attenuation was a function of the interplay of both geologically controlled valley geometry and hydrologic response in headwater reaches at their sites. Thus, the rapid decline of enlargement in the uppermost reaches of the Buffalo Creek watershed is not likely to represent a trend intrinsically associated with conditions of urban land use. Downstream increases in sinuosity might also contribute to parallel reductions in peak discharge and channel enlargement, but substantial increases in sinuosity do not occur in the upstream zone of greatest channel capacity decline. Based on average values derived from the power function curve fits, some degree of urban channel enlargement persists downstream many kilometers until the proportion of drainage area categorized as rural increases to

Figure 9 (A) Percentage of watershed covered by impervious surface and percentage in rural land use (i.e., outside the municipal boundary) as a function of drainage area in the North and South Buffalo creek watersheds. (B) Scatterplot of percentage impervious land cover versus channel enlargement ratio for North and South Buffalo creeks.

<!-- image -->

around 60 percent (i.e., 40 percent urban) and impervious area percentage declines to about 16 percent. The latter value is similar to the effective impervious cover value of 10 percent that has been suggested by Booth and Jackson (1997) as a threshold value for major channel instability and permanent stream habitat degradation.

Moderate frequency variations in enlargement are sometimes spatially coincident with such changes as major tributary confluences, large zones of particularly high impervious area, and floodplain size variations. Storm water inputs from subwatersheds of the CBD and highly impervious industrial zones could enlarge the trunk stream until countered by greater low-density residential or rural landscape drainage. This might explain the coherent enlargement increase and subsequent decline between Muddy Creek and Jorden Branch tributary inputs along NBC (Figures 6 and 7). Floodplain widths and presumably

related flood-peak attenuation effects, however, also increase between Muddy Creek and Jorden Branch (Figure 8), potentially curtailing any local enlargement effects produced from the highly impervious Muddy Creek watershed. Floodplain and valley width controls might also be evident along SBC around the 90-km 2 drainage area. The lowest values of enlargement observed at SBC begin at this point just downstream of the municipal boundary and correspond with even larger floodplain expansion than at NBC (Figure 8).

High frequency variation could represent real variation in channel capacities, random error in LiDAR-modeled cross section dimensions, or, perhaps most likely, both combined. In addition to the sorts of extrinsic hydrogeomorphological controls on channel dimensions discussed so far, as well as intrinsic variability always present in fluvial systems, there are many possible sources of local variability, particularly in urban environments, that could increase high frequency variability in channel dimensions. Urban environments feature complex palimpsest land uses, stemming from sometimes long, complex histories, not all of which can be accounted for. The most local of these, such as old infrastructure crossings, variations in bank vegetation and stability, and local storm water outfalls might account for much apparently random variability in channel dimensions (Hammer1972; Ebisemiju 1989; Roberts 1989; Gregory, Davis, and Downs 1992; Chin 2006; Grable and Harden 2006).

Also of importance are more areally extensive channel modifying influences, including historical channelization impacts and old stream impoundments such as mill dams. Although muchreadjustment has occurred in those upper urban reaches known to have been channelized, it is probable that LiDAR-model channel capacities in at least some of these remain larger than average, and this would serve to exaggerate the rapid decline in enlargement observed at low drainage areas. The powerfunction regression equations for our watersheds, however, are insensitive to removal of local high values, preserving the trend of rapid decline in enlargement. With regard to impoundments, Walter and Merritts (2008) and Merritts (2011) have remarked on the influence of often-unrecognized mill dam sediment accumulations on channel morphology in the eastern United States. Deep incision into pond sediments following dam removal could manifest as local increases in enlargement ratios. Of the sample points nearest five former mill dam locations along NBC and SBC (triangles in Figure 6), none exhibit high enlargement ratios. Walter and Merritts (2008) estimated an average frequency of between five and ten mill dams per 100 km 2 for this area, and such a frequency would make dam sediments important in only a small number of reaches. Further detailed studies of the stratigraphy of bank sediments in the Buffalo Creek drainage, however, would allow a better assessment of the full impacts of such historical features on channel morphology.
sections.Conclusion:
This study demonstrates that channel terrain models derived from 3-m point-spacing resolution LiDAR data do not accurately represent specific cross-sectional shapes in detail at most points but can be used, at least at our sites, to estimate reach-averaged channel capacities. Based on these modeled capacities, enlargement ratios decrease downstream of urban areas with a trend best fit by a negative power function. A large proportion of the total decrease occurs within or relatively close to the urban boundary as a result of the interplay between diminishing runoff augmentation by reduced impervious cover and the occurrence of geologically controlled wide floodplain reaches and commensurately strong reservoir effect. The power function relationships describing declines in enlargement ratio indicate that full return of channel capacity to rural dimensions does not occur until over half of the watershed area is rural or about 16 percent of the watershed is impervious.

Although generally decreasing, enlargement ratios appear to fluctuate in response to significant increases in contributing drainage area at major tributary junctions, with the directions of the fluctuations influenced by the nature of land use in the tributary's watershed. These relationships are not always clear, though, and the high complexity of the urban environment and its history of human modifications and of fluvial processes in general continue to present

many challenges to understanding the impacts of urbanization on channel morphology.

Limitations of both the data set and technique reduce the general utility of our outcomes, and it would be inadvisable to apply our model uncritically to any other geological or hydrogeomorphological environment. Similar studies of different streams in the Piedmont and elsewhere are advocated for determining whether averaging model-derived dimensions is a robust approach, although more current LiDAR data would be needed for this. Future exploration is also recommended with regard to the use of raw LiDAR data. The development of algorithms to specifically target bare-earth points in riparian settings, as well as the exploration of other interpolation options (kriging, etc.), could be invaluable in the development of models that more accurately capture channel dimensions at a local scale. Such models would be of great benefit in studying all kinds of landuse impacts on stream channel change. /squaresolid

records.title: Reasons for Returning and Not Returning to Rural US Communities
records.abstract: Population loss persists in nonmetropolitan America, especially in isolated counties with limited natural amenities. Communities in these counties experience high levels of outmigration among high school graduates, but low in-migration is more important in distinguishing declining from growing nonmetropolitan counties, and return migration is a much more prominent component of in-migration to these locationally disadvantaged areas. This research uses a multisited, interview-based methodology to understand the factors that influence decisions of people in their late twenties to late forties to move back to rural communities and the barriers that keep others from making such moves. The life course segment considered here captures a critical settling down period when career and family obligations overlap and return migration peaks. Interviews at high school reunions, the only venues where stayers, return migrants, and nonreturn migrants are found together, show that limited rural employment opportunities are barriers for nonreturnees. Others intent on returning find ways to secure or create employment but are primarily influenced to move home by family concerns. Connections to the larger social and physical environment of the community are important as well. Interviews affirm that factors affecting migration decisions work in combination, and ties to both people and place are critical for understanding rural return migration.

*   Title: "Reasons for Returning and Not Returning to Rural US Communities"
    *   Abstract: Focuses on population loss in nonmetropolitan America. Uses a "multisited, interview-based methodology" to understand factors influencing decisions to move back to rural communities. Mentions interviews at high school reunions.
    *   Data and Methods section: 309 interviews conducted at 27 reunions in 21 communities across 17 states.
    *   Study Area section: Describes how the study area was identified using Z-scores for geographic isolation and the Natural Amenities Index. This part uses quantitative/spatial data to *select* the sites.
    *   Reaching the Study Population: Describes the sampling process.
    *   Identifying Nonreturn Migrants and Return Migrants: Describes the interview questions and categorization of participants.

    *   The *goal* of the research is to "understand the factors that influence decisions... to move back to rural communities and the barriers that keep others from making such moves."
    *   The *primary analytical engine* used to answer this question is the "multisited, interview-based methodology."
    *   The quantitative/spatial part (Z-scores, Natural Amenities Index) was used for *site selection* (identifying the study area), not for the main inferential claim about *why* people return or don't return.
    *   The main findings are derived from the interviews (e.g., "Interviews at high school reunions... show that limited rural employment opportunities are barriers... Others... are primarily influenced to move home by family concerns").

    *   `qual`: Qualitative methods (interviews, ethnography, etc.).
    *   `quant`: Non-spatial quantitative methods (regression, etc.).
    *   `mixed`: Qual AND Quant carry comparable weight.
    *   `spatial`: GIS, spatial stats, etc.
    *   `descriptive-empirical`: Original empirical work describing a phenomenon without inferential testing.
    *   `theoretical-conceptual`: Conceptual essay.
    *   `unclear`: Cannot be determined.

    *   The core of the paper is the analysis of 309 interviews.
    *   The spatial analysis was a precursor to the interviews (site selection).
    *   The inferential claims (reasons for returning/not returning) come from the qualitative data.
    *   Therefore, the primary analytical engine is qualitative.

    *   Is it `mixed`? The spatial part is just for sampling. The quantitative table (Table 1) is descriptive of the sample, not an inferential engine.
    *   Is it `spatial`? No, the spatial methods were used for site selection, not to produce the main claim.
    *   Is it `descriptive-empirical`? It goes beyond simple description to identify "factors" and "barriers," which is typical of qualitative research aiming for thematic inference. However, `qual` is a more precise fit for an interview-based study.

H undreds of communities throughout rural America face the difficult challenge of adjusting economically and socially to a dwindling demographic base. In most years, more people move into nonmetropolitan America than move out. At the county level, however, these net migration gains are unequally distributed, so that over half of nonmetropolitan counties persistently lose population due to net outmigration. A strong correlation exists between nonmetropolitan population loss on the one hand and low population density, low urban accessibility, and lack of scenic amenities on the other (McGranahan and Beale 2002).

Communities in such areas are attuned to a relentless, and quite visible, annual phenomenon, as a large proportion of each high school graduating class leaves town in pursuit of further education or other life experiences. Rural areas experiencing population decline, however, are distinguished less by high rates of outmigration of high school graduates and more by low rates of in-migration of people in their late twenties and thirties (Gibbs and Cromartie 1994). Compared to areas with higher locational advantages, these areas attract fewer newcomer in-migrants, depending to a greater extent on their ability to lure back return migrants during life course stages overlapping with the 'settling down' period (White 1992; McGranahan, Cromartie, and Wojan 2010). For rural communities, return migration is a less visible and more gradual process than outmigration.

To gain an understanding of the reasons for and barriers to rural return migration, this study used a multisited, interview-based methodology to evaluate individual and household migration decisions. Interviews took place in small towns at ten- to thirty-year high school reunions, the only venues where stayers, return migrants, and nonreturn migrants are found together, allowing simultaneous recording of reasons for returning and reasons for not returning. The dominant conceptualization of migration used here-migration as a family-related and deeply community-embedded process-draws most heavily on social network theory, especially as formulated in new interview-based research on return migration in transnational settings (e.g., Conway, Potter, and St Bernard 2008; Ralph 2009; Reynolds 2009). The project's overall design and much of its analytical strategy, however, builds on life course perspectives that dominate current empirical research on U.S. domestic migration (Chen and Rosenthal 2008; Whisler et al. 2008; Cromartie and Nelson 2009; Plane and Jurjevich 2009). The personal views of rural return migrants and their fellow classmates who faced, and continue to consider, similar return migration reveal the complex interplay of economic circumstances, family incentives, and social and place settings that are a hallmark of life course perspectives.

Few interview-based studies of domestic return migration in the United States have been conducted (Cuba and Hummon 1993; McHugh and Mings 1996; Stack 1996). Recent case studies of international return migration, however, have significantly broadened knowledge about the social context of return migration. Although myriad geographical, historical, and institutional factors differentiate domestic and international migration processes, the reasons for making return migrations, especially as voiced by the migrants themselves, are uncannily similar across a wide spectrum of race, class, and space. Return migration to rural areas of the United States operates in settings very similar to those described in international migration studies. In both contexts, returnees typically leave more dynamic labor markets for home places with fewer employment opportunities, suggesting that factors other than job seeking come into play. Across diverse geographic contexts, the core questions for exploring return migration are the same: What are the motivations to move back to a place for people who left earlier in life, often for better opportunities elsewhere? What reasons and barriers keep others from moving back?
sections.Background:
Return migration has long been recognized as a prominent feature of human migration within both domestic and transnational migration streams throughout the world(Eldridge 1965; Gmelch 1980; Long 1988). Current understanding of internal return migration in the United States and Canada draws from a rich tradition of census-based analyses and survey research showing strong geographic variation in return migration levels and the socioeconomic characteristics of returnees (DaVanzo 1976; Miller 1977; White 1987, 1992; Shumway and Hall 1996; Newbold 1997; Wilson et al. 2009). Sizable differences in the geography of return and differences in the relative importance of economicversus family reasons have been extensively documented (White 1987; Long 1988; von Reichert 2002; U.S. Bureau of the Census 2009b; Niedomysl and Amcoff 2011). Survey and census-based research on return migration in the United States supports findings from similar quantitative research on life course migration showing the significant extent to which migration reasons vary by destination (Plane and Jurjevich 2009).

A recent and burgeoning literature on causes and consequences of return migration focuses on international return migration, much of it directed toward understanding the family context and broader social dynamics of international labor migration circuits in a globalizing age. Continuing theoretical challenges to traditional economic frameworks, creative use of new data sources, and increased efforts on the part of researchers to let migrants speak for themselves have

added much needed information regarding the causes of return migration and the critical role it plays in overall migration dynamics.

This new emphasis is not surprising, given the very high incidence of return migration in both international and domestic, rural-urban labor circuits (Bailey et al. 2002; Constant and Massey 2002; Olesen 2002; Zhao 2002; Wenfei Winnie and Fan 2006; Dustmann and Weiss 2007). Renewed attention to return migration also follows logically, given the sharp move away from economics-based migration theories that view migrations as discrete events (Sjaastad 1962; Greenwood 1969; Todaro 1969). Early theorizations severely constricted explanations of return migration, most typically viewing it as 'failed migration' (DaVanzo 1976). An inordinate emphasis on assimilation processes at the destination masked evidence of counterstream dynamics (Ley and Kobayashi 2005). Beginning in the 1970s, researchers remodeled migration into socially constructed, network-connected events, geographically embedded in an ongoing dynamic linking individuals, families, and multiple locations (Bach and Schraml 1982; Wood 1982; Cromartie and Stack 1989). The full emergence of critical theories in population geography and the very strong move toward qualitative approaches has contributed to a broad-based social science agenda that has served to bring return migration out of the shadows (McHugh 2000; Bailey 2009).

Notions of return are constitutive of terms that have come to replace migration in much of the literature: transnationalism typically embodies the idea of a continual grounding in home communities, as does the more broadly applicable description of migrants as translocal (Bailey et al. 2002). Within agendas set by critical migration theory and the desire for migrants to speak for themselves, the topic of return migration often takes center stage. Included are ambitious, mixedmethod projects that place migration in the details of everyday life (Bailey et al. 2002; N´ ı Laoire 2007; Conway, Potter, and St Bernard 2008; Phillips and Potter 2009). Additionally, these and several other studies focus on untying complex theoretical and conceptual knots, addressing such questions as 'What constitutes a return move?' and 'What is the meaning of home in a translocal age?' (Christou 2006; Ralph 2009; Barcus and Brunn 2010). Another large component of the literature focuses on the impacts of return migration, including its role in entrepreneurship and economic development in poor nations (Goulbourne 1999; Murphy 2000; Olesen 2002; Zhao 2002; Black and Castaldo 2009). It is clear from several of these accounts that returnees contribute in different ways to the economy of their home countries (Thomas-Hope 1999). In many cases, they bring back significant entrepreneurial skills and are supported in these endeavors by transnational social and business networks (Cassarino 2000).

Most relevant to our study is the growing body of interview-based case studies that explicitly address reasons for making return moves, as voiced by the mi- grants themselves (Murphy 2000; Lidgard and Gilson 2002; N´ ı Laoire 2007; Phillips and Potter 2009). These studies largely confirm the necessity of framing return migration in a family strategy perspective, mediated by life course decision making. The family strategy perspective on migration pulls from overlapping theoretical strands, including social network theory, social capital theory, and life course approaches (Boyd 1989; Findlay and Li 1999; Bailey 2009). Applied to migration, social capital theory shows how diverse and ever-changing connections with families and friends are crucial resources for migrants in generating and maintaining 'networks and relationships of trust and reciprocity' across space (Reynolds 2009, 801).

Embeddedness in social networks is a key influence on the decision and timing of return moves. Reciprocal trust, feelings of social connectedness, and the many ways families provide support to migrant communities constitute the social networks of families (Tannenbaum 2007). Even when the research agenda is not explicitly focused on capturing reasons for return migration, family-based motivations are usually part of the story (Wenfei Winnie and Fan 2006; N´ ı Laoire 2007; Phillips and Potter 2009; Ralph 2009).

Children play an important role in almost all return migration contexts, although this aspect remains understudied. Intergenerational ties and the educational needs of children are a central factor in explaining the unique dynamics underlying migration circuits between Hong Kong and Canada (Ley and Kobayashi 2005). In a recent survey, a desire for children to grow up in New Zealand was cited as a major reason for returning home from abroad (Lidgard and Gilson 2002). A survey-based model of Turkish families in Germany shows that the presence of children influences decisions to return and the effects differ for sons and daughters (Constant and Massey 2002). Working from a traditional economics framework, Dustmann (2003) endeavored to show that return decisions are inherently linked to life course decisions connected with children. If altruistic concern for children is the dominant motivator, it can lead to diminished return migration when career prospects for the parents are perceived to be better away from home or it might lead to increased return when parents think that the home area provides a more appropriate environment.

Return migration is a complex social process that nonetheless shows common patterns over the life course and operates under very similar conditions in different geographic settings. Family ties show up as a primary factor in all interview-based case studies that explicitly address motivations for returning home, but the form and underlying motivations of family-based strategies vary geographically and shift over the stages of the life course. Given its social complexity, multilocational nature, and sensitivity to time, return migration can only be understood through an accumulation of knowledge from case studies employing a diverse set of creative methods (McKenzie and Mistiaen 2009).

This research sets out to add to this base of knowledge about return migration by focusing on a certain

set of regions for which return migration is especially important: demographically struggling and geographically isolated rural U.S. communities with limited natural amenities. It focuses on a particular segment of the life course, namely, on people in their late twenties to late forties, capturing people in the labor force and typically in the family stage. It uses a qualitative methodology based on interviews at high school reunions.
sections.Data and Methods: High school reunions provide the only opportunity to speak with common cohorts of stayers (who never moved away), return migrants (who moved and later returned), and nonreturn migrants (who moved away and still live elsewhere). In 2008 and 2009, 309 interviews were conducted at twenty-seven reunions in twenty-one communities across seventeen states, at evening mixers, school tours, family picnics, and other events taking place on reunion weekends. On average, we spoke with fifteen reunion attendees per community, with the highest number being twenty-eight and the lowest being five. Fewer interviews took place on visits limited to a single reunion for one high school class attended by one interviewer. More interviews were possible in the six communities that had multiple class reunions on the same weekend (e.g., simultaneous ten- and twenty-year events) and during the five community visits attended by more than one interviewer.
sections.Study Area: Interviews took place in nonmetropolitan counties that were both geographically isolated and had relatively limited scenic and recreational amenities, two characteristics strongly associated with persistent popula- tion loss (McGranahan and Beale 2002). These counties attract far fewer newcomers than metropolitan areas or other nonmetropolitan counties; thus, their in-migration flows are highest for migrants between ages thirty and forty and contain much higher proportions of returnees (McGranahan, Cromartie, and Wojan 2010). To identify the study area, Z-scores were combined for three measures of geographic isolation: (1) a gravity-type, urban accessibility measure; (2) distance to regional airports classified by size; and (3) distance to interstate highways. The presence of attractive physical characteristics-pleasant climates, mountains, bodies of water-was measured using the Economic Research Service's (ERS) Natural Amenities Index (McGranahan 1999). The resulting study area consisted of 942 nonmetropolitan counties with combined urban access and natural amenity scores below the national average, which also experienced net outmigration between 2000 and 2007 (Figure 1).
sections.Reaching the Study Population:
A high school database overlaid with the study area yielded approximately 2,400 potential reunion sites. Prior experience showed (von Reichert 2000) that very small schools typically opt for all class reunions that include far fewer participants in our targeted age groups, so we chose only to consider visits to the 1,570 high schools with more than 150 students. From that set we developed a sample that was national in scope and representative of the range of community sizes found in our study area. Eight of the visits were to towns with fewer than 2,500 people; one visit was to a city with more than 10,000 people; and the other twelve were to intermediate-sized towns. Visits were made to ten- to thirty-year high school reunions, for interviews with people in their late twenties to late forties. The age cohorts considered here include peak ages of return migration from twentyfive to thirty-five (Miller 1977; Long 1988). In most geographical settings, the bulk of rural return migration occurs during this critical settling-down period associated with childrearing and career maturation. As shown in Figure 2, derived from Current Population Survey data (U.S. Bureau of the Census 2009a), migration propensities for life stages after the settling-down period are much lower (Rogers and Castro 1981; Plane 1992). This implies that locational choices made while settling down, between the late twenties and the forties, have greater permanence and bearing on community population levels and characteristics.

Over 95 percent of reunion interviews were with non-Hispanic whites. In large part, this focus corresponded with the racial and ethnic composition of the relevant high school graduation years (1978-1999). In 1990, a meaningful census year for this graduation interval, 85 percent of the study-area population was non-Hispanic white, 9 percent were non-Hispanic African American, and 4 percent were Hispanic. We visited one of the 124 study-area counties in which African Americans made up 20 percent or more of the 1990 population and one of the sixty-five counties with similarly high Hispanic percentages. At reunion visits in the rural South, we interviewed a small number of African Americans, far too few to consider any of the very important racial dimensions of rural return migration. Similarly, we encountered and interviewed very few Latinos. Although several of the communities visited have gained Latinos in recent years, there were relatively fewer Latino high school graduates in the ten- to thirty-year reunion classes we visited. Given that, findings from our work are mostly telling of nonHispanic whites.

Receiving permission to attend reunions hinged on establishing rapport with reunion organizers, who were identified from phone calls to schools, newspapers, city governments, chambers of commerce, and potential reunion venues. Reunion-related social networking websites, such as Classmates.com, were rarely used in rural areas in 2008, but the use of personal social networking sites-for instance, Facebook-had noticeably increased in 2009. Phone calls with reunion organizers proved more effective than e-mails in establishing trust and receiving permission to attend reunion events. Beyond a few exceptions, the collaboration of reunion organizers was remarkable and their introductions and assistance throughout the community visit were vital for the success of the project.

Recorded interviews were conducted near the beginning of reunion events, to minimize intrusion. Conversations ranged from a few minutes to a half-hour, for an average of eleven minutes. Interviews were open-ended, including questions that varied by migrant type. We asked returnees about reasons for leaving and for returning. Nonreturnees laid out their thoughts about leaving, returning, and not returning, and stayers spoke about the draw of their hometown. The interviews were transcribed and imported to NVivo (QSR International 2009), a software package helpful in organizing text data, keeping track of attributes, and coding themes as they emerged from interviews.

Before or after high school reunions, we spent several days in each town collecting information on economic and social conditions and gaining a sense of community dynamics. We conducted nearly 100 interviews with community leaders outside of reunions,

including several group interviews. A few community leaders were in their mid-thirties, but more typically they were older than the reunion interviewees. Primarily, these conversations were meant to provide broader contextual information about the social and economic factors influencing the decision to return or not return. Many persons contacted as community leaders were themselves returnees, and their stories were included in our findings. We also had twenty-one interviews with returnees outside of reunions. Such interviews were often longer, ranging in length from twenty minutes to over an hour, and frequently provided a more detailed understanding of reasons for returning and the decision-making process.
sections.Identifying Nonreturn Migrants and Retur:
The question 'Where do you live now?' revealed that nearly 60 percent of reunion interviewees (183 out of 309) now live elsewhere, not in the town of high school graduation (Table 1). Almost all live in much larger cities or towns. These 'nonreturnees' make up a critical and unique component of this study. They are potential returning migrants to rural areas who are extremely difficult, if not impossible, to track down and interview outside reunion events. By asking them 'Have you thought about moving back? Why or why not?' we learned of the potential appeal and most common barriers to rural return migration.

As expected, nonreturnees are diverse with respect to migration histories. Most moved away right after high school to larger urban places, and many made additional moves. Some returned to their home community and later left again, and some returned to the region but not close enough to be classified with other returnees. We spoke with a small number of couples who had lived elsewhere before returning to the other spouse's hometown, a move that certainly qualifies them as a return couple but not from the perspective of the graduating class and the community being studied.
