I n this article I critically examine the role of food sovereignty interventions in the mitigation of the impacts of neoliberal economic policies on poor farmers in the Telengana region of India. The Telengana region has experienced high levels of agrarian distress, especially after India introduced neoliberal economic policies in the 1990s (Ghosh 2005; Nagaraj 2008). The commodification of agriculture has intensified processes of environmental degradation, land fragmentation, and water stress, which, combined with decreasing state supports and safety nets, have made rural livelihoods increasingly precarious.

Food sovereignty is put forth as a principal strategy to counteract the negative outcomes of the commodification of agriculture, which is blamed on the global corporate food regime, a system that favors particular Western nation-states and corporate interests in food and agriculture (McMichael 2005). Food sovereignty seeks to curb this trend through a strategic focus on upholding small farmers and agroecological practices (V´ ıa Campesina 1996; McMichael 2005; Desmarais

2007; Altieri 2009; Patel 2009; Martinez-Torres and Rosset 2010; Wittman, Desmarais, and Wiebe 2010). It distinguishes itself from the productivist food security paradigm that emerged after World War II as a state-sponsored strategy to increase food production to achieve food self-sufficiency, revive economies, and increase political legitimacy (McMichael 2005). Where food security is dominated by its focus on high production and efficiency, food sovereignty is animated by the principles of equity and ecological integrity. Food sovereignty's promotion of 'the peasant way' as the solution to the ills of the corporate food regime is also critiqued, however, as being a set of principles with little political analysis of how they would translate in practice (Akram-Lodhi 2013; Trauger 2013; Bernstein 2014; Edelman 2014).

This research supports emerging critiques of food sovereignty and seeks to contribute to debates on food security. Findings based on eighteen months of ethnographic research in the Telengana region reveal that small and poor farmers face socioeconomic and

cultural constraints in the adoption of food sovereignty practices and ideals. These include compulsions to participate in the market economy, changing geographies of labor, and shifting values and knowledge relating to agriculture. Food sovereignty prescriptions based on localized, sustainable, and subsistence agriculture paradoxically constrained farmers' chances of maintaining viable rural livelihoods in a harsh economic climate. Based on these findings, I argue that contrary to assertions by advocates that food sovereignty is a precondition to genuine food security, farmers must first have food and livelihood security (hereinafter food security) to exercise true food sovereignty that allows them more control over their livelihoods.

To examine the disjuncture between food sovereignty and food security, I draw on historical and contemporary critiques of neopopulist ideas promoted by alternative agricultural movements as well as more recent empirical research examining food sovereignty in the Global South. This research supports recent assertions that food sovereignty is an idea that fails to consider the complex nature of peasant societies and as a result is unable to offer concrete alternatives to the existing market and state-led programs for food security.

In the following section, I chronicle debates surrounding food sovereignty and food security. I then describe the field site and provide a brief history of agrarian transitions in the region. This is followed by a discussion of my findings on the outcomes of food sovereignty interventions in the Telengana region. I conclude by discussing the contradictions between food sovereignty and food security and highlighting the myriad problems rural dwellers face in the Telengana.
sections.Drawing the Lines: Food Security and Foo:
The ideological basis of food sovereignty implies control and autonomy over the food system, something that is not addressed by food security paradigms. The term attained global significance after V´ ıa Campesina, a transnational peasant coalition, deployed food sovereignty to oppose the General Agreement on Trade and Tariffs (GATT) as compromising the rights of nations to produce their basic foods and being inimical to the interests of peasant farmers (Edelman 2014). Since then, food sovereignty has been widely adopted, and its definition expanded, reflecting its growing appeal as a discursive weapon to protect the interests not only of small food producers but increasingly of consumers and states (Wittman, Desmarais, and Wiebe 2010).

Food sovereignty is a call to address the failings of the food security paradigm that do not address who produces the food, how food is produced, and who benefits from its production and sale (Desmarais 2007). The diverse array of ideological positions and class interests of those advocating for food sovereignty make it challenging to define what it actually entails, but most call for supporting small and peasant farming systems and agroecological practices-a neopopulist ideal-as essential to resist the corporate food regime (V´ ıa Campesina 1996; McMichael 2005; Windfuhr and Jons´ en 2005; Desmarais 2007; Patel 2009; MartinezTorres and Rosset 2010). Advocates highlight how the commodification of agriculture has impinged on the sovereignty of states, communities, and individuals to determine their own food policies. Food sovereignty's most identifiable battles are those that oppose the research, marketing, and cultivation of genetically modified crops, landlessness, corporate 'land grabs' for biofuels, large-scale commercial agriculture, resource extraction such as mining, and other large-scale development that displaces poor farmers or impedes their ability to make a livelihood from farming.

As food sovereignty is a relatively new concept, only recently have scholars made attempts to theorize it. Although most scholars support its progressive agenda in that it questions the unsustainability of neoliberal agriculture, they highlight how food sovereignty ideals represent a resurgence of agrarian populism and hence do little to respond to the varied, complex, and contradictory problems faced by different classes of rural dwellers (Kay 2008; Bernstein 2014).

In its simplest form, populism is defined as 'a mode of thought opposed to orthodox large-scale concentrated production in favor of small-scale individual enterprise' (Watts 1983, 80). Contemporary agrarian populists have foisted ecological sustainability onto this ideal and envision peasant farmers as supporters of a decentralized socialism who base their practices on ecological values (Cochrane 2007). Populist economic doctrines date back to the work of Russian neopopulists such as Chayanov from the early 1900s (Watts 1983). E. F. Schumacher (1993), author of Small Is Beautiful, and influential writers and scholars such as Wendell Berry and Michael Lipton and others kept these ideas alive in the 1960s and 1970s (Watts 1983).

Critiques of neopopulism highlight that strategies that uphold a localized, smallholder farming model are ahistoric and static as they fail to adequately acknowledge how the economic logic of small farms are not distinct from those of other capitalist production systems (Watts 1983; Byres 2004; Brass 2005; Bernstein 2009). Rural society is dynamic. Peasants accumulate surpluses and diversify out of agriculture. This dynamic necessarily includes the accompanying structural change, the inequality of access to resources, the necessary relations between agriculture and industry, the role of the state in these processes, as well as the relationship of peasants to other classes (Watts 1983; Byres 2004; Kay 2008; Bernstein 2009; Borras 2010). Yet, it is common for food sovereignty advocates to make claims about small farming systems that capitalist market relations are external to indigenous and peasant communities, whereas noncapitalist relations, based on a moral economy of reciprocity and production for subsistence, exist on the inside (MartinezTorres and Rosset 2010, 154).

Recent empirical research in the Global South examining food sovereignty stresses that food

sovereignty as it is currently defined is at odds with farmers' lived realities and does not enable them to achieve food security. Boyer's (2010) research in Honduras among peasant organizations belonging to V´ ıa Campesina found that there were historical, cultural, and structural constraints that prevent the acceptance of food sovereignty ideals among Honduran peasants. He concluded that Honduran peasant understandings of food security were at odds with V´ ıa Campesina's discourse of food sovereignty.

Bhattarai (2013) found that in the context of an increasingly monetized economy in rural Nepal, even a voluntary shift to agroecological farming practices by farmers who want to cut the cord of corporate dependence is not enough to provide food security that included access to education, health care, and housing. Furthermore, the younger generations' aspirations of progress moved them away from agriculture. Thus, Bhattarai calls for an expanded version of food sovereignty that does not base its solutions only in agriculture. Gartaula et al. (2013) similarly found that in rural Tamil Nadu, food sovereignty practices would not address the particular challenges farmers faced within a neoliberal agrarian economy nor meet their needs and aspirations. They found that food sovereignty was too narrow and ideological and needed to include sustainable development policies that went beyond agriculture.

Therefore, critiques of the neopopulist vision of food sovereignty are borne out by empirical research that in the context of developing countries, food security and food sovereignty ideals are contradictory. Empirical research highlights that food sovereignty strategies based solely on small farming ignore the changing realities of the contemporary countryside where the move to commercial farming and the diversification out of farm-based livelihoods is integral to achieving food security. That many 'peasants' no longer can (or want to) depend only on agriculture alone (Bernstein 2009) is also true of the Telengana region, which, as the following two sections demonstrate, pits the food security struggles of small farmers against food sovereignty ideals.
sections.The Telengana Context:
Research was conducted among fifteen villages of the Western Medak district of the Telengana region, with two villages being the focal point of the ethnographic research. Food sovereignty interventions have been actively promoted by a nongovernmental organization (NGO), Rural Development Initiatives (RDI), in seventy-five villages in the area since the early 1990s. This research used a political ecology approach that combined a place-based study of local actors contextualized with a historical analysis of the capitalist transition of agriculture and a multiscalar treatment of food sovereignty. Methods included focus group discussions, surveys, semistructured interviews, life histories, informal discussions, and participant observation.

Secondary data in the form of land records, crop histories, and local news articles were also used.

The Telengana region (see Figure 1) forms part of a contiguous semi-arid belt and is considered 'backward' in terms of its human development (Nagaraj 2008). The region is characterized by rain-fed agriculture, poor soils, drought, and cultural and economic marginalization. Since India adopted neoliberal economic policies, already vulnerable farming systems have given way to widespread agrarian distress in the form of farmer suicides (Nagaraj 2008).

The region still primarily cultivates food crops such as sorghum, lentils, and oilseeds in nonirrigated lands and commercial crops such as sugarcane, potato, and banana in irrigated lands. Genetically modified (GM) cotton, considered by local farmers to be a high-risk crop, has in the past been cultivated by mainly large farmers. Yet, within the last seven to eight years, GM cotton and hybrid corn sold by Monsanto's local affiliates have been adopted on a large scale, even by small and marginal farmers.

Distress is not new to small and marginal farmers 2 in the region. Historically, lower castes have dealt with extreme oppression, exploitation, and hunger. Under late-Mughal rule, land and power were highly concentrated among the high castes, while untouchables and lower castes provided wage and unfree labor (Pavier 1981). Examples of earlier hardships were recounted several times during life history interviews by Dalit and lower caste families at the field site. They talked about the indignity of being hungry into the 1970s and 1980s, of having to beg for food and the compulsory unpaid labor called vetti.

The era of state-led development after independence brought some positive changes with land reforms, abolition of feudal institutions, investments in agriculture, the provision of safety nets resulting in agricultural growth, and increased food security. Many interviewees benefited from land reforms and became owner-cultivators. They reported that the availability of subsidized rice and rural employment programs greatly contributed to their food security. For the lower castes, these developments brought self-respect as culturally sanctioned poverty and social exclusion lessened.

The adoption of neoliberal economic reforms in the 1990s led to massive cuts in farming subsidies, reduced safety nets, and privatization and disinvestment in several key institutions for agriculture including credit, seeds, research, and extension services (Ghosh 2005). Costs of cultivation rose substantially as a result, leading to high debt. The reforms had differentiated impacts for the poor at the field site. Increased market engagement created new opportunities but also increased vulnerability in the face of ecological and market perturbations. Although most small farmers continued to struggle to meet their basic needs and their lives were extremely vulnerable, a majority of Dalits felt that they were better off than the past. Maniamma, an elder Dalit farmer who recounted hardships during a life history interview in 2009, explained:

Figure 1 Map of study site, Medak District in Andhra Pradesh State of India. Map credit: Charles Daveny, Cartographer, Department of Geography, University of Hawai'i at M¯ anoa. (Color figure available online.)

<!-- image -->

Things are better now. We are eating well because of subsidized rice, state-provided rural employment, and the ability to cultivate our land. Our own hard work brings in wages that are high. Before we could not work in our own fields and had to work the landlord's fields. If we did not work for them they would not give us the grain we needed to survive.

This comment suggests that a combination of higher wages that came with neoliberal reforms, state welfare measures, and the breaking down of traditional feudal institutions have allowed them to cultivate their own land and sell their labor freely. These have been key to their improved food security. Small farmers are still up against insurmountable obstacles in their quest to eke out a livelihood in the Telengana region, however.

It is within this context of historical vulnerability, hunger, and marginalization and rapid commercialization that food sovereignty interventions have been promoted by RDI among small and marginal mainly Dalit women farmers. Their strategies reflect food sovereignty's overarching model for resisting the neoliberal agro-food regime, promoting localized agroecological farming that intends to improve farmers' capacity to subsist, focusing on traditionally cultivated food crops such as sorghum, millets, oilseeds, and lentils.

The majority of small and poor farmers, however, were unable to adopt localized subsistence-focused agriculture even if it improved their ability to subsist. Farmers faced many constraints including (1) compulsions to participate in an increasingly monetized economy with all the opportunities and risks that markets bring, (2) changing geographies of labor, and (3) changing values and knowledge relating to agriculture.
sections.Constraints to Adopting Food Sovereignty:
Debt, Risk, and a Monetized Economy

Chinnapuram 1 Village was the locus of the 1995 anticotton protests led by the NGO with the participation of local farmers. The protests were an attempt to draw attention to the displacement of food crops by cotton and the increasing commercialization of the countryside. RDI was prescient regarding the potential of cotton to cause major upheavals in a primarily food-crop cultivating area. When they staged the protest, mainly rich farmers were cultivating cotton. Today, however, small farmers are rapidly adopting cotton cultivation, andsomelandless farmers are leasing land at exorbitant

Figure 2 Spraying a genetically modified cotton field with pesticides. Source: Author. (Color figure available online.)

<!-- image -->

rates to cultivate cotton, a trend not seen in the field site before. Historical crop reports for one research village show that cotton was first planted in 1996. Until 2003, it averaged less than 10 percent of the cultivable area. By 2004 almost half of the cultivable area was planted in cotton, representing drastic shifts in cultivation.

Cotton and corn (corn is another new commercial crop grown for chicken feed; it is not considered a food crop in the field areas) are displacing food crops like sorghum, pigeonpea, and other lentils, as well as certain high-value food crops like chickpea. Farmers explained that cotton is the only crop that brings such high returns in nonirrigated areas (Figure 2). They are well aware of the risks but also want to profit from agriculture. Balappa, a small Dalit farmer who owns two acres of nonirrigated land, explained:

Traditional crops are not being cultivated as much because with a crop like cotton one can make twenty to thirty thousand rupees in profit as opposed to very low profits from traditional crops.

Localized agriculture focused on food crops imposes limits. For example, one of RDI's most celebrated Dalit women farmers noted in a focus group discussion:

Although we have control over our agriculture, and are secure in food, shelter, and agriculture, we do not have enoughcashtoeducate our children, for marriages, sickness, and so on.

Over the last fifteen to twenty years local economies are becoming increasingly monetized. Villages have moved beyond subsistence and needs for cash are more urgent than before. In most Dalit households at the field site, children are being educated for the first time and farmers reported that health and education costs had increased dramatically. Of the 150 households surveyed, 50 percent borrowed money for costs of cultivation (including leasing land and sinking borewells), about 40 percent for marriages and other ceremonies, 30 percent for housing construction, and 25 percent for education and health.

Muniamma, a small woman farmer, noted during an interview:

If we had more land then we could afford to plant food crops, but since we have only one acre we plant only cotton to maximize our earnings.

Small farmers like her have no choice but to maximize their cash-earning opportunities and are more constrained in their cultivation choices.

Those who planted cotton and corn, however, were not happy with the absolute dominance of private actors in the seed sector. Farmers complained that the state had abdicated its role in providing the research and extension support they felt was crucial to their success as agriculturists. They preferred to buy their seeds from state extension outlets but complained that the seeds were of poor quality, making it even riskier.
sections.Changing Geographies of Labor:
Since the RDI established itself in the region nearly thirty years ago, local geographies of labor have changed in ways that have had direct impacts on households' abilities to mobilize labor for labor-intensive farming practices. Food sovereignty practices tend to be more labor intensive in all aspects of the agricultural cycle, including selecting and storing seed, preparing

Figure 3 Woman farmer weeding a field during a drought-high labor for poor returns. Source: Author. (Color figure available online.)

<!-- image -->

the land, building soil fertility through the application of organic matter, controlling weeds and pests, harvesting, processing, and storing grain. Because agriculture is becoming increasingly feminized in the region, this work burdens women more.

Before subsidized rice became cheaply available in the early 1980s, most poor households ate traditional food such as millets. Preparing millets is time consuming and women especially appreciated the reduced labor needs of preparing a rice-based meal. Anaamma, a landless Dalit farmer who depends primarily on wage work and safety nets for food security, explained:

Subsidized rice has made things easy for us. We had to do a lot of work to prepare foxtail millet, finger millet, and other grains, pounding them with our hands to dehusk the grain.

Farmyard manure is a key input into agroecological farming and a household's ability to maintain livestock depends on labor availability. Children have traditionally taken care of livestock, but they are increasingly unable or unwilling to tend to animals. When asked why they were not growing traditional crops, Maisappa, a small Dalit farmer belonging to one of RDI's project villages, explained in a focus group discussion:

If we want traditional agriculture and food security we should not send our children to school. We can only have animals if we have people to graze them. This was done by our children. Animals give us farmyard manure that we can use on our fields. In school children are not learning anything, neither are they useful at home . . . . If I go to graze cattle then who will earn the money?

As Maisappa indicates, the formal education system not only takes children physically away from agri- cultural work, but it also leads youth to devalue an agriculture-based livelihood.

The prevalence of higher wages in the area presents high opportunity costs for small farmers who would rather earn wages than expend time and labor growing food crops that would limit them to a subsistence lifestyle (Figure 3). Lalamma, a small woman farmer in an RDI project village, for example, remarked:

From one acre I can get three bags [300 kg] of sorghum. . . . If I weed my field, I lose my daily wages from other work. To hire bullocks for ploughing costs Rs. 300 a day. The investment is so high for only three bags of sorghum. For this reason many small farmers prefer doing wage work to cultivating their own fields.
sections.Shifting Values Around Traditional Agric:
Within households, there is a shift in knowledge and values around traditional subsistence crops due to the introduction of the subsidized rice program, increased material wealth, changing food preferences, and shifting values on a subsistence-focused lifestyle.

Indicating that increased material wealth has changed their diets, Somamma, a small woman farmer, recalled changed food habits during a life history interview:

Nowweeatmorewhite sorghum, subsidized rice, green gram, pigeonpea, and chickpea and less uncultivated greens like punti koora, doggal koora, and payal koora [referring to uncultivated greens from the Amaranthus and Hibiscus families]. Those days we ate more greens and less dal [prepared lentils] and hardly any vegetables. Now we eat more vegetables and also eat mutton one or two times a month.

For many Dalits, traditional foods and systems of cultivation were associated with exploitative labor institutions, hunger, and social exclusion. Valiamma, an elderly small Dalit farmer, shared her perspective on traditional foods in one of RDI's project villages:

Ambali [finger millet porridge] is poor peoples' food. It is associated with the hungry days. In those days, there was no summer work and that was the hungriest season. Now that there is chai and government subsidized rice, there is no need to make ambali.

Older farmers like her associated traditional foods and farming with the marginality and poverty of the past. Within households, there is a clear generational shift in food tastes away from traditional subsistence crops, especially the coarser grains. The younger generation frequently sought to distance themselves from traditional foods, which were perceived as a signifier of progress. Farmers confirm that because their children are not interested in eating these coarser traditional millets there is less incentive to cultivate them; as a consequence, knowledge about traditional food crops is waning. In a focus group discussion of male small farmers, the older farmers said that their diets were 50 percent rice and 50 percent sorghum bread, whereas the younger farmers said that their they preferred rice to sorghum bread and it made up around 25 percent of their diets. Although some forms of sorghum are widely eaten in the region and form a staple along with rice, the more drought-resistant or nutritious varieties are not as preferred because they are considered to be coarser, do not taste as good, or do not make white flour or soft rotis. AsoneDalitwomansmallfarmersuccinctly stated, 'People do not even eat yellow sorghum because it is not white.'

The director of RDI, who has actively promoted food sovereignty initiatives for the last two decades, shared that one of their biggest challenges is motivat- ing the younger generation to value traditional agriculture, as their situations are vastly different from their parents' and grandparents' generations. He explained:

Most of the farmers we originally worked with were farm labor and were earning small wages, sometimes as grain. They have felt hunger and complete deprivation. Attaining food security [with RDI] is precious for them. But we are not sure what will happen twenty years from now when the children go to school. The two generations that we have worked with will continue to practice traditional and agroecological cultivation.
sections.Discussion: Disjuncture Between Food Sec:
The constraints previously discussed underscore that food sovereignty prescriptions were not rooted in the changing material conditions of peasant existence in the Telengana region and depend on an essentialized notion of peasant motivations. At the field site, all those who practiced farming, regardless of their socioeconomic standing, gender, and caste, wanted more control over their agriculture. This control, they explained, would come from access to credit, support prices, subsidies on seeds, fertilizer, power for irrigation, research and extension services, market supports, and safety nets-for which they put faith in and assigned responsibility to the state. For poor farmers and the landless, their already precarious livelihoods would be far more difficult without existing state supports, such as summer work (Figure 4), subsidized food, and other welfare measures.

In addition to state supports, the farmers' ability to negotiate their position within the market economy is crucial for achieving livelihood security. This is in contrast to food sovereignty's foundation that farmers are better served if they can limit their engagement with

Figure 4 Farming is not enough: Women farmers demanding summer wage work from the state. Source: Author. (Color figure available online.)

<!-- image -->

the market economy through a focus on agroecological farming and subsistence food crops. Unless farmers are completely isolated from the market and live subsistence livelihoods, they cannot but feel pressured to participate in an increasingly monetized economy, and move to commercial crops. Many were supportive of agroecological agriculture in principle but did not think it would allow them to gain food security. Food sovereignty thus had little to do with localization and self-sufficiency strategies promoted by RDI.

A political ecology analysis of food emphasizes the importance of power, place, context, and difference at the conjuncture of social, political, and environmental relations (Jarosz 2014). In the Telengana region, rural dwellers are confronted by several problems, including (1) chronic food insecurity and nutritional insecurity of the very poor; (2) highly ecologically unsustainable farming practices especially of high-input crops such as cotton; (3) high cost of farming and debt; (4) water stress and climate change; (5) the loss of control over biological resources and loss of biological diversity with the corporatization of agriculture; (6) social inequity; and (7) livelihood insecurity and the inability of farming to provide it and a consequent desire to leave farming. Therefore, achieving food security, supporting farming, increasing ecological sustainability of farming, and resisting the corporate global food regime might need different strategies especially in the context of landscapes where small farmers are food insecure and where agrarian landscapes are experiencing rapid commercialization.

Analyzing this disjuncture between food sovereignty andfoodsecurity highlights that both food security and food sovereignty narratives are hegemonic. A hegemonic food security narrative with its focus on productivist modes of agriculture has enabled corporate capital's control of the food system and is laying waste to our ecosystems, bodies, local knowledges, and communities (Goodman 2014). In the Telengana region, the impact of corporate capital's foray into agriculture has had profound impacts as seen in the high number of suicides among small farmers (Nagaraj 2008).

Is the food sovereignty narrative also not hegemonic in that it privileges the views of those who favor a neopopulist vision of agriculture over the needs and aspirations of small farmers? Food sovereignty narratives link environmental and social justice concerns with food security and serve as an important critique of the corporate food regime and the food security paradigm. When myriad and complex rural issues are conflated by food sovereignty advocates, however, they do not serve to improve the lives of small farmers.

This does not mean that the food sovereignty model is not viable, only that it is limited. When food crops are grown locally and sustainably, it does increase access to food for the most marginalized, especially women, and brings other benefits to the local economy. Thus the answer to the myriad and complex problems of rural Telangana might lie at the conjuncture of food security and food sovereignty and not within one or the other approach. Peasants to- day negotiate their lives within the constraints and opportunities posed by state, market, and civil society, and these should be the starting point of initiatives that aim to help them (Bebbington 2000). Unless food sovereignty movement proponents are able to recognize the constraints faced by small farmers, the limits of their radical horizon are weakened. Food sovereignty ideologues need to be willing to test their ideas against critical, empirically grounded research to consider how food sovereignty plays out in specific localities for impoverished farmers, particularly the pressures and challenges they face to shift toward commercial agriculture and high-capital-input crops (Louis 2013). /squaresolid

sections.Wendy Jepson and Emily Vandewalle:
Texas A&M University

This article examines household-level characteristics that predict water insecurity in low-income rural and periurban communities on the Texas -Mexico border. We employ two logistic regression models (binary and ordered) to identify household characteristics that are more likely to result in water insecurity. Our analyses yielded unexpected fi ndings: Whereas socioeconomic factors are weak predictors, immigration status of household members is a signi fi cant variable that contributes to household water insecurity. Policymakers need to pay more attention to marginalized communities as ' universal ' water access still leaves populations without adequate, reliable, and affordable water in the Global North. Key Words: colonias, household water security, logistic regression, Texas, water resources.

T he pervasive view that households in developed countries have universal, indoor plumbing and secure water belies everyday experiences in lowincome and marginalized communities, where access to and bene fi t from adequate, affordable, and safe drinking water are daily struggles. In the United States, more than 600,000 households, or approximately 1.5 million people, live without complete plumbing facilities (American Communities Survey 2012). Many are homeless or belong to migrant or economically distressed populations. In Europe, Roma settlements lack access to safe water and sanitation (Harper, Steger, and Fil  c  ak 2009; Laurent 2011). For economically distressed households with access to water infrastructure, water service might not be affordable and water reliability and quality might be inadequate (Cory and Rahman 2009). In Detroit, thousands face water shutoffs due to an inability to pay their monthly bills (Lukacs 2014), and in the United Kingdom, almost 24 percent of households are ' water poor, ' paying more than 3 percent of household monthly income for water and sanitation services (Bradshaw and Huby 2013). Water quality threatens human health and well-being for rural communities and the urban poor. Small rural water suppliers chronically violate federal statutes protecting safe drinking water (Balazs et al. 2011; Satija 2014), and Native American communities face increased risk of drinking water contamination in water systems (Mascarenhas 2007). Yet, as some have pointed out, the poor in developed countries ' do not count among the world ' s 1.1 billion who lack access to safe drinking water or 2.4 billion who lack access to improved sanitation ' (Wescoat et al. 2008, 802).

Technical challenges are regularly cited as the cause of domestic water service delivery problems in the Global North. Poor water-system design, lack of trained operators, and insuf fi cient economies of scale for rural community water systems are cited as the causes leading to chronic boil water advisories (Patrick 2011a, 2011b). Geographic isolation, paired with poverty, is also posited as a reason for poor drinking water access (Wescoat, Headington, and Theobald 2008). In other places, dishonest land developers, minimum enforcement of plumbing codes, inadequate lowincome housing stock, and water pricing schemes are

cited as contributing factors to poor water service in low-income areas in the United States (Ward 1999; Olmstead 2003).

Although previous studies on drinking water access are meritorious, current explanations narrow the discussion to technical gaps or pricing problems that interrupt physical fl ows of water to consumers despite the growing scholarship in human -environment geography that examines water provision as more than infrastructure. Drinking water is part of a larger hydrosocial waterscape, de fi ned as a system bound together by dynamic circuits of knowledge, measurements, devices, organizations, institutional practices, and governance regimes (Linton and Budds 2014). Social and political processes constitute and mediate these circuits that allocate water fl ows and hydrological services through communities and across regions to water users and bene fi ciaries. Thus, our starting point is to frame the problem of drinking water provision in the Global North in terms of relational patterns of water access, everyday water practices, and the experiential or subjective dimensions of the hydrosocial cycle that dynamically reconstitute the waterscape (Sultana 2011; Jepson and Lee 2014). The challenge is how to operationalize the relational approach in a manner that is analytically robust, while offering opportunities to translate results into public policy that can materially improve drinking water quality for the marginalized in the Global North.

This article contributes to recent work on domestic water provision among marginalized communities in the Global North. First, we build on previous studies to advance the multidimensional concept of water security as a promising metric to assess the everyday experiences of water (Jepson 2014). Water security, de fi ned in terms of human development, is considered adequate, reliable, and affordable water for a healthy life (Lundqvist, Appasamy, and Nelliyat 2003; Wolf 2011; Cook and Bakker 2012). One can re fi ne water security for human development into three dimensions: water access, quality, and water affect (Wutich and Ragsdale 2008; Jepson 2014). This framework allows for the assessment of how gaps in water reliability, quality, and affordability erode the functioning for basic human activities. Water security includes, but is not limited to, water access; other characteristics such as affordability, quality, and the subjective experiences of domestic water provision are equally important. This is different than the concept of water poverty, which primarily addresses water access as a function of scarcity in terms of infrastructural and environmental issues at larger scales. Second, we examine the question of water security at the household level. By documenting water security variability among households in similar low-income populations, we might reveal contributing factors to water insecurity that have been previously overlooked at other scales.

Nowhere else does the relationship between domestic water provision and social exclusion come into such stark relief than in communities called colonias.

Colonias are impoverished and mostly unincorporated subdivisions populated by Mexican Americans located on urban fringes or in rural areas along the 2,000-mile U.S. -Mexico border. Although conditions have improved over the past decades (Durst and Ward 2013), colonias, home to more than 400,000 residents, are typically characterized by inadequate water and sanitation services, lack of electricity, and unpaved roads (Ward 1999; Donelson and Esparza 2010; McDonald and Grineski 2012; Of fi ce of the Attorney General 2012; Korc and Ford 2013). Recent work has examined the complex and dynamic social life of water prevalent in border colonias (Jepson and Lee 2014; Vandewalle and Jepson 2014). This article poses a further question: What household-level characteristics predict water insecurity within border colonias?

After placing the study in its regional context and describing the study ' s qualitative research and survey methods, we propose a novel measurement to assess household water insecurity and then employ two logistic regression models (binary and ordered) to identify household characteristics that are likely to result in household water insecurity. In the binary logistic regression model, the dependent variable is water insecurity. In the ordered logistic regression model, we use the natural order of dependent variables (water secure, marginally water secure, marginally water insecure, water insecure) where higher categories indicate increased household water insecurity. Our analysis, although preliminary, is signi fi cant because it is the fi rst regression model using a measurement of water security at the household scale.

Our results yield some unexpected fi ndings concerning the relevance of immigration status to household water insecurity. Notwithstanding some weaknesses in the study, it is clear that adequate, reliable, and affordable water for a healthy life is a ' material emblem of citizenship ' (Bakker 2010, 55); for colonias communities on the border, immigration status might in fl uence household water insecurity more than previously expected. Broadly, these results underscore the need to examine the social and political determinants of household water insecurity in marginalized communities rather than ascribing water insecurity to technical gaps in water delivery systems.
sections.Household Water Insecurity Along the U.S:
The waterscape on the Texas -Mexico border is de fi ned by complex hydrosocial interactions among institutions, organizations, and technologies that allocate the fl ow of water across the region and through infrastructure to different water users (Jepson 2012; Jepson and Brannstrom 2015). Rio Grande water eventually fi nds its way to poor households through circuits of irrigation-district canals, quasi-public community water networks, inadequate household connections, water vending machines, and garden hoses

Figure 1 Study sites: El Paso County and Hidalgo County. (Color figure available online.)

<!-- image -->

to be stored in fi fty-gallon barrels, buckets, or fi ve-gallon plastic bottles. A fragmented regime of water governance institutions, water markets, housing codes, and private corporations direct the water fl ow to households in border colonias. The focus of this study is two of the poorest regions in the United States: (1) Hidalgo County in the Lower Rio Grande Valley, with the largest concentration of colonias (over 240,000 people), and (2) El Paso County in West Texas (Figure 1). The boxes indicated in Figures 1

and 2 are sections of each county selected for consistency and to minimize exogenous factors. Demographic data compare study census tracts levels of poverty and households without complete plumbing 1 (Table 1, Figure 2).

Residents in border colonias have few reliable, affordable, and adequate options for drinking water. They face a ' no-win ' waterscape. Existing domestic water provision is available but expensive, highly variable, and unreliable, and water quality is demonstratively precarious. Residents face service interruptions due to lack of payment, unreliable water service, and concerns over tap water quality. Some households avoid existing water utilities altogether and use garden hoses to connect to a neighbor ' s water meter (Figure 3).

Several households not connected to community water service might live in areas not served by a water supply corporation. For example, 4,500 residents living in sixty El Paso colonias are not connected to community water systems. In other cases, households cannot afford the water connection costs, or they cannot afford the household improvements necessary to comply with building codes, a prerequisite for waterline hookups. Instead, residents rely on water delivery trucks to fi ll large 1,500- to 2,500-gallon plastic storage tanks. Trucked water, despite claims to the contrary, is not considered potable, and many residents experience skin rashes due to contamination (Graham and VanDerslice 2007; McDonald and Grineski 2012; Figure 4). Finally, most households, whether connected to a community water system or not, depend on unreliable water vending machines because of generalized tap water quality concerns (Chaidez et al. 1999; Schillinger and Knorr 2004; Figure 5).
sections.Household Surveys: Qualitative research was conducted in Hidalgo County during nine visits between January 2009 and August 2011. The fi rst author led a research team, including a local community health worker ( promotora ), as they conducted forty-one semistructured interviews and two focus groups. The fi rst author used qualitative information to develop a household water security survey, which was then completed for seventy-one households in Hidalgo County (sixty-eight households used in study) in July 2012. The second author conducted sixty-six household surveys in El Paso County and Do ~ na Ana County (New Mexico) in July 2013. We used the State of Texas colonia classi fi cation system to stratify our sample of households (Parcher and Humberson 2009). We selected households in eleven different colonias in eastern Hidalgo County and fourteen different colonias in eastern El Paso, with households representing each colonia classi fi cation: red, yellow, green, and unclassi fi ed (Table 2). We also surveyed colonias not classi fi ed in the Texas database. We removed six household surveys from adjacent counties in New Mexico when we ran the logistic regression models to limit our analysis to Texas counties. The surveys were conducted in Spanish or English with the available head of household. The survey, which took between thirty and forty- fi ve minutes, was divided into four parts: (1) household demographics (age, occupation, health care access, country of origin, etc., for each household member), (2) water usages and practices, (3) series of yes -no questions related to the three water dimensions, and (4) income and wealth. Descriptive statistics of households are provided in Table 3.
sections.Data Analysis:
We analyzed household survey data using three techniques. First, we used an experiential scalogram technique (Guttman 1945) to draw inferences about a latent variable (water insecurity) in the observed data (Guttman 1945; Guest 2000). In this study we created three scalograms for each dimension of water security. Guttman scalograms provide a measurement of cumulative or progressive objective, subjective, and biocultural experiences; it has been particularly useful when related to domestic water access and food security (Wutich and Ragsdale 2008; Hadley and Wutich 2009; Stevenson et al. 2012). For Hidalgo County, we used household scales and classi fi cations from previously published data (Jepson 2014), and we followed the same procedure to create the water security scales and classi fi cation for households in El Paso.

Survey item responses were entered 0 or 1 into a respondent-by-item matrix for each dimension of water security, with each row representing a household respondent and each column representing an indicator for each dimension of water security (water access, water quality acceptability, water distress). Guttman scalograms order item responses such that the individual who responded more positively will rank higher than an individual who responded negatively, and the positions of the item responses and individuals are given numerical values. Three conventional measures of reliability for each scale were calculated: coef fi cient of reproducibility (CR), coef fi cient of

We did not explicitly ask immigration status of household members; however, a combination of responses from several survey questions -place of birth, sources of income (including public bene fi t), time of residency, insurance coverage -allowed us to deduce and estimate documented or undocumented status. We noted households receiving Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, Social Security (including SSI Disability), and Supplementary Nutrition Program (SNAP, or food stamps) because monthly bene fi ts require documented status. We also noted whether the distribution of these bene fi ts varied between and within each household. For example, we surveyed households in which all of the children under the age of eighteen would be eligible for Children ' s Health Insurance Program or Medicaid but not all of them receive the bene fi ts. Similarly, a household might receive SNAP bene fi ts for some children but not as a household or at the maximum eligible under current state provision. We recognize that SNAP eligibility for adults is variable, but since July 2002 children under eighteen who are legal residents are eligible for bene fi ts (Wight et al. 2014). This intrahousehold variability, paired with other data on birthplace, strongly suggests whether the household is a mixedstatus or all-undocumented household. If no proxy evidence for residency status was obtained, we classifi ed the household as all documented.

An odds ratio less than 1.0 indicates a negative effect or a lower likelihood that the outcome will occur. Second, we performed an ordered logistic regression (OLR) model, which is similar to the binary logistic regression model but for multiple outcome variables that are categorical (water secure, marginally water secure, marginally water insecure, and water insecure). OLR models the relation between the previous independent variables and the four household water security classifi cations while controlling for the covariates. Regression results are reported as adjusted odds ratios (ORs) and 95 percent con fi dence intervals (CIs) for moving to higher water insecurity categories versus remaining in the same category. That is, OLR models cumulative probability, or the factors that increase or decrease the likelihood of being in a higher category of household water insecurity. For the OLR, an odds ratio higher than 1.0 for the explanatory variable indicates a greater likelihood of being in higher water insecurity categories versus remaining in the same category. Conversely, an odds ratio less than 1.0 indicates a negative effect or a lower likelihood of being in higher water insecurity categories versus remaining in the same category.

First, we employed a binary logistic regression, which estimates coef fi cients and reports an odds ratio for explanatory variables on the outcome variable. sections.Binary Logistic Regression:
Table 7 summarizes the outcome and explanatory variables used in the regression models. Table 8 presents the results from the logistic regression model for household water insecurity. Overall the model is reasonably strong as indicated by the likelihood ratio chi-square value, which is statistically signi fi cant ( p < 0.05).

Household immigration status is an important factor to consider in household water insecurity. The analysis indicates that ' mixed status ' households were 4.2 times more likely to be water insecure than households with members who were all documented (legal residents or U.S. citizens). Households in which all members are unauthorized residents increase the likelihood (1.2 times) of water insecurity, but the results were insigni fi cant. Birthplace, which is different than legal status, also signi fi cantly affected household water insecurity. Households with both U.S.- and foreignborn members are 20 percent less likely to be water insecure than households in which all members were born in the United States.

Other socioeconomic variables such as size of household increase the likelihood of household water insecurity, but the results are all insigni fi cant. Poverty level runs in the direction anticipated. Households between 50 percent and 99 percent of the FPL are almost twice as likely to be water insecure than those above the FPL, and the households below 49 percent of the FPL are 1.5 times more likely to be water insecure than those above the FPL. Households with members that include children, adults, and elderly are 6.3 times more likely to be water insecure than households with only adults or only elderly. Although the p value is slightly more than 0.01 ( p value D 0.127), it approaches signi fi cance and therefore is an important fi nding.

The model also considers residential factors on household water insecurity. Living in a manufactured home (recreational vehicle [RV] or mobile home) was not an important predictor of household water insecurity. The model con fi rms expectations, however, that households in ' red ' colonias were more likely (4.7 times) to be water insecure as compared to households in the ' green ' classi fi ed colonia. Although living in a colonia classi fi ed ' red ' signi fi cantly increased the likelihood of water insecurity, the other colonia classi fi cations are poor predictors of household water insecurity. sections.Ordered Logistic Regression:
The OLR model reports many similar relationships between the independent and dependent variable (household water insecurity) as the fi rst binary logistic regression but with some notable differences (Table 8). Households with residents of mixed documentation are 2.4 times more likely to be classi fi ed in a higher category of household water insecurity than households with all members documented. Although signi fi cant, this is less than predicted in the binary logistic regression model. The OLR model also indicates that households with all undocumented residents are three times more likely to be classi fi ed in higher levels of household water insecurity. Although this fi nding was not statistically signi fi cant, the p value was approaching signi fi cance and therefore we consider an important relationship between all undocumented households and water insecurity. Households with mixed U.S.- and foreign-born residents are 38 percent less likely to be classi fi ed in higher levels of water insecurity than households with all U.S.-born residents, which is a higher likelihood than in the binary logistic regression. Households with all foreign-born members are also less likely to be in a higher water insecurity category than all U.S.-born households. Although insigni fi cant, it is notable that this is a shift in direction from the binary logistic regression model.

Similar to the binary regression model, other socioeconomic variables, such as size of household, increases the likelihood of household water insecurity, but the results are insigni fi cant. In addition, relative poverty level runs in the direction anticipated, but results from our analysis are all insigni fi cant. Households between 50 and 99 percent of the FPL are about twice as likely to be in a higher household water insecurity category than those above the FPL, a very similar result from the binary regression. Households below 49 percent of the FPL are 2.6 times more likely to be in a higher water insecure category than those above the FPL, which is notably different than the result from the binary regression. Similarly, households that receive public bene fi t run in the negative direction to household water insecurity but, as with the binary logistic regression model, this is statistically insigni fi cant. As in the binary logistic regression model, households with members that include children, adults, and elderly are more likely to be water insecure (2.8 times) than households with only adults or only elderly. Although the p value is more than 0.01, it approaches signi fi cance with a p value of 0.163

and therefore is an important fi nding. The OLR model con fi rms that dwelling type and time in residence are poor predictors of household water insecurity.

The OLR model presents a clearer relationship between households living in ' red ' colonias and higher levels of household water insecurity than those in the binary regression. These households are 7.8 times more likely to be in a higher category of household water insecurity and with a stronger signi fi cance value. In the binary regression model, households in ' yellow ' colonias are less likely to be water insecure than households in ' green ' colonias, but the OLR model changes sthe direction of this relationship. There is an increased chance that a household in the ' yellow ' category will be observed in a higher category of household water insecurity but, again, the p value value indicates that this is not signi fi cant.
sections.Discussion:
Our research suggests that households living in border colonias -communities that are both connected to community water service and not connected to community water service -face signi fi cant levels of household water insecurity. Water insecurity varied, however, within similar subdivisions; thus, our work challenges the notion that colonias households form a homogenous group in terms of living conditions and access to resources. Our analysis attempted to determine what household-level characteristics would predict water insecurity in colonias households. The binary logistic regression modeled signi fi cant predictors for presence of household water insecurity; the OLR modeled the odds for a household moving to higher water insecurity categories versus remaining in the same category. Overall, household water insecurity is dif fi cult to predict with statistical signi fi cance, but there were some unexpected results in our fi ndings, particularly if we examine our preliminary fi ndings in comparison with recent scholarship on experience of insecurity of everyday life on the U.S. -Mexico border.

First, we would have expected relative poverty to increase the likelihood of water insecurity, but our results indicate that the degree to which a household lives in poverty might not strongly in fl uence water insecurity among this population. Although the reasons need to be investigated further, one can deduce that water is not affordable for most of the households because most are impoverished, and a majority of the surveyed households experience problems buying water or engage in practices to economize water use. Therefore, differences in terms of household water insecurity might re fl ect the experiences related to the other dimensions of water insecurity (quality and distress) and not to different levels of affordability or access.

Second, we would also expect that living in a mobile home would increase the likelihood of water insecurity because those units can be more easily located on land

that does not necessarily follow water and sanitation codes. Moreover, colonia residents more frequently rely on the secondary market to buy aging mobile homes and RVs (Durst 2014); therefore, the internal infrastructure could be signi fi cantly depreciated, degrading water quality through the connection between the housing and the water supply. In addition, the literature would suggest that an increase in residence time might decrease the likelihood of water insecurity because of housing consolidation and dwelling improvements made over the life course (Durst and Ward 2013). Yet, our analysis indicates that factors related to the dwelling (e.g., dwelling types [mobile or RV vs. house] and time in residence [years]) do not increase the likelihood of household water insecurity to any signi fi cant degree.

Although we were not surprised that households in ' red ' colonias have a higher likelihood of being water insecure than households in ' green ' colonias, the result that other state-mandated colonias classi fi cations were poor predictors of household water insecurity was unexpected. In many cases, especially in the El Paso ' red ' colonias, lack of either water or sanitation services set the stage for household water insecurity, whereas in Hidalgo County, households in ' red ' colonias lacked mainly sanitation. Moreover, although classi fi cation was a predictor, we documented various household levels of water insecurity in ' red ' colonias. Therefore, we can only conclude that the colonia classi fi cation system, although perhaps helpful in identifying the worst-case scenarios, is an inadequate proxy to assess the larger and more diverse experiences of household-scale water insecurity.

Finally, our analysis revealed a major unexpected predictor of household water insecurity -immigration status of household members -with mixed-status households as the most signi fi cant predictor of household water insecurity. Our fi ndings, paired with existing research on mixed-status families, suggest that the quotidian behaviors and choices in response to precarious immigration status might ' spill over ' into other insecurities, including household water insecurity. Negotiating the immigration regime is de fi ned by avoiding exposure to authorities. This can be achieved in terms of location of residences, and many colonias provide this protection as they are within the sparsely patrolled rural and periurban areas. Connection to public services might also be a perceived vulnerability and exposure point. Another form of ' protection, ' con fi rmed anecdotally in fi eld research, is the reliance or dependency on private water delivery -either trucked or vending machines. This allows individuals to manage chronic problems of water access and quality without directly addressing problems with the water supply corporations or municipal services. The impact could include increased costs of water, dependency on unregulated water sources, and increased water distress. Exploring these speci fi c interactions is beyond the scope of this study, but we believe that future research should explore how immigration status might in fl uence interactions with local water governance regimes as a signi fi cant factor in water insecurity.

Several important limitations should be considered when reviewing the results of this study and could inform future research. Although the study included an adequate number of households, a larger sample size might improve the robustness. Second, housing tenure -either rental, ownership (title), or contractfor-deed ( fi nal or interim) -would be another important variable to include in future surveys. Our current survey did not delineate the speci fi c status of housing tenure, so we could not include this variable in our current model. As time in residence, the variable we used, might autocorrelate with housing tenure, future research would have to determine the best independent variable. Third, our analysis provided preliminary means to assess gaps in water reliability, quality, and affordability, but we recognize the need to re fi ne the scalogram and classi fi cation analysis. For example, household water security classi fi cations were generated based on experiential scales re fl ective of each place studied yet were aggregated in the regression analyses. That said, our study is in line with the experience-based scales, as these communities are similar in terms of culture and socioeconomic demographics.
sections.Conclusion:
Ourstudy advanced current research on domestic water provision among marginalized communities in the Global North by applying methods to quantify household water insecurity. The empirical focus of this study was low-income, periurban and rural communities in two impoverished regions on the Texas -Mexico border: the Lower Rio Grande Valley and west Texas. The novel scale and classi fi cation system offered a systematic means to assess the three dimensions of household water security in a common measurement for households for two study areas. The results reveal notable regional differences. Households in both regions have an equal percentage classi fi ed as water secure, but there is a higher percentage of households surveyed in El Paso classi fi ed as marginally water insecure or water insecure. We also used household water security classifi cations developed from household survey data to run two statistical analyses: binary logistic regression and OLR. We determined that demographics, poverty, and housing infrastructure are relatively weak and statistically insigni fi cant predictors of household water insecurity, whereas immigration status signi fi cantly increased the likelihood of household water insecurity. Our study suggests that future research should investigate why immigration status might be a predictor of water insecurity, repeat the logistic regression analysis with a larger sample size, and broaden the geographical distribution of study areas to advance our knowledge of the unevenness of household water insecurity. These research directions will enable further tests of the

household water security measurement as a robust, reliable indicator, similar to the food security measurements, in the Global North. &

sections.Historical Political Ecology of Water: A:
Martha G. Bell

Leiden Institute for Area Studies

Historical political ecology provides a powerful framework for understanding nature -society relations in the past. This approach is applied to municipal drinking water governance in early colonial Lima, Peru, with a focus on how power dynamics in fl uenced sociospatial patterns of water access and control. Sixteenth- and seventeenth-century archival sources are analyzed for material aspects of Lima ' s drinking water pipeline network and for the management strategies employed by the municipal government. Access to water is demonstrated to have shaped, reinforced, and re fl ected colonial social divisions and to have been linked to the spatial development of the city, including urban -rural relations. Key Words: colonialism, historical political ecology, Peru, water governance, water infrastructure.

The public utility in the fair distribution of waters . . . has excited in all times continuing controversies.

-Ambrosio Cerd  an de Landa, Lima Water Judge (1828, 3 -4)

H istorical perspectives have long been considered integral to political ecology (Zimmerer and Bassett 2003; Peet and Watts 2004; Robbins 2004), although how and to what end historical content and analysis could be incorporated into this research approach has not been fully resolved and remains an ambiguous pursuit (Offen 2004). In general, the historical political ecology approach calls for the application of historical perspectives within a broadly de fi ned political ecology point of view and has been de fi ned as ' a fi eld-informed interpretation of society -nature relations in the past ' (Offen 2004, 21). This includes using historical material to contextualize current environmental con fl icts, especially the continuing in fl uences of European expansion and colonialism, often with the explicit motivation of improving social justice or environmental conservation in the present (Brannstrom 2004; Offen 2004; D. K. Davis 2009). Historical political ecology might also include asking questions about environmental change or natural resource use in historical periods, either recent (e.g., Swyngedouw 1999; Biehler 2009; Carey 2010; Lane 2011; Carey, French, and O ' Brien 2012) or more distant (e.g., Watts 1983; Sluyter 1999; Zimmerer 2000; Carney 2001; M. Davis 2004; End fi eld and Fern  andez Tejedo 2006; D. K. Davis 2007; End fi eld 2008). Although this latter purpose -using a political ecological analysis to closely examine nature -society relations in the past and not just provide context for current-day issues -is lesser used, it represents a powerful framework for historical research.

In this article, I apply such a framework to municipal drinking water access and governance in colonial Lima, the capital city of the Viceroyalty of Peru. I draw on approaches and questions inspired by political ecology to examine patterns and politics of water use in a colonial context, focusing on the in fl uence of power dynamics on sociospatial patterns of resource access and control (following McCarthy 2002; Ribot and Peluso 2003; Turner 2009). Using material analysis of water infrastructure and technology recorded in sixteenth- and seventeenth-century archives, I explain how water access formed, reinforced, and re fl ected

colonial social divisions, as well as in fl uenced the spatial development of the colonial city.

The city of Lima, originally called Ciudad de Los Reyes , was founded in 1535 as the seat of the Spanish Viceroyalty of Peru. It can be considered one of the most prominent of the Spanish colonial cities, second perhaps only to Mexico, the capital of New Spain. Lima is located on the central coast of Peru in a desert climate where true rainfall rarely occurs. All water used for drinking, irrigation, sanitation, and industry must be drawn from river watersheds and related aquifers. The urban design of Lima followed the wellknown Spanish colonial grid pattern, and the city was speci fi cally sited along the banks of the Rímac River and in relation to the numerous pre-Hispanic irrigation canals drawn from this river. 1 The Spaniards, however, established their own drinking water pipeline infrastructure. This underground pipe network, fi rst inaugurated in 1578, was controlled by the Cabildo (City Council) and was one of the earliest in the New World. The Cabildo, or municipal branch of colonial government, was of fi cially charged with managing Lima ' s water and, not surprisingly, the careful division of measured amounts of drinking and irrigation water occupied much of its energy. 2 Although the Cabildo ' s explicitly stated objective was to provide access to clean and copious drinking water for the entire urban population, this goal was only partially achieved. Therefore, this article seeks to examine how municipal governance strategies contributed to inequality in access to drinking water among colonial Lima ' s urban residents. The methodological approach to answering this question incorporates two major components: fi rst, asking questions inspired by political ecology and, in particular, the political ecology of water and, second, applying data collection and analysis techniques appropriate to the historical period being studied.

Three key themes drawn from the recent literature on the political ecology of water inform my interpretations of the Lima case. Most important, unequal water access (Swyngedouw 2004; Bakker 2011; Loftus 2011) and the related politics of surface water or aquifer management (Swyngedouw 1999; Norman and Bakker 2008; Brooks and Linton 2011; Jepson 2012) have proven integral themes in understanding current-day water systems and have been shown to have both important historical antecedents and long-term legacy effects. Second, analyses of urban development and urban -rural relations related to water demonstrate strong urban bias, with urban uses often privileged in cases of con fl icting multiple uses of water (multifunctionality). This bias, or unequal relationship between urban and rural areas, is evidenced by the urban hydraulic reach (or water footprint; Swyngedouw 1997, 2004; Bakker 2003; Kaika 2005; Scott and Pablos 2011). Third, combining spatial, social, political, and economic aspects of the previously mentioned themes, Bakker (2003) indicated that water supply in urban areas, especially urbanizing areas of the Global South, should be understood in terms of archipelagos instead of networks, given the discontinuous and partial coverage of public water supply and the frequency of multiple and overlapping methods of public and private water delivery mechanisms. Together, these themes provide a foundational perspective from which to examine urbanization, water supply, and inequality. They suggest the primacy of urban water use and indicate unequal infrastructural coverage and access to water within urban spaces.

Although these topics, questions, and themes from political ecological research can be easily transferred to historical contexts, the research methods typically used by political ecologists might not always be applicable, especially when more distant historical periods are studied. For such older cases, it is necessary to combine multiple methods and data sources, which might include fi eld-based ethnographic and landscape observations, archival analysis, archaeological investigation, biophysical data, mapping, and more. The multidisciplinary research area called hydraulic archaeology provides a framework for analysis of (pre) historical water systems (Kirchner and Navarro 1996; Glick and Kirchner 2000; Barcel  o 2004; Glick 2005). Here, practitioners seek to reconstruct the design, layout, construction, and modi fi cation of hydraulic systems, to identify the social groups participating in the use of these systems and thus to determine the relative political and demographic strengths of these groups as demonstrated by their ability to access water resources. The major unit of investigation in hydraulic archaeology is the concept of hydraulic space (Barcel  o 1996), which is basically equivalent to what Swyngedouw (1999) termed the ' waterscape ' and can be de fi ned as a landscape of water use, at once both natural and social. It is a space designed to take advantage of a natural fl uvial system, and incorporates (1) the aquifer or drainage area, (2) the local and regional topography in relation to desired water conduction, and (3) the irrigated parcels or other uses of water. It includes the biophysical context controlling the quantity of water available and the direction of its fl ow, as well as the human division of water among houses, fi elds, orchards, and other uses. The orientation and design of a hydraulic space is based on features of the fl uvial system, but the conduction and distribution of water in canals and pipes follows patterns that are neither natural nor casual. This water infrastructure is closely linked to the organization of productive activities and therefore to social, political, and economic relationships.

The focus on infrastructure (e.g., canals, pipelines), achieved through consideration of a range of data sources (e.g., archaeological survey and excavation, historical documents and maps, legal traditions, toponyms, and remotely sensed imagery), makes hydraulic archaeology a useful guide for pursuing historical political ecology work on water in colonial Lima. Given the nearly 500 years of Lima ' s urban development, few material or archaeological remains of colonial water infrastructure can still be found (or

reasonably accessed), so in this case archival sources contain the best information. The major source for the analysis of Lima ' s hydraulic space is the Libros de Cabildos de Lima (the books of the City Council of Lima, hereafter LCL ). These books, which record the minutes from the weekly or biweekly meetings of Lima ' s Cabildo, span almost the entire colonial period, from the city ' s foundation in 1535 to after Peru ' s independence in 1821, 3 and provide an incredibly comprehensive and continuous record of the Cabildo ' s actions related to drinking water governance. 4 In this article I examine the period 1578 to 1700, which was the interval during which most of Lima ' s public and private drinking water infrastructure was installed, the vast majority of potable water connection licenses were issued, and the most signi fi cant water management and governance strategies were developed. Speci fi cally, I analyze all references to springs, reservoirs, pipes, tanks, fountains, petitions for water connections, and other related topics in the LCL of the period in question to determine both spatial and temporal aspects of water supply in the pipeline network. I consider such basic questions as these: Where were pipelines constructed and when? Which residents and populations did these pipelines serve? How reliable was water supply in the network overall? This included mapping the pipeline routes and the locations of public and private running water connections. 5 I used this analysis of written descriptions of material aspects of Lima ' s hydraulic space to interpret the biophysical, social, political, and economic signi fi cance of patterns of drinking water access and control in the early colonial period and to evaluate the Cabildo ' s role in contributing to or alleviating inequality in water access.
sections.Lima's Hydraulic Space and Its Governanc:
In 1671, Lima ' s solicitor general called water ' the element most necessary after air ' ( LCL 29.X.1671), 6 and indeed it was the natural resource most frequently discussed by Lima ' s Cabildo. The provision of drinking water was considered one of the principal responsibilities of the Cabildo: ' the fi rst thing given attention in the foundation of all of the cities of the world [is] that this element, inexcusable for human life, is provided with cleanliness and security ' ( LCL 17.XI.1649). To this end, the Spanish located their capital city along the banks of the Rímac River, to provide residents with water for irrigation, drinking, sanitation, and industry. The Rímac dominates Lima ' s hydraulic space (Figure 1). Like all of Peru ' s coastal rivers, it fl ows westward, cutting down from the glacial lakes of the high Andes to the Paci fi c, descending from a height of over 5,500 m above sea level to its mouth near Lima ' s port El Callao over a distance of about 130 km. Its fl ow varies seasonally, increasing during the highland rainy season (October -April), when it often threatens to overrun its banks, and all but drying up during the dry months (May -September). The Rímac was the source of the irrigation canals that supported all agriculture in the region around the city (Domínguez 1988). It was also the source of numerous springs used for drinking water during the colonial period. Seepage and fi ltration from the river and the Andean cordillera fi lls the large alluvial aquifer -of approximately 390 km 2 in area and 100 to 500 m in depth -located underneath the city and its surroundings, recharging this resource on a seasonal basis (Lerner et al. 1982; Quintana and Tovar 2002).

The Spanish designed and built their linked agricultural and hydraulic system ( fi elds, canals, reservoirs, and pipelines) around the natural topography as well as the pre-Hispanic canals already in existence. This multipurpose hydraulic space linked Lima ' s urban core with its rural surroundings and was of fi cially controlled by the Cabildo, which exercised jurisdiction over the urban zone (approximately 2.6 km 2 ), as well as the surroundings of the city (approximately a 113km radius around the city). A diverse population resided within this larger territory, primarily made up of Spaniards, Africans, and Indians. 7 Although the Cabildo claimed great authority over the city, it actually governed through a complicated relationship with other branches of colonial government, especially the Viceroy (the Spanish monarch ' s representative in Peru) and the Real Audiencia (Royal Audience, the highest court in Peru). With respect to water administration, responsibilities of the Cabildo included protection of the urban riverbank and construction of levees, distribution of rights to irrigation waters, canal maintenance, concession of milling licenses, and, of primary importance here, construction and maintenance of a municipal drinking water pipeline network and allocation of permits to install private connections to this network for homes and other institutions. To manage all aspects of municipal water governance, a water judge ( Juez de Aguas ) was elected annually from among the city councilmen ( Regidores ). The water judge post was established in 1556, with power to enforce the water ordinances for the city and surrounding countryside. It was a lucrative position, with a salary of 800 pesos a year, yet election as water judge rotated among the councilmen and did not seem to require much specialized knowledge (Bell forthcoming).

To provision the city with drinking water, Lima ' s Cabildo carried out three functions: (1) It secured the source of the water in springs on the outskirts of the city; (2) it installed and maintained a network of reservoirs, tanks, and pipelines; and (3) it awarded licenses for running water connections from the pipes to private houses, monasteries and convents, and other institutions. For this, beginning in 1611, each year the Cabildo named three or four pipeline commissioners ( Comisarios de Ca ~ nerías ). 8 These pipeline commissioners were councilmen or mayors, and in fi fty-eight of the seventy-nine years for which we have data in the seventeenth century, one of the commissioners was simultaneously the water judge (or
