sections.Alexander B. Murphy and Anne Hunderi-Ely:
University o f Oregon

In  1994, support for European Union (EU) membership was highly variable across Norway, Sweden, and Finland. The 'no' vote was strongest in rural areas eligible for substantial EU subsidies.  Moreover,  the majority voted against EU membership in Norway. To explain these outcomes, this article focuses on the ways in which local and national differences mediated  interpretations of  the issues raised  during the campaign. The  analysis  highlights important forces shaping northern Europe today and their implications for the EU in the years ahead. Key Words: Nordic countries, European Union, electoral geography, urban-rural.

uring the fall of  1994, the voters in NorD way,  Sweden, and  Finland  went  to  the polls to decide whether their countries should join the European Union (EU). The outcome of  the  vote  revealed  significant political  and cultural differences both between Norway and its neighbors and between the urbanized  core of  northern  Europe  and  the  rural  periphery. There has been little post-referenda analysis of the electoral geography of the Nordic vote on EU membership,  however. As a  step  toward filling this void, this article focuses on the nature and significance of the general patterns of support  for  EU  membership  that  emerged from the referenda. The Nordic  vote is deserving of attention because the final outcome has important implications for the individual countries of the  European north  and because it offers insights into issues facing Scandinavia and  Europe  today. Moreover,  since many  of the 'no'  votes on EU membership came from individuals  living in regions that were expected to receive substantial subsidies within the EU, the Nordic vote highlights the need to go beyond neoclassical economic expectancies to explain voting behavior.
sections.Background:
The first Nordic country to vote on EU membership was Finland (Table 1). On October 16, 1994, 57%  of  the Finnish population voted in favor  of  membership.  The  'yes'  and  'no' votes  were  not  evenly  distributed  across  the

As Figure  1 reveals,  'no' votes were concentrated heavily in the northern part of the country, whereas those living in the  more  urbanized,  densely populated  south voted  in  favor  of  membership.  The  Swedes followed a similar pattern when they voted on membership  on  November  13,  1994.  Once again EU membership was carried by those in the more  urbanized areas: the Stockholm, Goteberg, and Malmo metropolitan areas. The margin  of  victory  in  Sweden  was  narrower than  in  Finland,  however, with  only  52%  of the population favoring EU membership. The Norwegians,  by  contrast,  rejected  EU membership by a vote of 52% to 48% on November  28,  1994. Once again, those  voting  'no' were concentrated  in the rural north, whereas those favoring EU membership were concentrated  around Oslo.

Voter turnout was relatively high in all three Nordic countries  voting  on EU membership. Surprisingly, Finland  had  the  lowest turnout (74%), even though a majority of the Finns felt that they were participating in the most important  decision  their  country  had  made  in  decades (Pesonen 1994, 10).  In Norway and Sweden,  well  over  80%  of  the  population  cast a vote.  Given  these  high  participation  figures, the  final vote  provides  a  good  picture  of  the views of most Finns, Swedes, and Norwegians on EU membership in the fall of  1994. One of the most striking features of those views is the extraordinary  continuity  in  the  geography  of the vote from country to country. In each case the majority of those in the densely populated urban core-particularly the national capitals-favored membership, whereas the majority  of  those  in  the  areas  far  from  that  core rejected the European Union (compare Figs. 1 and 2).

The extent to which the vote was polarized along urban-rural lines can be seen by looking more  closely at the  relationship  between  the strength  of  support  for  EU membership  and the  population  densities  of  the  Nordic provinces  or  counties.  Figure 3- a plot  of  that relationship-shows a  strong correlation  between population  density and  the strength  of the  'yes' vote.  Even  more  significantly, the figure  shows that strong 'no' votes  occurred solely  in  relatively  low-density  counties  and provinces (group E), whereas all of  the largest cities  (group A) favored  EU  membership. There was some diversity of voting preferences in  low-  and  medium-density counties and provinces (especially group D), but in all cases where  a  majority  of  the  population  voted  in favor of EU membership, the county or province either contained a large city or was closely tied to a large city. The latter point can be seen in  Figure  4,  which shows that those  counties and provinces in  group B are all immediately adjacent  to  large  urban  areas, and  that  those counties and provinces in  group  C are within the hinterlands  of these urban  areas. Figure 4 thus  confirms  that  support  for  EU membership  was  closely tied  to  distance  from  major centers  of business,  finance,  transportation, and communication.

An  analysis  of the  relationship between population density and voting at the county or province level is  suggestive only of  very general patterns.  Moreover, in  many cases where EU membership lost or won by a narrow margin, population  density cannot be viewed as  a strong predictor  of voting attitudes. Nonetheless,  the  fact  that  no  low-to-medium  density area  voted  for  EU membership  and  that  the 'yes' vote  was  strongest  in  and  around  the large cities shows that the arguments raised in favor  of  EU  membership  were  most  sympathetically  received  by  those  whose  lives  and livelihoods are tied to the economic and political centers of gravity of  the Nordic countries. This  would  seem  fairly  straightforward  if  it were not for one rather striking fact: the areas with the strong 'no'  votes were precisely those areas that had been designated for special EU assistance  in the treaties specifying  membership terms for each of the countries (Msnnesland  1994, 68). Indeed, a map of areas eligible for special EU assistance under a pro-

The  proposed  EU  subsidies  for  northern Europe  are  more  than  cosmetic; regions  that can take advantage of them stand to gain substantial economic benefits (Molle 1994).  Moreover, analyses focused on the Nordic countries show  that  EU  membership  would actually work against the  economic interests  of  industrial and manufacturing concerns concentrated

Since  these economic realities would leave urban  areas in a  vulnerable  position within an integrated European  Union,  Halvorsen  concluded  that peripheral Norwegian regions would fare much better  than their urban counterparts within the

The Norwegian vote-and indeed the Nordic vote  more  generally-thus cannot be  explained by reference to simple economic forecasts. Those living in areas that were predicted to reap the greatest fiscal rewards from a decision  to  join  the  EU  generally voted  against membership, whereas those living in areas ex- pected to suffer some negative economic consequences from membership voted overwhelmingly in favor of membership. To make sense of  the  outcome,  consideration  must  be given  to  the  political,  social,  and  economic contexts within  which  the vote  took  place. A focus  on  context  is  important  if  the  social forces  underlying  voting  patterns  are  to  be discerned and if the implications of those patterns  are  to  be  grasped  (see,  e.g., Johnston 1986; Murphy  1990; Agnew 1996). A concern with  these  matters  led  Agnew  to  argue  that

A broad contextual approach makes sense in studying  the  Nordic  referenda  on  EU  mem- bership,  where  the debates  leading up  to  the vote focused on everything from lifestyle changes to economics to sovereignty. The arguments advanced for and against membership were interpreted  differently depending on the historical and geographical context from which

they were viewed. To demonstrate  the nature and significance of  this point, we turn first to the principal issues that were raised during the campaign. We then  look at how those  issues were viewed  at two  different  scales: the  state and  the  local.  Examining the  problem  at two scales  is  important  because  both  are  foci  of political identification that influence, in different  ways,  people's  perceptions  of  the  world around them.
sections.Issues and Attitudes in the Nordic Refe: The campaign on EU membership dominated political life in Norway,  Sweden, and Finland for many months (see generally Pesonen  1994; Center  for European  Policy Studies 1994). In Finland  and  Sweden,  coalitions  favoring  EU membership  were  much  better  funded  than their opponents (Dahle 1994).  Moreover, most prominent politicians and business leaders came out in favor of E U   membership. In Norway,  by contrast, the 'no' coalition was  comparatively  well  funded  and  some  important public figures came out against E U  membership.  Consequently,  the  Norwegian debate tended  to be more even-handed.
sections.The 'Yes ' Campaign:
Throughout  Norway,  Sweden,  and  Finland, those  favoring  EU  membership  focused  on three key issues during the campaign: access to EU markets,  enhanced  political  influence  in Europe,  and  the  importance  of  the  EU  as  a framework  for  ensuring  peace  and  security. Turning to  the  first  issue, Norway,  Sweden, and Finland export 64% of their goods to the EU (Waller 1994, 12), and access to EU markets  therefore  looms  large  in  the  European north. Easy access to EU markets is especially important for Finland and Sweden, which have suffered through  a serious recession in recent years and face high unemployment rates. Norway's economy has fared much better  because of  its  reliance  on  exports  that  are  always  in demand  (oil  and  gas).  Nevertheless,  even  in Norway those who cast a  'yes' vote cited access to EU markets as the second most important  reason  for  voting  the  way  that  they  did (Dagbaldet 1994).

The second issue in the campaign-political influence-is important  in  the  Nordic  countries  because  Norway,  Sweden,  and  Finland became subject to most European Community (EC)  directives  and  regulations  without  any direct  input  into  the  policy-making  process when  they  joined  the  European  Economic Area  (EEA) (see generally Wallace 1992).  The decision to join the EEA actually followed the decision of  the governments of Norway, Sweden, and Finland to apply for EC membership. Joining the EEA was seen as a step that would ease  the  transition  process  and  ensure  good trade relations with the  rest  of  Europe.  Once the  Nordic  countries  became  a  part  of  the EEA, however, the push for full EC (later EU) membership  intensified.  This  occurred because  Norway,  Sweden,  and  Finland  found themselves  in  an  economic  bloc  over  which they  had  little  control;  the  only  way  to  gain that  control  was  to  become  a  full  EC/EU member  (Strem  1992). This  point  was  frequently made by advocates of EU membership as  Norway,  Sweden, and  Finland  moved  toward the fall  1994  vote. Indeed, in the months leading up to the vote, increased participation in decision making and closer cooperation with the rest of Europe on issues of trade, environmental protection, and security were the most frequently  cited  reasons  for  joining  the  EU (Dagbaldet 1994).

The third focus of the campaign in favor of EU membership was the potential importance of the EU as a framework for promoting peace and security in Europe. Peace has been one of Sweden's  greatest foreign policy  concerns, with that  country's  Social  Democrats constructing  much  of  their  international  agenda around  peace  issues.  Peace  and  security  are also issues in Norway, where government leaders  have  repeatedly  expressed  concern  over NATO's  declining  importance.  For  Finland, peace and security were of paramount importance  as  that country moved to extricate itself from the Soviet shadow. Playing off these concerns, the 'yes' coalition argued  that  extending the  EU into  the  Nordic countries  would ensure that European problems would be dealt with in a nonviolent, cooperative manner.
sections.The 'No Campaign:
Those  campaigning  against  EU  membership in  Noway,  Sweden, and  Finland  focused  on three  principal  issues:  loss of  sovereignty, the decline of  rural  areas, and  the  economic cost of membership. The sovereignty issue loomed largest  of  all.  Opponents  of  greater  Nordic participation  in the  EU painted a  picture  of  a distant,  unresponsive bureaucracy in  Brussels dictating  rules  and  regulations  that  had  long been  within  the  purview  of  individual states (Raza 1994).  During  the campaign,  Anne Enger Lahnstein from Norway's Center Party even called  the  EU 'undemocratic' (Segaard 1994). Her concerns reflected a  belief that,  if Norway  joined  the  EU,  important  decisions

about the  country's economy would  be  made by  the council of  the EU, which is comprised of  officials  who  are  not  directly  elected  and who meet in private (Hansen 1994).  Moreover, many noted  that the country would have only 3 votes out of 90 on European Council matters that  do not  require  unanimity, including economic,  social,  and  environmental  directives and regulations that could greatly affect Norway's  fishing  and  timber  resources (Nationen 1994b).

Closely related  to  the  issue  of  sovereignty was  the  concern  advanced by  the  'no' campaign that EU membership would precipitate the  depopulation  of  the  rural  sector  and  the destruction  of  rural  culture.  Those  opposing EU membership argued that EU regional subsidies  are  targeted  for  such  matters  as  infrastructure renewal and job retraining;  they are therefore designed to help poor regions to develop and, more generally, to ease the process of  economic restructuring  (Almbs et al.  1994, 14).  Supporters  of  the  'no' campaign  noted that  peripheral  regions  might  benefit  financially from EU subsidies, but only at the price of a form of economic restructuring that would be  devastating to local  areas. They painted  a picture  of  massive  rural-to-urban  migration and  the  devastation  of  traditional  modes  of livelihood in the rural sector (Syverud  1994).

On the economic front, the ''no'' campaign argued  that  EU  membership  would  expose Nordic products to intense  competition  from other  EU Member  States (Nytt Fra Norge 1994). Attention  focused  particularly  on  the agricultural sector, where production  costs per acre are generally higher  in northern Europe than farther south. Opponents of EU  membership expressed great concern that the importation  of  cheap  agricultural products  into Norway,  Sweden, and  Finland  would  undermine the economies of the Nordic countries, as well as contribute to rural change as outlined above. In a  somewhat different vein, the 'no' campaign also argued that EU membership would not  bring  the  economic boon  that  the  'yes' forces were claiming because Norway, Sweden, and  Finland  would  have  to  give  more  to the EU in  the way  of  subsidies than  they  would receive in return (Nationen 1994a).  T o   substantiate the point,  they highlighted the comparatively large contribution to the EU that Denmark has made in recent years.

In  summary, proponents  and  opponents  of EU membership stressed different points during the campaigns. A s in  any campaign, exaggerated claims were made on both  sides. The point of  this  overview is  not to probe  the accuracy of the  statements  made, however; it is instead to shed light on why people voted the way  that they  did  and to consider what those votes suggest about ideas and attitudes in contemporary Europe. Toward that end, it is useful  to  consider  the  issues  raised  in  the  campaign  in  light  of  electoral  outcomes  at  the national and subnational levels.
sections.Mediating Factors at the National Level: Norway, Sweden, and Finland have distinctive political, economic,  social, and  cultural  attributes and, for many, these influenced how the arguments surrounding EU membership were understood  and interpreted. A brief  examination  of  the  situation  of  each  of  the  Nordic countries  that  voted  on  EU membership  can thus provide insight into the variable successes of  the  'yes' and  'no' campaigns in  northern Europe.
sections.Finland:
In many respects Finland's human  geography would seem to lend itself to the kinds of local and regional issues advanced by the 'no' campaign. Large segments of the population have long  enjoyed  considerable autonomy  because of  the  scattered character of settlement in the country and the modest pace of modernization (Msnnesland  1994). A relatively dispersed settlement  pattern  has  been  sustained  even  in modem times by  a need  for seasonal labor in peripheral locations and by the desire to niaintain  settlements  in  strategic  areas  along  the border with Russia. People cleared virgin land for farms as late as the  1950s, making parts of Finland  the most  recently  settled  agricultural frontier in Europe, and agriculture remains an important  source of  livelihood  for  many  (Johansen  1993).

As is  evident  from  Figure  4,  many in  Finland's agricultural and resource-extraction communities were concerned about the implications of  EU membership, but the impact of the local and regional arguments raised by the 'no' campaign was  outweighed by the strong

national desire to move away from Russia  and toward  Europe  (Westengen  1994). Finland's uneasy relationship with Russia has profoundly affected the country's politics, economics, and especially foreign policy in the post-Soviet era. Resentment  of  the  long period  of  Soviet hegemony  runs  deep;  with  the  collapse  of  the Soviet Union many in Finland have been anxious to distance themselves as much as possible from  Russia  (Sutela  1994). Moreover,  recent political  and  economic  upheavals  in  Russia have fueled a sense that Finland's best hope for the  future  is  to reorient  its political economy toward  the West.  For many  Finns,  then, the vote  on EU membership  represented  an  important symbolic moment in the country's history.  The  impact  of  this  way  of  thinking  is evident in Figure 3. Other than Helsinki,  the Finnish  provinces  that  lie  the  farthest  above the regression line-Lappi, Mikkeli, and Kymi-all border  on Russia. Many in eastern Finland  apparently  feared  that  rejecting  E U membership would consign their country to a 'twilight zone' between East and West.

Beyond  the  geopolitical  realm, Finland's economic position  favored the  arguments being advanced by  the  'yes' campaign. Finland does  not  have  as  strong  an  export-oriented economy as neighboring Sweden, but Finland is  the  fourth  greatest  pulp  exporter  in  the world,  and  exports  of  iron  and  steel,  ships, clothing,  and  footwear  are  important  as  well (Solsten and Meditz  1990). Moreover, Finland has suffered through  a serious recession in recent  years,  with  unemployment  figures running  as  high  as  18%. Against  this  backdrop, EU membership  offered  the  prospect  of  an expanded export market  and  an improvement in the general economic picture. That prospect was  not  strong enough  to  allay  all  concerns about  membership,  but  a  comment  by  Finland's Foreign Minister prior to the  vote summed up the sentiments of many. He stated that  he was  'skeptical of  the  EU, but  willing to  sacrifice  most  of  Finland's  agriculture  in exchange for membership and the hope of better prospects for the country as a whole' (Nationen 1994~). A majority of  the Foreign Minister's fellow citizens apparently agreed.
sections.Sweden:
By  most  conventional indicators  Sweden is in the best position to benefit economically from

EU membership. Sweden's economy is export oriented  and  the  country  has  much  to  gain from  expanding  its  trading  possibilities  with the rest  of  Europe  (Stalvant 1993). Moreover, Sweden has been in a deep recession in recent years that is unlikely to be overcome without an  expansion  of  external  trade.  Hence,  the macroeconomic picture  in  Sweden provided a significant impetus  to membership.  It was  arguably  strong  enough  to  blunt  some  of  the concerns about rural  change advanced by  the 'no' campaign.  Such  concerns  were  further blunted  by  the  very nature of  Sweden's economic  and  settlement  geography  (see  Mead 1981). Over the  centuries  Sweden's relatively flat,  traversable  terrain  has  facilitated the  development  of  efficient transportation  systems and  the  large-scale exploitation  of  resources. Easily accessible forest resources, for example, led to early mechanization of the timber industry, which in turn favored the development of large-scale operations. At the same time, Sweden's economic policies in recent decades have favored large-scale farming and a combination of  high technology and service  industries. Taken together, these developments have promoted comparatively  rapid urbanization in Sweden  and  a concomitant decline  in the country's  small-scale  farming  and  resourceextraction sectors.

Given  this  history, it is  not  surprising  that arguments  about  rural  change  and  hardships for  the  agricultural  sector  had  only  limited success in Sweden. As one Swedish farmer put it,  'the  EU  cannot  possible  do  any  greater harm  to  Swedish  agriculture  than  the  Social Democrats  already  have  done'  (Kvadsheim 1994, 6). With 80% of the population living in the  southern  third  of  Sweden  (Mannesland 1994), there  are  simply  not  enough  Swedes living in classic peripheral, resource-dependent communities  where arguments about rural change would be expected to hold sway. Even in the Swedish north, the sense of local particularism is blunted by a  comparatively  high level of  interregional  connectivity.  Since  the  rural economy has already been greatly transformed, the  debate  over  membership  focused  more heavily on macroeconomic considerations, and these favored the arguments being raised by the 'yes'  coalition.  Hence,  it  is  not  particularly surprising  that  the  majority  of  the  Swedish population voted in favor of EU membership.
sections.Norway:
Norway's long, fragmented coastline and rough inland terrain historically made communication  difficult  and  resulted  in  a  relatively high  degree  of  interregional  differentiationboth  among regions in the periphery  and between  those  regions  and  the  capital  (John 1984).  The depth of Norwegian regionalism is reflected in  the  linguistic geography  of Norway,  which  is  more  diverse  than  that  of  any other Nordic country. Although transport and communications  developments  have  brought the  regions of  Norway  closer together  in  the modern era, regionalism remains strong. Moreover, many of the peripheral areas of the country are simply too remote and inaccessible to  have  succumbed  to  rapid  modernization. Consequently,  urbanization  proceeded  more slowly in Norway than in neighboring Sweden, and resource extraction  communities  were more  successful in  resisting  the  trend  toward mechanization and outside control (Halvorsen 1993).

Given these geographical circumstances, it is not  surprising  that  the  rural  change  issues highlighted  by  the  'no' campaign received  a more sympathetic hearing in Norway than  in Sweden or Finland.  Regionalism is  strong  in Norway,  and  many  felt  that  joining the  EU would amount to a surrender of local identities to  an  abstract  bureaucratic  entity.  The  'no' vote in Norway was  made  all  the  more likely by the absence of a strong economic argument in  favor  of  membership, particularly as  compared with  Sweden and Finland. Membership would probably have helped Norway's fish exports, but little else. Moreover, North  Sea oil has  buffered  Norway  to  a  degree  from  the serious  economic  problems  that  have  beset Sweden and  Finland  in  recent  years.  Hence, the  'yes' campaign  could  not  make  a  strong argument  about  the  importance  of  membership for resolving existing economic problems. That left them with  the argument  that failing to join the  EU  would  isolate  Norway in Europe.  Yet  that  argument  ran  up  against  a strong sense of commitment to the concept of Norwegian sovereignty-a legacy of  centuries of outside domination of  Norway that did not end completely until  1905. In the face of that commitment,  the  'yes' campaign  simply was unable to counteract the forces pushing toward a  'no' vote  among  the  majority  of  Norwegians.
sections.Mediating Factors at the Local Level:
Beyond  national  differences  among  Finland, Sweden, and Norway, the remarkable continuity in  the internal  spatial character  of  the  EU membership vote across all three countries requires  explanation.  For  those  living  in  the more densely populated areas of Norway, Sweden,  and  Finland,  the  arguments  in  favor  of membership were apparently persuasive-persuasive enough  even to overcome projections that EU membership would have negative economic  consequences  for  the  larger  cities  of Finland,  Sweden,  and  Norway.  These  arguments  were  clearly less  effective in  the  rural periphery,  even when  combined with  projections  showing  the  rural  periphery  benefiting from  EU subsidies. The reasons behind  this outcome can be discerned from the preceding discussion.  The  urban areas  of  the  Nordic countries  are  dominated  by  those who  define their interests more in national terms and who therefore  were  more  easily  persuaded  by  the macroeconomic  and  political  influence  arguments  of  the  'yes'  campaign.  By contrast, those  living in  more  remote  rural  areas were more  likely to  be  swayed  by  the  prospect  of diminished local control and the restructuring of  the rural sector.

The negative reaction to EU membership in the  Nordic periphery  was  exacerbated  by  the relationship that currently exists between core and  periphery  in  Norway,  Sweden, and  Finland. The  psychological distance between those  in  the  capital  cities  of  the  European north and those in outlying areas is significant (John  1984). The extent  of  that  distance became  clear  during  the  campaign  over  EU membership.  It  manifested  itself  most  obviously in a general disuust of  statements emanating  from  Oslo,  Stockholm,  and  Helsinh about the benefits of EU membership. In particular, substate regionalism is associated with a  suspicion in  many  rural  areas  that  the  national  governments  of  Norway,  Sweden, and Finland would  use EU subsidies as  an excuse to  cut  state  subsidies (Dug ug Tid 1994a). In Norway  such  suspicions were  heightened  by decades of north-south polarization that can be traced  back  to  the  efforts  of  the  Norwegian government to develop the country's industrial potential  after World  War I1 by discouraging northerners  who  had  been  brought  to  the south  during  the  Nazi  period  from  returning

home  (Mmnesland  1994). As  a  result,  when the  Agricultural Minister  failed  to  come  forward with any information on the level of subsidies  that  Norwegian  farmers would  receive after the five-year adjustment period that Norway would have gone through had it joined the EU, those in the periphery worried  about betrayal (Nytt Fra Norge 1994). Regional antipathies were sufficiently  strong that they affected how  economic  predictions  were  understood and interpreted. For many, such antipathies led to  a  rejection  of  the  economic  benefit  argument that was being advanced by advocates of EU membership in the urbanized core.

Beyond concerns about the amount of  economic benefits rural areas might receive, many voters  were  concerned  about  the  form  those benefits  might  take  if  Norway,  Sweden,  and Finland  joined  the  EU.  In the  Nordic  countries,  particularly  Norway,  the  goal  of  state regional  subsidies  in  recent  decades has  been to sustain a decentralized settlement pattern by creating  jobs  and  production  possibilities  in rural districts (Jussila and Malinen  1993). Regional funding is  used  to compensate  for the extra  cost  of  producing  goods and  services in these regions, and selective support to firms is therefore  not uncommon. To many, the prospect  of  substituting this  approach  to  regional assistance for the  EU approach-even if  total subsidies were greater-was unacceptable (Almk et al.  1994). As  they saw it, restructuring would bring social and psychological costs that would far outweigh any theoretical shortterm economic gain.

It should be clear from the foregoing, then, that local concerns played an important role in the  campaign for  E U  membership.  They are certainly evident in the positions of particular counties  and provinces  in  Figure  3.  For  Finland, the province lying farthest below the regression line is Vassa,  a western province that is  not strongly tied to the urban core but that is  distant  from Russia  and  therefore  less concerned with Russian influence than its counterparts  farther  east. In  the  case  of  Sweden, the counties lying the farthest below the regression line  are  Jamtland, Blekinge,  and  Goteborg. Jamtland is the county  with perhaps the strongest  sense  of  local  particularism  in  the Swedish  north-a consequence  of  close  historical  ties  with  adjacaent  parts  of  Norway. The other two counties are less distinct, but in each  case  the  inhabitants  expressed  concerns over the impact of EU membership  on sensitive  local industries. As  for Norway, the counties  that  lie  the  farthest  below  the  regression line are either well north of  Trondheim (Troms,  Nordland),  in  the  remote  area  between Bergen and Trondheim (Sogn og Fjordane,  Mme og  Romsdal), or  in  the  isolated southeast (Rogaland).  There is one Norwegian county well  below  the  regression  line  that  is more  urbanized-the county  of  Hordaland where  Bergen is located-but there  are longstanding  divisions  between  the  Bergen  area and the Norwegian core. Hordaland is thus in a very different  position  from  the Norwegian counties that lie the farthest above the regression line-Akershus, Buskerud, Oppland, and Hedmark-which are in a ring around Oslo.
sections.Implications and Conclusion:
The vote on EU  membership in Norway, Sweden, and Finland revealed a significant degree of  polarization  between  the  populous  south and the rural north. To understand that polarization it is  important  to look beyond  the  expected financial impacts of EU  membership on different  regions.  The interpretation  of  such impacts is  mediated  by  other issues and  concerns, which themselves are rooted  in the historical  and  geographical contexts from  which they are viewed. The history and geography of states and local areas help to explain not only the reasons for a rejection of EU membership in  the  Nordic  periphery,  but  also  why  that rejection  was  forceful  enough  in  one  caseNorway-to overcome  the  economic  arguments that were being advanced in support of membership.

The  significance  of  analyzing  the  Nordic vote  on membership  goes beyond what it can tell us about political and social issues in Norway,  Sweden, and  Finland,  however. The regional and local issues that emerged during the campaign  and  that  played  such  a  significant role  in the vote are signals of wider issues the EU faces in the years ahead. Sweden and Finland are now part of the EU, but that does not erase the  fact that  a  substantial percentage  of their  populations  voted  against  membership. The Swedish Prime Minister  Ingvar Carlsson recognized this when, the night  after the  referendum,  he  expressed  sadness  that  'fortyseven percent of  the Swedish people had lost' (Dag o g Tid 1994b). Those  47%  still  live  in

Sweden, and there  is  no indication  that  they have  changed their  views.  Indeed,  opposition to EU membership seems to have grown. In a post-referendum  opinion  poll  conducted  in Sweden  between  January 10  and 14,  1995, 55% of the population claimed that they would vote against EU membership if  given another opportunity (Fyllinngsnes 1995).  There are indications that  opposition  to  EU membership has grown in Finland as well, and the majority of  Norwegians remain opposed to joining the EU (Nytt Fra Norge 1995). Embedded  in  the Nordic vote over EU membership, then,  is  a great  challenge  for  the  Union  in  the  years ahead. That challenge is to move the integration  process  forward in  a  way  that  does  not exacerbate the  interregional  tensions  that  are so vividly  displayed in  the map of  the Nordic vote. If that is to occur, it is imperative that the guiding  vision  for  the  EU  not  be  one  that posits  the  Union  as  a  centralized  superstate sitting astride the European continent. Instead, the EU must work to facilitate  cooperation and interaction in ways  that acknowledge regional differences and  that  respect  local  social  and cultural practices.

records.title: LANDSCAPES OF CULTIVATION IN MESOAMERICA ON THE EVE OF THE CONQUEST
records.abstract: Pre-Columbian Amerindian agriculturalists developed technologies and management practices with which to crop a wide range of ecological conditions, giving rise to a multiplicity of cultivated landscapes. This variety was particularly evident in Mesoamerica, where agricultural practices ranged from swiddening to multicropped, hydraulically transformed wetlands. Here we explore these indigenous cultivated landscapes as they existed about the time of the Columbian Encounter. We illustrate them through the examination of three transects approximating the courses of the initial Spanish entradas through this diverse region: the first extends from the Gulf coast to central Mexico; the second traverses the Yucatan peninsula from north to south; and the third climbs into highland Guatemala from the Pacific coastal plain. Second, we broadly sketch the major changes that took place in these landscapes during the first phase of Spanish domination and some of the forces that shaped these changes. Three processes were especially significant: the Amerindian depopulation, the introduction of exotic biota and technologies, and the reordering of land and the rural economy. Ultimately, however, reconfigured hybrid landscapes resulted that reflected the union of cultures. Last, we argue that the scale of environmental transformation of Amerindian agriculture has not always been fully appreciated, the scale of environmental degradation associated with Spanish introductions has been overstated at times, and the contrasting ideologies of nature between the two cultures has been over-simplified.

sections.Landscapes of Cultivation in Mesoamerica:
Thomas M. Whitmore* and B. L . Turner II**

*Department of Geography,  University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, NC 27599, e-mail trnwhitmo@uncvxl  .oit.unc.edu

**Graduate School of Geography, George Perkins Marsh Institute, Clark University, Worcester,  MA 01610,

Fax 508193-7780, e-mail bTurner@uax.clark.edu, omnet B.Turner

Abstract.  Pre-Columbian Amerindian  agriculturalists developed technologies and management  practices  with  which  to  crop  a  wide range of ecological conditions, giving rise to a multiplicity of cultivated landscapes. This variety was  particularly evident  in Mesoamerica, where agricultural practices ranged  from swiddening to multicropped, hydraulically transformed wetlands. Here we explore these indigenous cultivated  landscapes as  they  existed about the time of the Columbian Encounter.  We illustrate them through the examination of three transects  approximating  the courses of the initial Spanish entradas through this diverse region:  the first extends from the Gulf  coast to central Mexico;  the second traverses  the  Yucatan  peninsula from  north to south;  and the third climbs into  highland Guatemala from the Pacific coastal plain.

Second, we broadly sketch the major changes that  took place in these  landscapes during the first  phase of  Spanish domination and  some  of  the  forces  that  shaped  these changes. Three  processes were  especially significant: the Amerindian depopulation, the introduction of exotic biota and technologies, and the reordering of land and the rural economy.  Ultimately,  however,  reconfigured  'hybrid'  landscapes  resulted  that  reflected  the union of cultures.

last, we argue that the scale of environmental  transformation  of  Amerindian  agriculture has  not  always  been  fully  appreciated,  the scale of environmental degradation associated with Spanish introductions has been overstated at times,  and the contrasting ideologies of nature between the two cultures has been over-

simplified.

Key Words: Amerindian agriculture, Mesoamerica, sixteenth century, Columbian Encounter.

HE  Columbian  Encounter  opened  the world  to  the  treasures  of  Amerindian plant  domestication, the impacts  of which would be global in reach and range far beyond agriculture per se.  The potato, for example,  increased the caloric base of  northern Europe, facilitating  its exponential  population growth after 1750, while maize, manioc, sweet potato, and  peanut became dietary mainstays for  much of  the  rest of  the world  (Hamilton 1976,856-57,860). Amerindian cotton was literally the fabric of the industrialization of textiles (Sauer 1976, 818), and tobacco claims the dubious distinction of 'vice of choice'  for much of the world.

Less  well  known is that  these  and  other Amerindian domesticates of global significance (e.g., avocado, bean, cacao, chile, papaya, squash,  and  tomato)  coevolved with  equally impressive systems of cultivation. Long before the Columbian Encounter, Amerindian agriculturalists had developed technologies and management practices with which  to crop a wide range of  environments  and ecological conditions,  giving rise to a variety of  landscapes of cultivation. This variety was particularly evident

in Mesoamerica, where advanced material culture and state organization extended from the southern border of the Bajio in  Central Mexico southeastward to  Guatemala,  including  parts of Belize, Honduras, Nicaragua, and Costa Rica (Fig. 1). Some of these cultivated  landscapes consisted  of  intermingled  or  patchwork-like microsystems, fine-tuned to small-scale  environmental variations, while others were dominated  by  zonal  patterns  keyed to  the  broad environmental zones created by elevation, aspect, and slope.

The conquistadores marveled at these  landscapes, even  a s they  sowed  the  seeds  of change. A new rendering of the land emerged at  a  pace only slightly slower than that of the conquest itself. Within  fifty years of Columbus's  initial  landfall,  Spanish  hegemony over Middle America (the Caribbean, Mexico, and Central America) was complete and, in  the course of the sixteenth century,  most of the cultivated  landscapes  of  Mesoamerica  had been forever altered from their former condition.  This  alteration  followed  not  only  from changes in control of  the  land,  but from the introduction of exotic biota, technologies, and management practices as well.

The cultivated  landscapes of the preconquest Amerindians and the implications of their transformation, especially  in  Mesoamerica, have  been  the  subject  of  rather  polarized views,  many of which  have  been empirically uninformed  (see  Denevan,  this  volume  and Doolittle, this volume). Amerindian agriculture has not  always been fully appreciated, the scale of environmental  degradation associated with Spanish transformation of this agriculture has been overstated at  times, and the contrasting ideologies of nature between the two cultures has been oversimplified.

Here we explore the  indigenous cultivated landscapes that were witnessed by the Spanish adventurers as they existed about the time of the Columbian Encounter. Our primary objective  i s  to  illustrate  the  variety  of  these  landscapes through the examination of three transects  traversing  different  environmental  and sociopolitical  terrain. Each  transect  approximates the course of one of the initial Spanish entradas through this diverse region: the 'Cortes  transect'  extends  to central  Mexico from  the Gulf  coast,  the  'Montejo  transect' traverses the Yucathn peninsula from north to south, and the 'Alvarado transect' climbs into highland  Guatemala from  the  Pacific  coastal plain  (Fig. 1). Second,  we  broadly sketch the major changes that took  place in these  landscapes during the first phase of Spanish domination  and  some  of  the  forces  that  shaped these changes. Our intent is neither to mythologize the accomplishments  of the Amerindians nor to  vilify  the conquerors, but  to  illustrate the magnitude  and  breadth  of  the  changes  that took  place  in  the  cultivated landscapes  of Mesoamerica a s   a result of the Columbian  Encounter.
sections.The Cortes Transect:
Cortes and his small band probably first saw the snowcapped summit of Orizaba (5,639 m) from ship's  deck in the vicinity of modern Veracruz, Mexico.  From that vantage point, they were observing the eastern flanks of the Aztec empire, a domain that stretched east-west  from the  Gulf  of  Mexico to the Pacific Ocean and north-south from the  Bajio to the  Isthmus of Tehuantepec (Figs. 1, 2). More properly identified with the 'Triple Alliance' of the city states of  Tenochtitlhn,  Texcoco,  and  Tacuba  in the Basin of Mexico (Gibson 1964, 17), the empire has taken its popular name from the dominant Mexica (Tenochtitlhn)  and their mythical homeland, Aztlan. The Alliance commanded a political and  economic realm unparalleled in Mesoamerican  history,  complete  with  a  supreme  ruler,  professional  armies  and  merchants, and a system of taxation and marketing that siphoned the wealth of the empire into its lacustrine heart. Population estimates for Central  Mexico,  roughly  corresponding with  the empire,  range  from <I0 million->50 million (Denevan 1976, 77-84;  1992).

This  transect  parallels the Cortes route and crosses virtually every major climatic and agroecological zone in Mesoamerica: the hot and  humid  tierra  caliente  of  the  Gulf  Coast Plains, the tierra templada (temperate land) of the  coastal  piedmont  and  the  basins  on  the altiplano or  Mesa  Central,  and  the  upper reaches of the sierras that separate the basins from  one  another  (Figs. 2, 3). sections.Gulf Coastal Plain and Piedmont:
The area of the Spaniards landfall  was inhabited by  the Totonac who mastered the seasonal rhythm  and  environmental  variation of  the coastal plain and  piedmont to produce crops for  local  subsistence  a s   well  as  tribute,  and possible  commerce,  with  the  Aztec  empire (Barlow 1949;  Hassig  1985,114,115;  Stark 1990, 269). The coastal plains and hills  offered a complex mosaic of microenvironmental opportunities  and constraints for agriculture.  The cultivated landscapes encountered in this complex natural terrain consisted of a patchwork of different cultivation types  interspersed with forests and  scrub  land.  It is even  likely that  the forests were managed and may have sheltered orchards. The Totonac orchestrated their yearround cultivation with the spatial and temporal variations in soil-water conditions,  working  the well-drained  lands  during  the  rainy  season, and the inundated lands in the dry season (Siemens  1988,  1992; Wilkerson  1983,  58).  The landscape  configured  by  these  practices  led Spaniards  to  describe  the  lowlands  around Zempoala as  'a  garden with luxuriant vegetation'  (Diaz del Castillo 1956,  87).

The mainstay of Totonac (and Mesoamerican agriculture generally) was rainfed  cultivation or temporal.  In  the Gulf Coast area,  such cultivation dominated the well-drained,  usually sloping,  terrain  and  incorporated  terraces  with rock-walled,  earthen,  and probably also earth and rnaguey (rnetepantli) embankments (Rojas

Rabiela 1988,  118;  Sluyter  1990,  20-37, 51-53; Wilkerson 1983,  64,  76).

Perhaps as  important,  however, were a variety of wetland adaptations that allowed cultivation during the  marked dry season  (Siemens 1983,  87; 1990,  117;  Vivio  Escoto  1964,  212; West 1964b,58). I n  some instances, the margins of wetlands and levees were cultivated as water receded in the dry season, facilitated by  the use of small drainage ditches. In  others,  more elaborate  networks of canals were  used to create field  systems  in  wetlands proper. Siemens (1982, 1983) believes that these more elaborate networks may also have functioned in a floodrecessional  manner.  Contemporary  flood-recessional  cultivation  in  the  Gulf  Coast  (and elsewhere) does not employ the elaborate and major canal networks found in the relics of the ancient systems. Thus we suspect that the cultivation  associated with wetlands  proper  may have  functioned  through  most  of  the  year rather than only during recession of the floods.

Relics  of  walls and embankments on  drylands and fields and canals in wetlands are abundant in the Gulf  Coast area,  although dating their continued  use  up to the  eve  of  conquest  is difficult  to  establish  (Sluyter  1990;  Siemens 1982,  1983). Indeed,  Siemens et al.  (1988,  107) found evidence  that at  least one wetland system in Veracruz was probably abandoned 500700  years  before  the  Columbian  Encounter. Further southeast,  however,  Spanish accounts describe conditions that imply wetland cultivation in the sixteenth  century (Pohl 1985). This evidence, the relatively large populations along portions of the Gulf Coast (Lopez de Gomara 1964,  91; Stark 1978, 214-19; Wilkerson  1983, 55),  and the amount of tribute extracted by the

Aztec  from the area (Barlow 1949),  lead us to suspect that  many of the relic agricultural  features  found throughout  the Gulf  Coast zone may have been operating  at the time of Spanish contact. These issues require further investigation.  In addition,  Wilkerson (1983,  81)  speculates that  runoff and other types  of  irrigation were used in the area.

It can  also  be presumed that two types of orchard-gardens  were found in the area:  the ubiquitous  solar  or  calmil, carefully  tended household gardens providing vegetables, fruits, condiments, medicinals,  and fiber products  (Siemens 1983,  97);  and orchards,  especially  of  cacao  and  various  fruits  grown  for commercial  purposes  and  tribute  (Bergmann 1969,  86,  88;  Millon 1955,  705;  Schmidt 1977, 57; Stark  1974,  204,  210; 1978,  215).  Orchard species  may  have  been  cultivated as  special plots (see Montejo Transect), and/or they may have been integrated within managed forests as  described by Alcorn  (1984) for the modern Huastec.

Field management  practices were probably similar to those used in  the altiplano,  including camellones (ridged or  furrowed soil)  and  possibly  transplanting  from seedbeds (almAcigos  or tlalacalli) Schmidt 1977,  57).  While  maize  dominated,  ethnohistorical  and ethnographic analogs suggest that fields were  intercropped with beans,  squash, cotton,  maguey  (Agave spp.),  tuna  (Opuntia montones (mounded soil) or (Rojas  Rabiela  1988, 33, 74-75, 82; spp.)  or  root  crops  (Rojas  Rabiela 1988,  93; Sluyter 1990,56,62;  Stark 1974,205;  1978,216).
sections.Sierra Madre Oriental:
The eastern versant of the Sierra Madre Oriental presented a formidable escarpment separating the Gulf  Coastal Plains and Piedmont from the mineral wealth and cooler climates on the  altiplano.  Its  ascent  took  the  Spaniards from the tierra caliente to the tierra templada and,  ultimately the tierra fria beyond the 20003000 m saddle of the range (Fig. 2). The slope i s steep  and rugged throughout,  dissected by the deep,  narrow canyons of the Gulf-bound streams  (West  1964b,  52-53). Much  of  the mountain slope receives large amounts of orographically-induced rainfall (2000 mm3000 mm annually), giving rise to cloud forests near the crest (Vivio Escoto 1964, 201).

This  escarpment  was  an  agricultural transi- tion zone perhaps shaped less by agroecological  conditions  than  by  declining  population pressures  between  the  piedmont  and  the upper slopes. The  piedmont apparently was a landscape of terraces,  and Siemens (1990, 145) quotes  a nineteenth-century German resident who described  'terraces .  . . on every slope.' As slopes grew steeper, however, the intensity of cultivation diminished to a shifting type,  although  fog  moisture  in  the  dry  season  supported two maize  crops  annually  in a  single field in some locations (Rojas Rabiela 1988, 78). Gutierrez  Ruvalcaba  (forthcoming)  notes  sixteenth-century  cultivation  frequencies  in  the Sierra Madre Oriental of 1  :8-1 :I0 (i.e, one year of cultivation and eight-ten  years of fallow for each milpa plot). Another source notes shorter cycle periods (1 :41:5) for the same region (the Colonial-era province of Meztitlan on the present-day Hildago-Veracruz border [Rojas Rabiela 1988,621).'  Local inhabitants  also may have employed a vertical  zonation strategy,  cultivating plots at different elevations to reduce risk and augment production (Gutierrez Ruvalcaba forthcoming;  Siemens 1990,144).
sections.Mesa Central:
Crossing the  Sierra,  the  Spaniards  entered the great semiarid  volcanic  basins and  ranges of the Mesa Central,  encountering landscapes that  they  found  more familiar  and  appealing than  those  of  the  tierra  caliente  (Figs.  2, 3). Here,  a  large Amerindian  population was  arranged in settlement hierarchies dominated by city-states  whose hinterlands  spread across basin  floors  and  up the  surrounding  slopes. Agriculture  formed  the  basis  of  subsistence and commerce among city-states and was central to the tribute extracted by the Aztec.

The Mesa Central is composed of broad, flatfloored  basins  ringed  by  imposing volcanoes and broad slopes (West 1964b, 42,47),  many of which offered fertile soils for agriculture (Stevens  1964,  195-296; West 1964b, 47).  Most of this  area  is  above  1800  m  (Figs.  2,  3).  Here, Mesoamerican crop production was limited by recurrent frosts and low levels of precipitation (Sanders et al. 1979, 230) (mean annual precipitation ranges from 250 mm-1000  m) combined with high annual variability (Vivi6 Escoto 1964, 199). Paradoxically, poor interior drainage gave rise to various wetlands on the basin floors.

While  each  basin  differed  according  to  its

features and occupation,  commonality of  use gave  rise  to  a  characteristic  pattern of  cultivated landscapes? The upper sierras remained in forest,  a source  of wood and  regulator  of water.  Below the forest  line,  rainfed terraced and semiterraced cultivation dominated. Various forms of  floodwater  irrigation were  pursued  within  ephemeral  water courses  and along  lands  adjacent  to  them,  including the edges  of  the  basins'  floors  into  which  the drainages emptied. On the basin floor proper, where  poor  drainage  was  common,  various kinds of wetland cultivation were  adapted to the perihumid conditions.

Small clusters of villages  and hamlets were scattered  across  the  landscape.  Their  intensively cultivated gardens produced food crops, condiments,  ornaments,  and medicinal plants (Evans  1990, 117, 126; Palerm  1955; Rojas Rabiela 1988, 92-93; forthcoming). Specialized orchards of avocado, nopal de grana (the cacti hosting the cochineal insect used for red dye, Opuntina  spp.), maguey  (agave  or  century plant,  Agave  spp.), tejocote  (Mexican  hawthorn  , Crataegus mexicana),  capulin  (capu  I  in cherry,  Prunus capuli) and other fruits  occupied favored  niches  (Rojas  Rabiela 1988,  93: forthcoming).

Rainfed  cultivation  dominated  spatially,  although its forms were adapted to the varying terrain.3  Upper  and  lower  slopes  were  embraced by flights  of  sloping metepanth (semiterraces) which  preserved soil  and  soil  moisture  (Donkin  1979,  131; Patrick  1985; Rojas Rabiela  1988: 118-19; Sanders 1981,192). More than a simple slope adjustment, metepantli incorporated food and fiber production into the terrace by using maguey or nopal  cacti as berm anchors  (Evans  1990,  125; Patrick  1985,  542; Wilken 1979). Maize,  beans, and squash were the mainstays of slope cultivation, but Mesoamerican cultivators grew a large variety of other cultigens, including amaranth (Amaranthus annuus),  chia  (Salvia hispanica), tomato,  beans, squash, and chiles.

Perhaps the most common irrigation works were  weirs or check  dams  that  captured silt and water within intermittent drainages, or that spread water onto adjacent lands for floodwater  irrigation  (Donkin  1979,  42, 44; Garcia  Cook  1985; Parsons 1971,  220; Rojas Rabiela  1988,  120; 1985,  202; forthcoming; Sanders et al.  1979,  222-81; Wolf and Palerm

1955,  266).  Perhaps  it  was  these  features  in Cholula that  Cortes  described  in 1520:  'the farmlands are very fertile and they have much land  and  the greater  part  is  irrigated'  (1945, 146). In  some  cases,  this  technique  was  extended to valley  floors,  which  were straddled by broad terraces that could be fed by channel runoff water  (Donkin 1979,  44; Rojas  Rabiela 1988,  120;  Sanders et al.  1979,  253;  Wolf  and Palerm 1955).

Small dams and diversion weirs coupled with canals  provided  permanent  irrigation  water from springs or permanent streams in selected locations  (Armillas  et al.  1956;  Doolittle 1990, 115;  Millon  1957;  Rojas Rabiela  1985,198;  1988, 121;  Sanders et al. 1979,260-62).  Thousands of small  contour  bench terraces  in the  Basin of Mexico are thought to have been irrigated in this way (Donkin 1979, 44;  Sanders et al. 1979, 251-52). I n some  cases,  lengthy  canals,  complete with aqueducts that spanned intervening barrancas (gullies), attest to the use of permanent  irrigation  (Doolittle  1990,  127; Donkin 1979, 42, 44; Parsons  1971, 220; Wolf  and Palerm 1955,  266). At  least one instance of the canalization  and  relocation  of  the  flow  of  a large stream for irrigation is known in  the Basin of Mexico (Doolittle 1990,  115-20). While terracing was  located throughout the Mesa Central,  i t s  association with elaborate  irrigation infrastructures  has  only been well documented for the Basin of Mexico.

Many of  the seasonal and  permanent wetlands and shallow lakes in the interior of the valleys of Tlaxcala, Mexico, and perhaps Puebla were transformed into a network of canals and planting  surfaces  (wetland  fields) on which year-round cultivation could be practiced (Parsons 1971,220;  Rojas Rabiela  1985,208;  Sanders 1972,  131-32; Sanders et al.  1979,  275;  Wilken 1969,1987). In some cases, hierarchial systems of canals channeled excessive water to the interior,  creating drained fields along the periphery of lakes or wetlands.

The latter form of wetland cultivation reached  its  zenith  among the  chinampas,  or 'floating gardens,'  of the Basin of Mexico, occupying thousands of hectares of the southern freshwater lakes  of  Chalco  and  Xochimilco (Armillas  1971,  653; Sanders  et  al.  1979,  275; West and Armillas 1952,171) (Fig. 2). The actual chinampa was a narrow artificial island (a raised field),  anchored by trees along i t s edges,  and

constructed from lake muck and biotic materials dredged from the shallow lakes themselves (Wilken 1985, 42). The effect was  to raise the planting  surface  relative  to the water  in the bordering canals,  providing subsurface  irrigation at  all  times,  but also  facilitating  surface regularly cleaned,  and  the  aquatic  muck was  used  to fertilize  the fields  (Armillas  1971,  653;  Palerm 1973;  West  and  Armillas  1952,  171;  Wilken irrigation  if  needed.  Canals  were 1985, 42) .4

By  the  sixteenth  century,  chinampas  were part of a state-designed and controlled hydraulic system that included dikes and sluice gates controlling water level and quality in  the southern  parts  of  the  lacustrine  network  (Palerm 1973).  Not  only  did  dikes  protect  the  two southern  lakes  from  brackish  Lake Texcoco, but an adjacent section of that lake was diked as  well,  making chinampa agriculture possible 2) (Calneck 1972;  Parsons 1976, 253;  Sanders et on  the  islands  of  the  Aztec  capital  (Fig. al. 1979, 154).

Individually and as  a system, chinampas  required significant  labor input to construct and maintain, but  they combined very high productivity  with  risk-reduction  (Armillas  1971,  660; Coe 1964,98;  Moriarty1968,473;  Parsons  1976, 244-46;  Sanders 1972,133;  Sanders et al. 1979, 390).  Irrigation reduced problems of drought, and the presence of water mitigated frost hazard.  Chinampas were probably doublecropped,  using different cultigens and transplantation from seedbeds (Rojas Rabiela 1985, 165;  1988,  79-80). Few  cultivation  systems  in the world could match their sustained level of productivity.
sections.The Montejo Transect:
The Yucatan Peninsula, home to the lowland Maya, provided a radically different experience for the Spaniards (Figs. 1,4).  As in  the Mexican case,  the northern Yucatan was well peopled, and the Maya were both skilled cultivators and active  in  long-distance  trade  (Andrews  1983; Chamberlain 1948;  Farriss 1984). Nevertheless, by such  measures as  the number and spatial domain of city-states, and level of sociopolitical organization and affluence (as measured by the scale and quality of monumental architecture),  the  condition  of  the  lowland  Maya  in

Yucatan at the time of contact was not on par of years  earlier  (Chase  and  Rice with that  of  their  Classic  Period ancestors some  500-700 1985;  Jones 1989;  Turner 1983a, b).

The  Yucatan  is  composed  of two environmental domains (Figs. 4,  5) over which a common set  of  cropping  practices were  differentially  employed  in  association  with  differing intensities  of  occupation. The  peninsula  is  a large limestone shelf with extreme karst conditions,  dominated by a tropical wet-dry climate (tierra caliente) in  which rainfall increases considerably from the northwest to the southeast (Finch 1965; Wilhelmy 1981; Wilson 1980). The northern periphery of the peninsula is a relatively  flat, lowly  elevated  plain, but  starting with the Puuc Hills (Figs. 3, 4),  a rolling hill or upland area extends southward into the P6ten (Guatemala).  Everywhere in  the  north, extremely shallow and rocky soils, an absence of surface  water,  and  a  pronounced  dry  season impeded agriculture.

At the time of the Columbian Encounter, the northern low plains were moderately to heavily occupied.  In  contrast, the central and southern uplands, an area that was once the heart of the Classic Maya civilization (Culbert 1973;  Turner 1990a),  were  very sparsely settled in  1492 (Jones 1989;  Means  1917;  Scholes  and  Roys 1968;  Turner 1990a,  b).
sections.Northern and Coastal Plains:
Spaniards officially discovered the  Yucatan in 1517  (Chamberlain  1948,  61-64; Clendinnen 1987,  17-18; Means 1917) only to find that at least two Spaniards, survivors  of a shipwreck, were present among the Maya. One of these men refused to return to his former comrades, but led the  Maya  in subsequent  military encounters  against them (Chamberlain 1948,  6164; Means 1917). The Spaniards bypassed the Yucatan for Mexico, so that the initial conquest awaited 1527,  while subjugation of the peninsula followed  some twenty years later  (Farriss 1984,  12).  Led  by  Francisco  de  Montejo (the Elder), the first entrada began on the northeastern coast of the peninsula and marched inland. The transect that we follow here roughly corresponds to the north-south course of Montejo's  route,  with some liberties taken to include the interior  uplands which Montejo's

The  littoral  of  northern  Yucatdn  was extremely  important economically to the Maya, who  had  converted  coastal  wetlands  (the cienaga) into the center of Mesoamerican salt production  and  trade. Salt  was apparently transported by canoe along the coasts to Mexico and Central America (Andrews 1983). The settlements controlling salt  production lay inland,  spread  throughout  the  northern  plains, as was  most of the Maya population. Here the Spaniards encountered large numbers  of Maya, arranged in small-sized polities consisting of sizable villages  and  well-tended  landscapes.

These villages and their lands had a common morphology. A small  plaza and public monument,  usually a small  pyramid or some  other shrine,  marked the  center of  a  village,  from which homesteads, each demarcated by stone walls enclosing orchard-gardens, radiated outward  (the  elite  lived  closest  to  the  center) (Clendinnen 1987; G6mez-Pompa et al. 1987). Homesteads gave way to open- or outfields in various stages of fallow, which in  turn gave way to forest, much of which may have been managed.  Here, culling and related activities may have supported forms of agroforestry (pet kot) (C6mez-Pompa et  al. 1987). This  spatial  arrangement was  repeated across the  northern plains, with the apparent exception of savanna areas.

Spanish  documents  refer  to  both  "plantations" and  "orchard-gardens'' in  the area, using  the  former  designation  frequently  for elite-owned  "cacao"  stands  situated  on  the edges  of  Maya towns  (Tozzer 1941,  194-95; Scholes  and  Roys 1968,  171-72).5 The  spatial arrangement and concentration of these plots may  have  given  the  impression  of  extensive orchards. Maya horticultural practices  were not well documented by the Spaniards, other than reports that the elite used slaves and servants to  care  for  their  orchards,  and  evidence  of monocropping  or  plantation-like  labor  organization  is  lacking  (Scholes  and  Roys 1968, 1  71 -72) .

Orchard-gardens played an  important  role among the Maya and the Amerindians of tierra caliente in  general (Killion forthcoming). Much of the Maya  food supply was grown in orchardgardens, a s   testified  by their spatial extent and the  quantity  of  remains o f orchard-gardens species taken from excavations of  Maya middens (Turner  and  Miksicek 1984). Indeed, Comez-porn pa and colleagues (1987) argue that the unusual distribution of useful species currently found within ancient walled plots throughout  Yucatdn  are  remnants of  ancient orchard-gardens  (see  also  Folan  et  al. 1979). Individual  trees  and  groves  were  apparently privately  owned  and  inherited  (Millon 1955, 700; Scholes and Roys 1968, 171-72).

Landa referred to the use of agaves,  chiles, beans,  and  cotton  in house gardens  (Tozzer 1941, 194-95). Maya orchard-gardens included a large  variety of native  trees, shrubs, and other species adapted to the wet-dry tropical climate of the plains (Clendinnen 1987,141; Chamberlain 1968, 52; Scholes and Roys 1968, 171-72, 328; Tozzer 1941,  179,  230). These  included agave  and cotton,  avocado, nance (Brysonima crassifolia ) , a  I Is  p  i ce ( f imen  ta dioica)  , guava (fsidium  guajava), sapodilla (Manilkara  zapote), and mamey zapote (Calocarpum  mammosum).

The prevalence of orchard-gardens notwithstanding, the staple crop of the northern Maya at  the  time of  the  Columbian  Encounter was maize. Considerable documentation by earlier

I

chroniclers  indicates that  the  bulk  of  it was produced  in  fields  distant  from  the  walled homesteads  and  orchard-gardens,  although walls  may  have  been  present  in these  "outfields" (walls  without occupation structures are common; see Freidel and Leventhal 1975). The cultivation  practices in these  "outfields" are uncertain,  a s   is the intensity of cultivation.  In the mid-I500s, Landa noted that the Maya prepared the land from January  to April (in  the dry season), planted with a digging stick,  and cultivated  by  "collect[ingl  together  refuse  and burn[ing]  it in  order to sow''  (indicating shifting cultivation?);  but  they  also  had  "improved" lands and "kept the land well cleared and free from  weeds"  (indicating  nonshifting  cultivation?)  (Tozzer 1941,62,64,97; Landa 1937,38).

Because of the  level of  population and the well-defined  boundaries of villages and provinces in the north, we suspect that a short-fallow rotational system was  used in which plot preparation focused on burning collected and dried vegetation in order to provide essential phosphorus for the soil before the rains began in April.  Plots were first  sowed to  maize and subsequently intercropped with squash and nitrogen  fixing  beam6  Interestingly, the  region was known for its cotton and hemp production at the time of conquest, although virtually  no descriptions of  its  cultivation  exist.  Weeding dominated the growing season labor until the fall harvest.

The outfields of each village  were apparently separated  from  those  of  the  next  by  forest which,  in addition to possible agroforestry activities, formed a reserve for wood fuel, hunting,  and  tame  animals.  Deer were,  perhaps, the  most important of the semitame animals, apparently controlled from birth through biological imprinting, and later herded from the village to feed  in the forest (Means 1917,  30; Toner 1941, 127).
sections.The Uplands:
Compared to the northern plains, the rolling karst hills of  the central peninsular area must have been a disappointment and aggravation to  the  Spaniards,  for here  the  population thinned dramatically  (Means 1917; Scholes and Roys  1968,  333),  and the  tropical  forest  provided a frontier  refuge for Maya fleeing Spanish  control.  The  distinctive  cultivated  landscape of the northern plain was replaced in  the uplands by extensive swidden systems,  possi- bly  similar  to  those  described  by  ethnographers in the  nineteenth  and twentieth  centuries.' This  slash-and-burn  or  milpa  (literally cornfield)  method involved basically the same tools  and  crops  as  in the  north,  but  utilized longer fallow  cycles  and  lower  labor  inputs, especially for weeding. New plots were cut in January to  allow  the  woody  species  to  dry sufficiently  for  burning  before  the  rains  of April. After several seasons of cultivation, a plot was  abandoned for a protracted period to escape  the  concentration of pests  and  weeds there  and  to  allow  regrowth  of  a  secondary forest.

The  role of orchard-gardens in the  uplands during this period is not clear. They may have existed  around  larger  settlements,  but  references to activity of this kind are sparse. House gardens were undoubtedly common. The forests were very much the product of past Maya activities  and were well stocked with economic species  from  which  extensive collecting took place.
sections.Alvarado Transect:
Pedro de Alvarado led the  Spanish entrada into the highland Maya realm of Guatemala in 1524,  charting a route southeastward from the Mesa  Central,  following  the  Pacific  coastal plain,  before turning northward into the welldefended highlands of present day Guatemala (Figs. 1,6). Following the experience of Cortes, Alvarado brought  thousands  of  Aztec and Tlaxcalan warriors  to  subdue  the  Maya,  who fought  the invasion in a  series of  bloody battles. The Spaniards found a  populous highlands divided  into  provinces  of  different  ethnolinguistic Maya stock. Each province had hereditary rulers, but no overarching state was  present,  nor were  there  many  large cities of  the material majesty found in the Aztec realm. The region, however, contained some of the finest agricultural soils in Mesoamerica and the lowlands of its Pacific versant gave the Spaniards a preview of yet another source of wealth-estate production of cacao.

The  climb  from  the  Pacific  Coast  to  the homelands of the highland Maya  transverses an array of broad agroecological  zones associated with elevation (West 1964a,  373). The  Coastal Plain (La  Costa) and the  Boca Costa or  piedmont comprise a 40-50 km-wide strip between the  ocean  and  highlands proper  (Figs.  6,  7).

The coastal plain (up  to about 100 rn elevation) and the lower Boca Costa (about 100 m-460 m elevation) are  tierra  caliente while  the  upper Boca Costa  (about 460-1500 m elevation) is tierra templada.  Precipitation increases inland and with elevation, such that  portions of  the Boca Costa receive in excess of 2000 mm annually (Viv6 Escoto 1964, fig. 10). Around 1000 m elevation,  the  mountain front  rises steeply to cinder cones and composite volcanos, some o f
