*  Beekeeping  promotes  rural  diversification and  hence  is  an  alternate source  of income and  employment,  particularly in areas  where  arable  land  is  restricted and demographic  growth is resulting  in insufficiently  profitable  landholdings.
*  Beekeeping  is an activity  that has successfully  been adopted by women in many  parts  of the continent (Clauss  1992).

*  Beekeeping  allows  for  a  degree  of risk  avoidance by  providing  a  reliable, highvalue  product  that  enables  rural farmers  to survive  in  times  of  economic  crisis. This is particularly true of beeswax,  which can  be stored  indefinitely.
*  Beekeeping  clearly  is a  low-cost,  sustainable  undertaking with a  low environmental impact. The spin-off of enhanced  plant pollination is an invaluable one.
*  Although  honey  is  not a  primary source  of  food,  it  can  be  used  as  a  dietary  supplement. In addition,  its cultural  significance  should  not be ignored.

Recorded  European  evidence  of traditional  beekeeping  in southern  Africa  dates back  to 1594 in  Angola.  David  Livingstone noted  the  presence  of  log  and  bark  hives  in the upper Zambezi  area  in 1854 (Clauss  1992). The relevance  today  of this form of economic activity  is evidenced  by statistics  from  a single  district,  Babati,  in Tanzania,  where some  6,ooo  bee  colonies  produce a  total of  60,000-go,ooo kilograms of honey  a  year, with  a  value  equivalent to  u.s.$11,ooo-$17,ooo (Ntenga and  Mugongo 1991). A growing  importance  of honey-based  self-reliance strategies is  suggested by  a doubling in the number of rural  beekeeping  clubs in Malawi,  from forty-two to ninety-two,  over  the  course  of only  two  years  (Mensing  1993a).  In  this  article  we first explore  the relevance  of locally  appropriate self-reliance  strategies  in southern  Africa,  then discuss  southern  African  bees  and  indigenous  beekeeping  and  the  potential  of  this  activity to  supplement  rural income.  Our focus then  shifts to  an examination of the limited support given by certain  aid agencies  to increase  the effectiveness  of traditional  beekeeping.  The Bondolfi Beekeeper's Association in Zimbabwe  is presented  as a case  study.
sections.THE MOVE TO SELF-RELIANCE:
Desperate  economic realities  in Africa  both oblige  and  compel  many  communities to seek  solutions to the circumstances  in which they  find  themselves.  According  to the United Nations, "for  almost goo million people, approximately  one-sixth of mankind,  the march  of human  progress  has  become a retreat. In  many  nations,  development is being thrown into reverse.  And after  decades  of steady  economic advance,  large  areas  of  the  world  are  being  thrown  back  into  poverty"  (Gooneratne  and Mbilinyi  1992,  22).  This  statement  is  particularly pertinent  in  Africa, where  the  effective  collapse  of  government  services,  infrastructure, and  social  provision  in  many  areas is coupled with hyperinflation,  vast debt  burdens,  and the disastrous  effects  of global  trade  and  structural  adjustment  packages  (Taylor and  Mackenzie  1992).  This situation  militates  against  any  significant  socioeconomic  intervention  on the  part  of national  governments.  Aside  from  often  tokenistic  interventions by  aid  agencies  and nongovernmental  organizations,  many communities are  forced  to look inward  at their own resources  and  potential  in order  to carve  some form  of future  for  themselves  and their  children.  Frequently, this  leads  to a reliance  on, or a rediscovery of, traditional  forms of livelihood and income generation.

The switch in applied  development  strategies  to a bottom-up approach  at both the community  and  policy  levels  accords with  W.  B.  Stohr's argument  that  the  failure

of modernization  approaches to  tackle  poverty  requires new  forms  of intervention, in which control  is  vested  in  the  host  community  (1981). Communities  need  to draw  on local skills,  resources, and indigenous  knowledge.  These  principles  are  endorsed  by recent  writings  that  discuss  the potential  of indigenous  technical  knowledge  (Binns 1995).  Research  undertaken  in various  parts  of Africa  reveals  that economic marginalization  is  encouraging a  new  or  enhanced focus  by  communities  and  aid  agencies on the development  of local potential through  indigenous  strategies  (Taylor  and Mackenzie  1992).  An  argument for  self-reliance is  inherent within  this  switch  in  focus, a  concept  that  finds  accord  in  the  writings  of  the  South  Commission, which  has  come out in support  of a  "revival of economic  growth  which  is  inward-orientated and  selfsustaining,  providing  full  employment  and  the  development  of both agriculture and industry" (Gooneratne  and  Mbilinyi  1992, 3).  According to J.  Galtung, self-reliance is "development  on the basis  of a country's  own resources, involving  its populations, and  based  on the  potentials  of its  cultural values  and  traditions" (quoted  in Gooneratne  and  Mbilinyi  1992, 3).  Traditional beekeeping  dearly  lies  within  this  conceptualization.

Numerous locally driven African development endeavors  are emerging that speak  to local  needs  and  encourage  greater participation by  the  indigenous  population (Gooneratne  1992).  Local  initiatives  that use indigenous  technology  not only help  to ensure  human  survival but  also  provide  a  basis  for  participation in  the  mainstream economy. High capital returns  can be generated  through local improvements in indigenous  techniques  and in the marketing  of produce.

Agricultural  activities  clearly  have  a  key  role  to play  in any  rural  development strategy:  "Agricultural development  is indispensable  to guarantee  local food security,  to generate  widespread  employment  and income sources  and conserve  environmental  resources"  (Gooneratne  1992,  5).  Overpopulation,  environmental  degradation, drought, marginal farming conditions,  and supplementary income needs require  production that is more than just subsistence.  Transportation  and storage difficulties,  however,  work against  the attempts  of small-scale  farmers  to compete as major suppliers of food to external markets.  Honey and beeswax, though, are  a  high-value commodity with which to complement  existing agriculture,  are  easy  to transport  and  store,  and  provide  subsistence  farmers  with a  valuable source of income.

Beekeeping  has considerable  merit  as  a  self-reliance  strategy  that  can  augment the income of small-scale farmers  with only a minimal financial outlay.  Traditional  beekeeping  is being  enhanced as a form of  rural activity and income through the introduction of small, technologically appropriate  improvements. Often  this is  due to limited,  nondictatorial  support  offered  by  aid  agencies  that  acknowledge the considerable  benefits which beekeeping offers. Intervention  has been designed  to remove  obstacles  and  increase  productivity  and  income, thereby improving rural  community self-reliance.  Evidence  from countries such as Malawi illustrates  how suitable  interventions  can  address  existing  constraints  (Mensing 1993a).

TRADITIONAL  HONEY-HUNTING AND BEEKEEPING IN SOUTHERN  AFRICA

Honeybees  and  their  products  have  been  an  important  part  of the  rural  economy  in parts  of Africa  for  hundreds  of years.  Honey  is  a  food source,  an  ingredient  in traditional  medicine,  and  an  additive  in  the  brewing  of  honey  beer,  and  beeswax  has  been important to local craftsmen  (Svensson  1991). In areas  where  beekeeping  is practiced,  honey also  plays  a  key  role  in traditional  rituals  such  as  initiation  ceremonies (Ntenga  and  Mugongo  1991).  Evidence  from  Zambia  suggests  that  more  than  50 percent of honey produced  by traditional  methods is sold or bartered  locally  within tribal  groups  (Clau4s  1992).

Honey has been collected  in southern  Africa  since ancient  times. Harald  Pager has  identified  a  large  number  of  Stone  Age  rock  paintings  depicting  honeybees,  honeycombs,  and  honey  hunters  (1973).  One  painting  from  an  overhang  near  Toghwana Dam, in the Matopo  Hills  of Zimbabwe,  clearly  shows  an  early  honey  hunter  using  a burning  stick  to protect  himself  from  stings.  More  than  one hundred  scenes  of bees and  associated  features  have  been  identified  in  the  Drakensberg and  Midlands  areas of  KwaZulu-Natal  in South Africa (Mazel 1982).  Farther  south, the name of the Outeniqua area  was reported  by Francois  le Vaillant  to mean "man  loaded with honey"  (Tribe  1982).  It  is  apparent that  "traditional beekeeping  has  always been  part of the life-style of  most families"  in many districts  throughout southern Africa (Jones  1995, 74),  although  there  is currently very  little  traditional  beekeeping  south of the Limpopo  River, except  in the Brachystegia-Julbernardia Woodland  of southern Mozambique (Guy  1971).

Techniques  of beekeeping  and honey collection  are  handed  down through  the generations  (Clauss  1992; Jones  1995).  Given  the range  of traditional  uses  of honey, beekeeping  often exists as a way  of life rather  than as a form  of commercial  enterprise,  although  commerce  is a  consideration  that  development  agencies  are  seeking to enhance (Clauss  1992).

If  honey  hunting  from  naturally occurring  honeybee  nests  has  been  widely  practiced in southern  Africa,  traditional  beekeeping  has  been  particularly prominent  in the northern, savanna  portions of the region under consideration (Ntenga and Mugongo 1991).  Traditional beekeeping  differs  from  honey hunting  in that  the colony of honeybees  is  not destroyed  but  manipulated: The  honey is  extracted  without eliminating  the honeybees.  The resource  is protected,  and repeated  harvests  can  be made  from  the  same  colony.  Traditional beekeeping  in  southern  Africa  is  most  widespread  in Zimbabwe,  Zambia,  Tanzania,  and Mozambique,  where the honeybees have  been kept in bark  hives.  The bark  hives  are  made  by ring  barking  the desired length from a large  tree. Ring  barking  entails removing  a section of bark  of even width from the circumference  of a tree.  The two ends of the hive are  then plugged with coils of woven  grass,  leaving  a small  hole as  an  entrance.  The  hives  are  hung  in trees, out of the reach of children,  pests, and predators.  Traditional  beekeeping, though frequently  carried  out on a small  scale  or as  a  supplement  to other  activity, can  range  from  an  individual  with  fewer  than  ten  hives  to a  beekeeper  who possesses up to one thousand hives (Ntenga  and Mugongo  1991; Clauss  1992).

The important  role  that  beekeeping  plays  as  a  source  of employment  is  clear:  Of the  approximately400,000  people  in  the  North-Western Province  of  Zambia,  nearly 15,000  are beekeepers  (Clauss 1992). The significant and potential  earning capacity of beekeepers  is  vividly  illustrated by evidence  from  Tanzania, where  the more  successful  beekeepers  can  earn  incomes  of up  to approximately u.s.$370  per  year,  compared  with a  state  official,  whose annual  earnings  average about  u.s.$s56. It  is  evident why "large-scale  beekeepers  in the villages  have solid social and economic position[s]"  (Ntenga  and Mugongo  1991,  3).
sections.SOUTHERN AFRICAN BEES: The  honeybees  of  Africa belong  to  the  species Apis  mellifera, which  is  subdivided  into ten  subspecies  or  races  (Ruttner 1988).  Four  races  of  honeybee  occur  in southern  Africa.  The  two  major  races  are  the  Cape  Bee,  Apis  mellifera capensis, and  the  Highland Bee,  Apis  mellifera scutellata. The other  two minor  races  are  a  little-known  bee from the coastal regions of Mozambique  and northern KwaZulu-Natal, Apis mellifera litorea, andApis  mellifera adansonii, which  occurs  in  Angola  and  northwestern  Zambia (Ruttner 1988;  Hepburn and Crewe 1991;  Radloff, Hepburn, and Villet 1997).  The Cape  Bee  is  largely  restricted to  the  fynbos  biome  along  the  southwestern and  southern  coast  of  South  Africa, which  stretches inland  to  the  mountains  of  the  Little  Karoo. The fynbos  biome is  a  heathlike  plant  community  with  high  biodiversity and  a  large number of endemic plant species.  Farther  north and east  the Cape  Bee hybridizes with the Highland  Bee.  The  vast  majority  of the subcontinent  is populated  by  Apis mellifera scutellata. The  main  difference between  these  two  races  is  that  the  Cape  Bee has  a  unique  trait  known  as  thelytoky, whereby  the  workers lay  diploid  eggs  in  the  absence  of a  queen.  Traditionally the  Cape  Bee  has  been  regarded as  smaller, darker, and less aggressive than  the Highland  Bee (Hepburn  and  Crewe  1991). All  of the  honeybees we discuss  in this article  belong  to the race  Apis  mellifera scutellata.
sections.ADVANTAGES AND DISADVANTAGES OF BEEKEEPI:
Honeybees  provide  direct  benefits  to beekeepers both as  a source  of food that  has  a high  nutritional  value  and  as  an  additional  source  of income  through  the  sale  of surplus honey and wax. Wax is an important  by-product  of beekeeping  that can be melted  down and  stored  almost  indefinitely. Tanzania produced  1,050  metric  tons  of wax in 1984,  of which better than one-thirdwas  exported (Crane 1990).  Honeybeer  is a valued commercial  product,  particularly in areas  such as northwestern  Zambia (Ngolofwana  1994).

A wide range  of other advantages  exist.  When practiced  on a small  scale,  beekeeping  is not particularly labor  intensive,  and  tending  can  be restricted  to periods outside peak  work times (Mensing  1993a). As a result,  the beekeeper  can carry  on with usual  agricultural activities,  such  as  growing  maize  and  raising  cattle.  Beekeeping therefore  usefully complements crop production and may lead to increased yields  and  cash  income  if  enough  honeybees  are  present  for  pollination  (Ntenga  and Mugongo  1991;  Murless 1995).

At its most basic  level,  beekeeping  commands  a relatively minimal financial  investment, especially  compared  with the many  cash  crops  that require  purchase  of plants or seedlings,  pesticides,  and fertilizers  (Mensing  1993a). A subsistence-level farmer  who keeps  honeybees  needs  not purchase  land  and  can  construct  hives  from locally available  material.  Bees can be obtained  by placing  empty,  baited hives in trees,  which are  then occupied  by  wild swarms.  A particular advantage  in southern Africa  is  that  beekeeping  can  even  be  carried out in areas  with  a  low  agricultural potential,  where  little or no arable  land exists  or  where  rainfall  is unreliable.

Beekeeping encourages the conservation  of local habitats (Ntenga and Mugongo 1991).  It is in the beekeepers' interest  to conserve  local nectar-  and pollenproducing  vegetation.  Beekeeping  is  a  passive  form  of agriculture, for  it  does  not require  that indigenous vegetation  be cleared  to make  way  for crops  (Murless  1995). Beekeepers  also  discourage  the  use  of  pesticides  on crops,  because  they  could  kill  the honeybees. In some areas,  as in northern  Malawi,  beekeepers  may actively  protect conservation  areas  (Mensing  1993b).

The practice  is a  culturally  accepted  one in most of the  region.  Almost  all  population  groups  in southern  Africa  have  some  knowledge  of honeybees  and  honey  collection (Guy  1971). In addition,  it can  lead  to the  empowerment  of women within a community. For  example,  both the chairperson  and the treasurer of the successful Bondolfi  Beekeeper's Association  in  Zimbabwe  are  women.  In  the  Kasempa District of Zambia  honey hunting is traditionally  a male-dominated  activity,  but in recent years  female  heads  of household  have  begun  to keep  bees  because  of the other  economic constraints  they  face.  Beekeeping can  therefore  encourage  gender  empowerment, allowing women an improved status and community role through their capacity  to generate  an  income.  Bernhard Clauss  (1992)  quotes  examples  from  Zambia,  where  women producers  are  harvesting  up to 500 kilograms  of honey  each  and are  now able  to pay  for their  children's education.

Beekeeping  is a mechanism that can help address  the employment challenges created  by  a  growing  population  and  increasing landlessness  (Ntenga  and  Mugongo 1991).  Employment  opportunities  are  also formed  for  craftsmen  who manufacture hives,  smokers,  gloves,  and other  beekeeping  equipment  (Sosu  1991).  For  example, participants  in a beekeeping  project  in the Mpumalanga  Province  of northeastern South  Africa  earn  additional  income  by  manufacturing hives  for  newcomers  to beekeeping  (Lundall-Magnuson  1997).

Beekeeping,  particularly when it is  undertaken as  a  part-time  activity, lends  itself to cooperative  action in collecting  honey and  purchasing  or manufacturing  equipment. The need for such action is enhanced  if beekeeping  is undertaken  on a semicommercial basis because of what can become a high cost of equipment. The practice and its labor requirements  also easily  graft onto traditional,  communal ways  of life  that  are  prevalent in  many  parts  of  the  region.  This  is  evidenced  in  the  recent upsurge  in the number  of beekeeping  clubs in Malawi (Mensing  1993a).  G. M. Ntenga and B. T. Mugongo assert  that "beekeeping  offers  great  opportunities  for both co-operation and self-reliance,  as it is normally  more successful  when prac-

ticed  collectively, and  is  an  avenue  for  generating  income  without government  support" (1991,  3).

Rural  beekeeping,  and  steps  to enhance  it,  do,  however, face  certain  constraints. Some of the most apparent  ones are:  If  honey is not marketed  or consumed  it may eventually  start  to ferment;  inadequate hive  management  may  lead  to the spread  of bee diseases  and  pests;  and  vandalism,  theft,  animals,  and  bush  fires  can  be a  problem.  Another  key  problem  is  that  the  construction  of  bark  hives  can  result  in  the  loss of a  tree  and,  sometimes,  in  the  demise  of valuable  bee-forage  plants  (Towry-Coker 1995).  Overexploitation  of trees  has  been noted in the Babati  District  of Tanzania, where a shortage  of traditional  materials  may  oblige  some beekeepers  to abandon traditional  beekeeping  altogether  (Ntenga  and  Mugongo  1991). The  members  of the rural  Bondolfi  Beekeeper's Association  in  Zimbabwe  found  that  the  construction  of bark hives led to the depletion of certain  trees.  As a result,  if bark  hives are constructed  they now tend to be made from fallen  branches  (Mutude  1997).  An additional problem is environmental  degradation  caused  by frequent  bush fires that inadvertently  start  when hives are smoked to collect honey (Guy 1971).  Tropical honeybees are known to be very aggressive,  which ideally  requires  beekeepers  to take precautions,  such as using protective  equipment and placing colonies away from dwellings  or animals.

Inadequate  research  into African  bees is decidedly  a problem.  Although  a vast amount of research has  been  done  on the  races  of  honeybees  in  temperate regions  of the  world,  the  same  cannot  be said  for  some  of the  races  in  tropical  Africa.  The  temperate  bee races  do not always behave  the  way  tropical  races  do.  Therefore, beekeeping techniques  developed  in temperate  areas  may  be inappropriate in tropical  ones. For  example,  whereas  temperate  colonies  are  able  to  survive  cold  periods  by  clustering and  building  up large  food stores  during  times  of plenty,  tropical  colonies  have developed  nomadic  tendencies  (Bradbear 1991). Apis  mellifera scutellata readily  absconds,  and  beekeepers  must constantly  ensure  that  hives  are  in good condition  to prevent  the bees from  moving on (Ngolofwana  1994).

A final,  potential  problem  is that  of the illiteracy of many  beekeepers,  given  the importance  of  keeping  records  on each  colony  of  honeybees.  Careful record  keeping enables  beekeepers  to determine  the amount  of honey  and  the  state  of the  colony  at particular times  of  the  year  and  allows  them  to  choose  the  best  time  to  harvest  honey. Illiteracy  also  makes  the dissemination  of information  to the  beekeepers  more difficult  (Makalo 1991).
sections.ENHANCING THE POTENTIAL OF TRADITIONAL:
Traditional beekeeping  is constrained  by  these  problems.  If  its  potential  is  to be enhanced,  positive  interventions  need  to be made.  It  is,  however, critical  that  any  program use appropriate  technology and not simply be imposed on the recipients. Improvements  should  be  worked  out  in  careful consultation  with  local  beekeepers in order  to enhance  their  capacities  for  self-reliance.

Ntenga and  Mugongo's  research in  Tanzania  (1991) and  our  field  observations in Zimbabwe clearly  indicate that the absence  of scientific  input in traditional  beekeeping  constrains  yields,  poses risks  to the  environment,  and  limits the economic return.  Traditional bark  hives  and  honeybee  colonies  are  frequently destroyed  when honey is  extracted.  The  need  for  reusable hives  is  clear, as  is  the  need  to  adopt  methods that do not threaten  the colonies or deplete  timber  resources.  In northwestern Zambia,  traditional  beekeepers  have  recognized  that  increased  beekeeping,  as  near Kabulamema,  has resulted  in the absence  of bark  resources  within an 8-kilometer radius  of the settlement  (Clauss  1992).  Low  yields  per  hive,  the  poor siting  of hives, and the poorly developed  nature  of marketing  systems  all constrain  the development  potential  of traditional beekeeping  at  present-but all  of  these  can  be  remedied (Ntenga and Mugongo 1991).

Such  problems,  as  well  as  language  barriers between  the  beekeepers  and  outside advisers, further restrict improvements and adaptation to modern beekeeping techniques.  According  to Robin Guy,  traditional  people are  "bound  by their cultures,  often  to  their  material  and  nutritional  disadvantage" (1971,18). Modern  Western  techniques,  hives,  and  safety  equipment  are  simply  too expensive  for  most rural communities, and  they  present  problems  of transportation, adaptability, and  complexity.  In order  to address  these difficulties  and  to increase  honey yields in a sustainable  fashion,  new,  technologically  appropriate hives  have  been developed  and promoted by nongovernmental  organizations.  The top-bar  hive  was developed  in Kenya  using  locally  available timber,  rather  than  tree  trunks.  Its  design  permits  the easy  removal  and  repeated  extraction  of honey  from  the  hives  with minimal  disturbance of the colony.  It  works  on the principle  that  combs  hang  down from  removable  slats  that  cover  the top of the hive.  They  can  easily  be lifted  off  and  the combs removed  (Figure  2).  Only  one slat  needs  to  be  removed  at  a  time,  limiting  disruption and reducing aggression.  The frame for the hive can be constructed  out of small branches  and  twigs,  covered  with a  mixture  of clay  and  cow  dung.  Local variants  include the Kupfuma  Ishunga,  Kenyan,  and Tanzanian  top-bar hives (Ntenga and Mugongo 1991; Towry-Coker  1995).  There  is,  as  a result,  very  little  necessity  for  dependence on foreign  technology.  If  beekeeping  becomes  popular,  some individuals may even construct additional  hives for sale at low cost. These new hives are reported to  be in use in Mozambique (Jones 1995) and Tanzania (Ntenga and Mugongo 1991);  and we observed  them in Zimbabwe  and Botswana  in 1997.  The principles applied have built on the reality  first identified  in Kenya,  namely that "with  beekeeping,  as with other agricultural  inputs,  the question ...  is not one of seeking  new  knowledge  only,  but rather  one of improving  and  implementing  what exists already" (Kigatiira  1976,144).  These interventions  serve  to enhance  the economic independence and hence self-reliance  of beekeeping  communities.

Programs  designed  to offer  guidance  and  improvements  to beekeepers  and  not to impose inappropriate changes  have  been  pioneered  by  the  Deutsche  Gesellschaft fur  Technische  Zusammenarbeit (GTz;  German  Agency  for  Technical  Cooperation) in Malawi  and  Mozambique  (Mensing  1993a;  Jones  1995). A notably wide-ranging  intervention  has been in northern  Malawi,  where the GTz has assisted  in the establishment  of more  than  ninety  beekeeping  clubs.  Advice is offered  on improved  beekeeping,  how to make  modified  hives,  safety  equipment, and marketing  skills  and outlets.  The  equipment  has  been  provided  in return  for a portion of the first  three  years' yields  from  the  hives.  The  success  of the initiative  is apparent  in its statistics.  The new hives  have  the  potential  to increase  honey yields from  6  kilograms  to 40  kilograms  per  hive  per  year. Annual  production  in  the  project area increased  from 1.4  metric tons in 1990-1991 to  5.5  metric tons in 1992-1993, largely  as  of result  of the  project.  Evidence  of improved  lifestyles  resulting  from  adaptations  of traditional  beekeeping  can  be  found  in  the  experience  of the  Nhkalanga Beekeeping  Club in the  village  of Karonga  in northern  Malawi,  where  income derived  from  honey sales  quintupled  in  just  five  years  (Mensing  1993a).
sections.THE BONDOLFi BEEKEEPERs AssocIATION, Z:
A prime example  of the potential  of rural  beekeeping  for  improving  socioeconomic conditions in  a  rural  community can  be  found  at  the  Bondolfi  Mission, near Masvingo  in central Zimbabwe. The area is semiarid, so opportunities  for agricul-

FIG. 3-Members  of  the  Bondolfi Beekeeper's  Association, Zimbabwe,  which has significantly improved  the status  of beekeeping  in the  community  and  provided  additional  income. (Photograph by  Mark  Robertson,  March  1997)

<!-- image -->

ture  are  restricted.  Low  incomes  are  exacerbated by  structural adjustment  and  poor growth  rates  in the  regional  economy.  Beekeeping has  always been  pursued  as  a  traditional  activity  but seldom as a  primary  form of income (Mutude  1997).

Residents  of the  community recently  realized  that  production  from  traditional hives  was  no  longer  viable  because  of the  negative  impact  of bark  stripping.  To  their credit,  they  concluded  that  outside  support  was  needed  to maximize  local  potential and  earnings  from  beekeeping.  This  coincided  with  an  interest  shown  by  an  external aid  agency,  the United Nations volunteer  program  in the area.  Material  assistance was also  provided  by  the  European Union (Chale  1997).  Based  on this  measured  advice, the residents  acquired  better  beekeeping  skills  and  marketing  strategies  (Mutude 1997). One of their first actions was to establish the Bondolfi Beekeeper's Association in 1995 to coordinate  activities  and undertake  the bulk collection and processing  of honey (Figure  3).

The association now has seventy  active  members,  forty  of whom are  women. The endeavor  assists  women,  who are  traditionally  disempowered  in Zimbabwean society,  to  acquire  an  independent  livelihood.  Fewer  than  ten of the members  still work  with bark  hives;  the  balance  use  the  improved  top-bar  hives  (Figure  2).  On  average  each  member  manages  two  hives,  although  it  is  the  intention  of the  United  Nations volunteer to increase  the number of hives to at least ten per member.  The production  of new hives has, in itself, generated  local employment  opportunities  for

carpenters,  who manufacture  hives at the association's  small shop in the village. Other direct spin-offs include the establishment  a beehive-smoker  enterprise  in Bondolfi.  A small leather-processing industry  has been established  that manufactures  gloves  for  beekeepers, and  a  sewing  group  produces  protective veils  for  the  collectors  (Chale 1997).

The association  now successfully  coordinates  the collection,  processing,  marketing,  and  sale  of honey and  wax,  eliminating  the  extreme  difficulty  that  individuals  previously  experienced  in trying  to sell their  produce.  The association  has also overcome  the constraints  that  individuals  encountered  in trying  to transport  their goods to Masvingo,  the  closest  major  urban  center. Honey  is  now  collected  and  bottled  centrally and  then  sold  in  bulk,  in  jars  bearing  the  association's logo.  In  addition to obvious savings  in time and effort,  the sale  of a product  that  has  become recognized for  its  quality  commands  higher  prices  and  turnover  than  individual  producers could have hoped for. Bulk sales to a trader  who markets  the honey on their behalf assists  with penetration  of the urban  retail  market,  ensuring  a greater  competitive  edge and  higher  prices  (Mutude  1997).  Increased sales  have  resulted; these, in turn,  have  had a cumulative  effect  in Bondolfi,  where  income and employment have  risen  and  additional  hives  are  being  constructed. Although  it is too early  to see noticeable material  improvements  in Bondolfi,  the attainment  of a more reliable form of income promises  considerable  long-term  benefits  for  the community.
sections.CONCLUSION:
Traditional  or enhanced  beekeeping  practices  can serve  as a reliable  means of increasing  rural  self-reliance. Although  beekeeping  per  se  will  never  become  a  panacea for  rural  development  problems  in  Africa, its  role  as  an  adjunct  to  other  development activities  is  not  to  be  underestimated. Low-technology  interventions  have  considerable  merit  in  enhancing  productivity and  efficiency. They  can  help  to  ensure  that  rural communities are better able to generate  meaningful income and eventually become even more self-reliant. The support  offered  by  aid  agencies  has  the  capacity to facilitate  beekeeping,  as  evidenced  in Malawi  and at Bondolfi.  Any  intervention undertaken  should not prescribe  to a  local  community  but  suggest  alternatives that can improve  traditional  techniques.  These  alternatives should  not introduce  costly, inappropriate, and  imported  First World  technologies.  This  conceptualization is  endorsed  by Guy,  who writes  that  "better beekeeping  will help  them [traditional beekeepers]  to live  in harmony  with both their  traditions  and  their  increasing  pressure for productivity" (1971,18).  This scenario was identified in the 1991  Banjul Bee Declaration,  which advocated  the use  of transitional  and  appropriate technology  and  the development of suitable support systems  and structures  (Bees for Development 1991).

Local  knowledge  of honeybees  through  honey  hunting  and  traditional  beekeeping exists  in most areas  of southern  Africa.  This  knowledge  needs  to be tapped  and aided through the introduction of low-technology,  high-return  beekeeping  projects.  Rural  beekeeping  is a sustainable activity  with  great  potential  for  boosting  the

incomes of poor,  small-scale  farmers  through  minimal  financial  outlay.  Beekeeping is an environmentally  friendly,  economically  viable,  nonintrusive  activity  that  can complement  existing  agricultural practices  in rural  communities.  "Increasing interest in tropical  beekeeping  is fueling  research into the  biology  and  behavior  of tropical  honeybees....  Armed  with understanding, we can  derive  ways  for  beekeepers to benefit  most  efficiently  from these bees" (Bradbear 1991,  23). These principles  have clear  developmental  ramifications that  governments  and  aid  agencies  should  recognize and pursue.

sections.MAURI J. PALOMAKI and ALLEN G. NOBL:
ABSTRACT.  Narpes Commune, South Ostrobothnia,  is the center of the  largest area of  greenhouse  horticulture  in Finland. Its  presence  is an  example  of local adjustment  to  agricultural  decline and increased  population pressure.  The empirical  horticultural  evidence is the basis for a  theory  of economic transition  for depressed  rural  areas.  Key  words: agricultural theory, Finland, greenhouses, horticulture,  regional  development.

etween Vaasa  and Kristinestad,  in the  Swedish-speaking  areas  of the South Ostrobothnia  coast of Finland,  the commune of  Narpes  is the center of the  largest  and most  important  area  of  greenhouse  horticulture in Finland  (Fig. 1).  The most  significant  in terms of volume and value of production,  it  supplies primarily  tomatoes,  cucumbers,  and lettuce  (Atlas 1982, 5.311).  The  development  of  this  agricultural specialization  illustrates a  process  of local and  regional  economic  adjustment  that is theorized for  depressed  rural  areas.  To  understand  the  relationship  of the case study  to  the  theory  it  is  necessary  to  examine  the  evolution  of  this horticultural  activity  in some detail.
sections.BEGINNINGS:
Poverty  in Finland was  widespread during  the late nineteenth and early  twentieth  centuries,  when  the  country  was  part  of  the  Russian Empire.  Especially  in South  Ostrobothnia,  evidence of the low economic status  included  large-scale emigration during  the  first  quarter  of  the twentieth  century  to the United States,  Canada,  and Sweden  (Atlas 1993, 3.9).  More than half of  all  Finnish  emigrants originated  in  South Ostrobothnia.

Many people  who  remained existed  at a  barely  subsistence  level. Farmsteads were small, even  by  the Finnish standards of the  time, and continued subdivision of land  by  inheritance made  agriculture  increasingly  less economical  (Atlas 1993,  3.5).  Thus conditions were  opportune for a new  and  promising agricultural  venture, however  radical in  approach. During  the nineteenth  century  a few  commercial  greenhouses had been established around Helsinki and Turku  to serve their  sophisticated and affluent urban markets,  but  greenhouse agriculture  was unknown elsewhere in Finland.

DR. PALOMAKI is a  professor  of economic geography at Vaasa  University,  Vaasa, Finland SF-65200.  DR. NOBLE is a  professor  of  geography at the  University of  Akron, Akron,  Ohio 44325-5005.

Greenhouse horticulture was  initiated  in  Narpes  by  an  emigrant, Valdemar  Mattfolk,  who  returned from the United States to Finland in 1916.  Accustomed abroad to  eating vegetables  at almost  every meal, he recognized  the  potential  in Finland  for  greenhouse produce;  at that  time, because of  poorly developed agriculture  and a  generally  low standard  of living, vegetables  were  rarely  eaten.

The  greenhouse  enterprises  of  Narpes  were  greatly  aided  by  the unforeseen market that  large  numbers of German  troops,  billeted in the nearby  Vaasa  area,  created  during  World  War  II.  Growth of the domestic market, on  the  other hand,  was  slow,  yet  steady,  as Finns  generally accepted  a basic  change  in their  dietary  habits.  By  the end of the 1950s greenhouse  horticulture had  spread  to 17  villages  in  Narpes  from the original  centers in  Finby  and  Pjelax  (Hindstrom 1978,  35).  Greenhouses on 617 farms  provided  a total of 306,963  square  meters of  growing space (Figs.  2  and  3).  The  pattern  of  diffusion  depended  not  only  on  the

In  the  village  of  Finby  Mattfolk  built a  greenhouse  for  the cultivation  of tomatoes and cucumbers  (Hindstr6m  1978,23-25).  His innovation  was not immediately successful, and ten  years passed  before other local farmers adopted  the idea. In 1926  two brothers,  Uno and  Georg  Lassfolk,  from  the neighboring  village  of  Pjelax,  erected  a  150-square-meter greenhouse.  The older brother,  Uno, had received  training  as a  gardener  at the  imperial household in St.  Petersburg,  Russia, and  may  have been familiar with greenhouse  horticulture  as  practiced there  (Hindstr6m  1978,28).  The  adoption  of  greenhouse  horticulture continued  to  be  very  slow,  and  by  1943  only five or six  greenhouses  had been constructed  (Walls  1968,39,  94).

sections.GREENHOUSE HORTICULTURE:
Greenhouse horticulture, which  had  achieved  considerable  acceptance  by  the  1960s,  has  brought  a measure of  prosperity  to the  Narpes area.  A  survey  conducted in 1963,  which  compared greenhouse  cultivators with  neighboring nongreenhouse  farmers, showed  a  significantly

higher  standard of  living among  the former  (Walls  1968,  78).  The difference in affluence  persists. Beginning  in 1967,  the income of  greenhouse farmers accelerated at a much faster rate than did that of  neighboring, nongreenhouse farmers,  and after 1971  the  disparity  was  sharply greater (Hindstrom  1978,203).  Although  no  specific  data  exist to confirm  presentday  income differentials, the  widely  held belief in  Narpes  is that such differences exist.

By  1974 the number of  greenhouses operating  in  thirty villages  of Narpes  exceeded  one  thousand.  Although  the number of  greenhouse farmers had risen  only minimally  since 1959,  from 617 to 636, the  space under cover had increased  almost 90  percent,  from  306,963  square  meters in  1959 to  579,698 square  meters in  1974  (Statistik 1994). Greenhouse horticulture  has continued to  expand,  but the results have been a mixed pattern  of  growth,  so much so that the term  consolidation  might  be more appropriate  than  growth.  The same  thirty villages  account for all of the greenhouses  in  Narpes  in  1995 as  in  1974, but  considerable shifts  in numbers of  greenhouses  in  villages  have  occurred.  Among  the  most pronounced  are the declines in Overmark  from 76 in 1974  to 37 in  1995, in  T6jby  from 81 to 31,  in Norrnas from 15 to 3,  in  Tjarlax from 21 to 6,  in Finby  from 61 to 34,  and in  Pjelax  from  69 to 46.  By  contrast,  increase  has been  equally  dramatic  in other  villages.  These include  Bodbacka,  from 1 to 13,  and Traskbole,  from 5 to 23.

The net  effect  has  been  to  even  out  the  distribution  pattern.  An examination of data on  greenhouses per village  for 1959, 1974,  and 1995 validates this assertion. In 1959 the  greatest  concentration occurred in Pjelax,  with 111  greenhouses,  and the smallest in  Rangsby, with 9.  By  1974 the  range  of 102  had shrunk  to 80:  the  upper  limit of 81 was in  Tojby, and the lower in the five  villages  with  only  one  greenhouse  each. In 1995  the range  had declined to 45. The  process  of diffusion was still  operating  in 1974,  but  by  1995  the  emphasis  was on consolidation rather  than  expansion.  Nevertheless,  a few  greenhouses  had been established to the northeast in  villages immediately  outside the  Narpes  commune  boundary.

Those  changes represented  a shift from  old,  small  greenhouses  to modern, much  larger  structures.  While the total number of  greenhouses in  Narpes  fell  by  almost one-third  between 1974  and  1995,  the area  under glass  increased  by  more than a  quarter.  Most affected were the  original centers of  greenhouse  horticulture,  as well as the  newest  villages  to  adopt it. In  intermediate  villages, change depended  on individual initiative and venturesome  spirit. Responding  to economies of scale,  greenhouse  farmers  have  built  ever  larger  structures. In  1974 the  average  amount of greenhouse  area  per  farm  in  Narpes  measured 803  square  meters,  and  by 1995 the  average  floor area  per  farm was  1,734  square  meters  (Statistik 1994).

Increased  size of  greenhouses  is a measure  of the  growing  influence of distant  markets.  Traversing the  commune  is  Highway  8,  a  main  north-south road that also connects  with  principal  truck-ferry ports.  The route  crosses Narpes  from Portom  through  Overmark,  Yettermark, and  Finby  to  Pjelax, all  villages  on  or  very  close  to  the  highway. Accessibility  and ease  of marketing,  together  with the fact that  the  highway  seeks the easiest route across  the  largest  lowland areas  of the  commune,  help explain  the unusual expansion  of  greenhouse  horticulture  in these  villages.
sections.CHANGES IN BUILDING AND HEATING PRAC:
Significant  changes  in the  greenhouse  horticulture  of  Narpes began  in the mid-1970s.  They  were  especially  visible in  greenhouse  construction. Traditional  wooden  framing gave way  to metal, and  glass began  to be replaced by plastic. Today  about 40  percent  of all structures  are covered by  translucent  plastic (Statistik  1994).  After the mid-1970s  greenhouses became  longer  and wider, as well  as  higher  to  support  the  larger  roof necessitated  by  horizontal  expansion.  A  recently  constructed  greenhouse may  be as  long  as 70 to 75 meters and as wide as 25 meters-a very large cubic area that must be heated in both the fall and the  spring growing seasons.

The fuel of choice  today  is either  heavy  oil or  light  oil, both of which must be  imported, usually  from North Sea oil fields. Some  greenhouse operators  burn  peat,  which is  locally  obtained. Coal was  formerly  used but had to be  imported;  it  currently  is little used because it is too  expensive. The  heating  is  accomplished by large  hot-water  pipes  that are laid on the  ground  to  separate  the  planting  beds  into rows.  Space heating represents  the most  significant  cost in  greenhouse  horticulture.
sections.GREENHOUSE HORTICULTURE TODAY:
Five  vegetables  are  currently  grown  in  Narpes.  Tomatoes  account for about two-thirds of the  greenhouse space,  cucumbers for about a fifth; because of market demand, tomato  production  is  increasing  faster than is that of cucumbers.  Today  68  percent  of all tomatoes and 45  percent  of all  cucumbers  grown  in  Finland come  from the  Narpes  greenhouses (Linde 1994).  Annual  yields  of tomatoes  may  be as  high  as 30  kilograms per  square  meter and  of  cucumbers as  high  as  50  kilograms.  Small amounts of lettuce, Chinese  cabbage,  and  parsley  also are  grown.  The lettuce is sold in  pots  that  are  kept  in domestic households and harvested as needed. In addition to the Finnish  market,  sales to Sweden, Germany, and Russia have been undertaken  successfully,  which is  important  in a country  hard  pressed  to  gain foreign exchange  and to broaden its economy.

Marketing operations  for  the  Narpes  greenhouse  horticulture are efficiently  organized.  A  local  growers' cooperative  and  three  private

packing plants  market the entire  production.  Tomatoes  must be  graded by  both size and color. The latter is  necessary  because Helsinki markets need new  supplies  two or more times a week. The size of the Helsinki market and the  high  turnover both  allow  and  require ripe, very  red tomatoes. In contrast,  shipments  to  Lapland  occur  only  once  every  several weeks  because  of  the  much  smaller market. These tomatoes  are shipped green  and  ripen  in transit  or at destination.  Foreign  markets  also have  specific  needs and demands that must be met  individually.

The  general prosperity produced by greenhouse  horticulture  in Narpes  has been balanced to a  degree by  the lack  of suitable  agricultural  land and  by  the  continued,  though  more  gradual,  subdivision of land  through inheritance.  Most  greenhouse  cultivators  also  practice  open-field farming to  protect  their investment  and  to  broaden their  risks,  as well  as  to augment  their incomes. The  grain yields  of these farmers  are  among  the highest  in Finland. One  long-term strategy  to solve  the  land-shortage problem  is  emigration.  Between 1951 and 1960 almost 15  percent  of the Narpes population  left for overseas, with most  going  to Sweden  (Hindstrom 1978, 126-127).  Since 1960  emigration  has slowed,  but it still continues.

The  Narpes greenhouses  also  grow  flowers for fresh  cuttings,  flowering  potted  plants,  and  seedlings  for  flower  gardens.  The market for flowers  and  plants  is  much more limited  than is  that for  vegetables, probably  because  purchases  of  flowers  and  plants  are a  discretionary expenditure.  The most  important greenhouse  flower is the rose, associated  widely  in Finland with school  graduation  and with the custom of bringing  flowers when invited to dinner or to  parties.
sections.CHALLENGE OF THE FUTURE:
The  probable  entry  of Finland  into the  European  Union casts  a  shadow of  anxiety  over the  greenhouse  horticultural  entrepreneurs.  Although  the Finnish market seems secure, other  potentially  lucrative  European  markets are not so.  Long  hours of darkness in late winter and  early spring, combined with the cold climate,  increase  the  production  costs of  heating and artificial  lighting,  in  comparison  with those in the Low Countries  and the Channel  Islands,  the chief  competing  areas.  For  example,  the Netherlands, the  strongest competitor,  has six weeks more  daylight  in fall and spring,  as well as  considerably higher temperatures.  The  longer  summer daylight  in Finland is not a  compensation,  because it comes at a time when field  vegetables supply  the market.  Transportation costs for  Narpes growers  to the  principal  European  urban  markets  are  also  higher  than  are those from  competing  areas.

Fuel cost is one of the  greatest  problems  for  Narpes  horticulturalists. The Dutch fuel cost is  currently  only  one-half that of the  Finns,  and the Dutch must use  only  about one-half as much fuel as do the Finns in a

normal  growing  season. Another chief  disadvantage  for Finnish  producers is that loans from the  government  for  development  and  expansion must  be  amortized in  ten  years,  whereas  Dutch  horticulturalists are permitted thirty  years  in which to amortize their  loans  (Hindstr6m  1978, 126-127).

Balanced  against  these deficiencies are several  positive aspects.  The quality  of the  greenhouse vegetables, especially  tomatoes, is  high,  and contamination  by  environmental  poisons  is lower than  in western  Europe (Horticultural  production  1993,  3).  Labor  costs are  lower in Finland than they  are  in most  competing European  areas,  and the work ethic and sense of  responsibility  are  very high  in Finland.  Another  positive  factor  for the Finns is that  expansion  of the Dutch  greenhouse  horticulture  will  require acquisition  of additional land. Because  of the  pressure  of  population  and the  fully developed  economy  of the Netherlands,  expansion  would  be very expensive,  which would add to the future  cost of  greenhouse vegetables there.  Perhaps  most  important  of  all,  the  Narpes entrepreneurs have  already  demonstrated their  ability  to  compete successfully  in the German and  Russian markets. Because of  its  proximity,  the  Russian market  appears  to be  especially inviting.
sections.A THEORY OF ECONOMIC TRANSITION:
The  successful evolution and  development  of  greenhouse  horticulture in  Narpes  illustrate  a  process  that  has  been  occurring  in Finland  and some other areas of  Europe.  Two excellent  examples  from other communes in western Finland are  fur  farming,  centered  on  Jakobstad,  and Konni  clock manufacturing,  in  Ilmajoki. Each  of these industries  represents  the  adjustment of a local area to  declining agricultural  resources and  increasing population, essentially  the same conditions that once  prevailed  in Narpes.

An inductive  theory explains  the occurrence  in rural areas of  highly specialized  industrial communities formed  by  similar small-scale enterprises, originally  with  quite  low  technological  levels  (Palomaki 1983). Thus far, empirical  results have  come  from Finland and from central Europe.  The  point  of  departure  is an older  agricultural  area,  where all available  agricultural  resources  have been used, so that  expansion  in  any traditional  way  is no  longer possible (Fig.  4).  The  economy  is so one-dimensional that  virtually  no other  ways  of livelihood exist.  Transportation is slow and  expensive.  No  possibilities  for  commuting  to  adjacent,  more developed  areas  exist because the  process  of urbanization  there  is still in an initial and  rudimentary phase.  Therefore,  livelihood  necessarily  remains centered on the local area.

The  population  is nevertheless  growing.  The birthrate  remains at a high  level,  but  because  of  improved  health care and  rising  levels  of hygiene  the death rate  is  decreasing.  The  rate  of  migration  is  low,  initially

FIG.  4-Model for  regional  agrarian change.

<!-- image -->

because of these conditions. As a result of continued subdivision of  land, farms  have become smaller  and,  especially during  famine  years,  production of food remains limited and  inadequate.  These conditions lead to a continually growing  population  pressure. Because an  expanded  labor force cannot be  used  in  agriculture, unemployment  with  unfavorable social  consequences  follows.

On the  positive  side,  these  conditions  sensitize  an  area to  accept changes  to  improve living  standards and the immediate economic situation. The diffusion of information about conditions  prevailing  outside the area  performs  a  key  function.  Knowledge  of  living  conditions elsewhere and information  about  possibilities  for  expansion  there  encourage mass  emigration, despite  the difficulties of  transportation.  Mainly  the young  and  more  venturesome  segment  of  the  population  departs. Though  effective,  this  pattern  is not the  most  advantageous  way  to relieve population pressure:  the area  loses the  part  of its  population  that is most likely  to  accept changes  and to  promote  in situ modifications.

At the same time, an information flow from outside  may  include the knowledge  of new  ways  of  production,  often with  details for  specific economic activities. A  person  with  special  skills and new ideas  may  come to the area or be aware of its  surplus  labor force and  tempted  to  exploit low  wage  levels. This  entrepreneur  initiates  production,  and if the enterprise  is  successful,  additional  workers  are  needed and  hired.  The  requisite skills must be communicated to these newcomers to the  industry.

<!-- image -->

1st  generation

2nd  generation

3rd  generation of economic  growth  and diffusion  in a local area. The X ind

Workers  are local  people,  most  likely  former farmers  and their  sons, who  are used  to  working  independently.  If the  firm continues  to be successful and the  original entrepreneur  becomes  financially  secure, the boldest and most  energetic  workers  may  demand an increased share of the returns.  One  way  to achieve this outcome is for  them to establish  new enterprises.  The new  entrepreneurs'  skills are  apt  to be limited to those proved  in the  original enterprise.  Therefore,  the new firm must be of the same  type  as the  original  one  (Fig. 5a).  If the  outgrowth  is  successful, additional firms will be started. The  consequences  are the  same, and a new  generation  of  firms  emerges.  The  process  can be  repeated many times.  Although  some  failures and other  interruptions  of  growth  will occur,  the total number of firms  steadily  increases.

The first  firm will  often  be  located  in  the  most  accessible  place, because  the  entrepreneur  has no  previous  ties to the  community  and makes a rational decision influenced  by  market forces  (Fig. 5b).  For the second-generation  firms of local  entrepreneurs,  the  deciding  locational factor  usually  is  prior ownership  of  the  land,  if  the  general  location satisfies other  preconditions  for the  activity.  Therefore,  the distribution pattern may  be scattered. Much later,  if  growth  is sufficient, the intense rivalry characterizing  these  pioneering  phases  will  ease  and be  supplanted by  cooperation  in  subcontracting, marketing,  traffic  arrangements, and  repair-shop arrangements.  The  changes happen  because the cost of these activities is  beyond  the economic resources of individual enterprises,  but  their  functioning  benefits  all  of  the  enterprises.  The entrepreneurs  will  find it  profitable  to start education and  training  in the field and to take care of roads, water  supplies,  and sewer  systems, as well  as other  components  of an economic infrastructure. Thus the benefits of  agglomeration begin  to  strengthen  the  position  of the new industrial area.

At the same time, other  changes  occur in the area. The  mobility  of people  increases  by migration,  because of better  information,  closer links to outside  areas,  and  greater  accessibility  to  transportation.  These same conditions  encourage  local  commuting  of workers to outside centers of employment.  The  productivity  of  agriculture  increases with new methods and  increasing intensity  of landuse in farms and  through  the same kind of  enterprise development  as is  experienced  in  industry.  The  whole process  of economic  change  leads to lowered  population pressure  and a better-adjusted  and better-balanced  population,  and the area  shifts from a local orientation to a  regional  one.

records.title: Settin' the woods on fire: Rural incendiarism as protest
records.abstract: Fire is a fundamental tool within a broad spectrum of vegetation-management strategies, from swidden agriculture to plantation forestry. Through the seemingly pyromanic activity of incendiarism, fire assumes additional significance in the human-environment relationship. Case studies from England, Algeria, and the southern United States serve to illustrate the circumstance of fire as an indication of agrarian discontent and a weapon of peasant resistance. Other documented cases of incendiarism reveal that use of fire in the landscape has expanded from a constructive ecosystem-manipulation technique to a destructive form of protest undertaken by the oppressed or disempowered.

sections.ROBERT KUHLKEN:
ABSTRACT. Fire  is a fundamental  tool within a  broad  spectrum  of vegetation-management strategies,  from swidden agriculture  to plantation forestry.  Through  the seemingly pyromanic activity  of incendiarism,  fire  assumes  additional  significance  in the human-environment relationship.  Case  studies  from  England, Algeria,  and  the  southern  United  States  serve to illustrate  the circumstance  of fire  as  an  indication  of agrarian discontent  and  a  weapon  of peasant resistance.  Other documented cases of incendiarism  reveal  that use of fire in the landscape has expanded from a constructive  ecosystem-manipulation  technique to a destructive  form  of protest  undertaken by  the  oppressed  or  disempowered.  Keywords:fire, land tenure,  peasant  revolt, political  ecology.

I'll  gas  up my  hot rod  stoker We'll get hotter  than  a  poker You'll be  broke  but  I'll  be  broker Tonight  we're settin'  the  woods  on  fire

-As  sung  by Hank  Williams,  1952

'ire has  long  been  a  cultural tool  for  modifying the  environment. Humans  and their  antecedent hominids have  used fire as  an  effective and  efficient method  of  converting  resources  for  250,000 years,  if  not  longer.  Carl  Sauer wrote  that  man  "learned early  that fire  aided  in collecting  food, both plant  and animal,  and thus  began  the practice  of setting  fire  to vegetation" (1975, 4). Omer  Stewart  counted  a number  of reasons  for prehistoric  and  what  he described  as  primitive  uses  of fire:  to facilitate hunting or travel  by removing  dense  vegetation;  to drive  or direct  game during  a hunt;  to improve  pasture  for  game;  to  increase the  yield  of  wild  plant  foods;  and  as  an act of war (1956) (Figure 1).

With the development  of agriculture, burning  became  an integral  maneuver  in opening up new lands  for  cultivation  or in clearing  pastures  for  domestic  livestock. Conversion  of wildlands  to agropastoral systems  around  the world has absolutely depended on fire,  and burning continues to play  a major  role in current  agrarian production  strategies. Swidden  is  still  the  dominant  land  use  in many  tropical  areas, and  bush-fallow  agrosystems utilizing  slash-and-burn methods  are  now  recognized as  successful  and  sophisticated  adaptations to the  rain-forest  environment.  Grazing is  another  tropical  land  use  that  relies  on fire  for  the  maintenance  of savannas  or  for enhancing forage  within wooded areas.  In modern forestry,  controlled  burning  is widely  used  as  a  silvicultural prescription, for  hazardous-fuel reduction,  and  for  watershed and wildlife management.  Fire  is also used extensively  in other managed ecosystems,  such  as  midlatitude  rangelands and  heathlands. Indeed,  fire  has  enabled human  occupation  and use of the earth (Pyne 1995, 1997).

m$' DR. KUHLKEN is an associate  professor  of geography  at Central  Washington  University,  Ellensburg,  Washington  98926-7420.

FIG.  i-Fire  was  often  used  by  American  Indian  tribes  to create  favorable conditions for  hunting,  as depicted  in Prairie  Meadows  Burning,  a  pencil  and  watercolor  by  George  Gatlin,  1832.  (Private  collection; reproduced  in Truettner  1979,  248)

<!-- image -->

Fire  has  been an  effective weapon  in  warfare  as  well,  at  least  since  the Greek  and Roman  Empires  (GoudsbloM  1992). But  there  is another  cultural  tradition  of burning,  a  similarly destructive  one that  has  developed  in  addition  to  outright  acts  of  war or deliberate  "scorched-earth" policies.  Through  the act of incendiarism,  humans have infused  fire  in the  landscape  with even more  meaning.
sections.FORMS OF INCENDIARISM:
An incendiary  fire  has  been defined  as  a  "wildfire willfully  set  by  anyone  to  burn,  or to spread  to,  vegetation  or  property  not owned or controlled  by  him, and  without consent of the owner or his agent"  (Forest  Service  1978, 9). Although  the popular Hank  Williams  song  used  "settin' the  woods  on  fire" merely  as  a  metaphor, these  illuminating  lyrics  are  clearly indicative  of  actions  familiar to  many  rural  residents.  Motives for  such actions  include  personal  grievances  against  landowners,  attempts  to devalue  property  for  speculative  economic gain,  incidents  of arson  by  unemployed firefighters who seek  work,  and  the  pyromanic  activities  of demented  individuals. The focus of this article  is on incendiarism  as  a tool of protest  or resistance.

Arson is  listed  by  James  C.  Scott  as  one of the  "weapons of the  weak"  that  "relatively  powerless  groups" utilize  against  ",those who seek  to extract  labor,  food, taxes, rents,  and interest  from  them"  (1985,  29).  Rural  incendiarism,  according  to George

Rude,  belongs  "to  that  shadowy  realm  between  crime  and  protest  where  it  is  often  no easy  matter  to tell  the two apart" (1978,  4). In  cultural-ecological terms,  destructive burning of the landscape  represents  seemingly  maladaptive behavior,  as  a result  of which the perpetrators themselves  become  victims.  But  a review  of the  literature of peasant resistance  stamps  this type of incendiarism  an act of desperation,  which must be seen as  part  of a  "rebellion  of hopelessness" (Scott  1976, 195). In  many  cases it is  a  refractory phenomenon that  occurs  wherever  an  established  agrarian order  is forced  to undergo change  that threatens  to disrupt  its particular  subsistence  ethic and its  traditional  resource-use  patterns.  These  inflammatory reactions  range  from isolated  incidents  of arson  to jacquerie,  or full-blown  peasant  revolt,  during  which incendiarism  may be widespread.  Frederick Gamst  found that "such  uprisings  of peasants  often  stem  from  increased rates  of  extraction of  the  fund  of  rent,  or  from  attempts to alter  the nature  of their  ties to the land"  (1974,  48).

In the wake of commercial agriculture,  the rise of export-driven  plantation space-economies,  and  postcolonial  modernization  of the  peasantry, rural  incendiarism persists  as a political-ecological  trait  operating  in defiance  of unpopular  government  policies  or  as  a  symbolic  and  immolatory  act  of  protest.  The  representative case studies reviewed  below, followed  by a brief assessment  of incendiary  activity elsewhere  around  the world,  serve  to illustrate  this idea.
sections.ARSON IN THE ENGLISH COUNTRYSIDE:
The  first  documented  widespread use  of incendiarism as  a  means  of  protest  began  in England  in the eighteenth  century  and  culminated  in the "Captain Swing"  revolt  of 1830. During  the  1700s,  rural  discontent  was  provoked by  enclosure  laws  and  ensuing competition for forest  resources: game,  timber,  firewood,  and  forage  for  cattle  and sheep.  Privatization of  traditional  commons  land  subsequently placed  unreasonable production  pressure  on remaining  "open" resources  and  created deep-seated  resentment. The government  reacted  to the  protest,  and  a  vicious  cycle  ensued.  Increased poaching  and  malicious  destruction  of deer  parks  and  hedges,  often  by  gangs  of men disguised  with blackened  faces,  led to the passage  of the Black  Act in 1723, making trespass  and poaching of Crown  game capital  offenses.  This forced  a conflict  between gamekeepers  and traditional  users  of the forest  and  contributed  to the radicalization of the peasantry.  Arson within emparkments  increased  as a gesture  of indignation  (Charlesworth 1983, 60). As  Edward Palmer  Thompson  explained,  "the resort  of deer  poachers  to more  highly  organized  force  may  be seen  as  retributive in character and  concerned  less  with  venison  as  such  than  with  the  deer  as  symbols  (and as  agents)  of  an  authoritywhich threatened  their  economy,  their  crops,  and  their  customary  agrarian rights" (1975,  64).

Continuing enclosure  of commons and wastelands  was part of the rise of an agrarian  capitalism  that endangered  the subsistence-based  economy of the peasantry.  Moreover,  as Scott points out, the "right  to subsistence" was perceived  in moral and social context,  so its inevitable  demise  was at the core  of peasant  revolt (1976, 33).  Between 1750 and  1850  the  English peasant became  a  proletarian farm  la-

borer,  cut  off  from  customary rights  to  land  and  confronted  with  ever-increasing agricultural  mechanization.  Agrarian unrest  resulted  in a  "tendency for  incendiarism to flare  up  occasionally and  to maintain  itself  at  a  very  high  level  during  certain  periods of disturbance" (Hobsbawm  and Rude  1968, 80). Such  cultural-ecological disturbances included extremely harsh winters, failed harvests,  and the return of 250,000 men looking for farmwork  after  the Napoleanic  Wars.  Particularly rebellious  years were  the  1790s,  1816,  1822-1823,  1830,  1834-1835,  and  1843-1844,  and  incendiarism  was an increasingly  frequent  tool of protest (p. 16).  Poor  wages for farm labor  became  the  leading  grievance, especially  in  the  eastern  counties,  where  setting fire  to haystacks was a common practice  (Peacock  1974, 31) (Figure  2).

The Captain  Swing  revolt,  named  after  a  mythical  sender  of threatening letters, manifested  two components:  attacks  on threshing  machines  as  the  perceived  cause of unemployment,  and  an  unprecedented wave  of incendiarism. This  was  "no  longer a  case  of isolated  attacks  on ricks" but  an  organized protest  for  higher  wages;  during November  1830 "all  of southern  England  seemed  in flames"  (Hobsbawm  and Rude 1968,  102, 84).  With  the  invention  of the  strike-anywhere "Lucifer match"  that  same year  (1830),  "technology it  would  seem  had  come  to  the  aid  of  the  protester at  just  the right  historical  moment"  (Archer  1990,  24).

These  fires  signaled  a  profound  change  in the  economic  geography  of a rapidly industrializing  nation. Peasants  found themselves  obsolete in the emerging  landscape  of mechanized  Britain. As  J.  P.  D.  Dunbabin  remarked, "agricultural labor  was in widespread  surplus,  a factor  underlying  many  of the riots,  fires,  and  threatening letters"  (1974,  297).  Differential  agricultural ecologies  within the country  created  a spatial  component for the protests.  In addressing the geography  of rural  incendiarism in England  at  this  time,  Eric  Hobsbawm  and  George  Rude  note that  the revolt "occurred  essentially  in the  regions  in  which  cereal  farming  was  combined  with  low wages"  and  list the counties  of North and  East  Kent,  Surrey, East  Sussex,  West  Norfolk,  Cambridgeshire, and  Lincolnshire as  particularly prone  to incendiarism  (1968, 173).

After 1830,  incendiarism  became the predominant  weapon in the arsenal  of agrarian revolt.  John  Archer  reported that  "from  October  1843 to  December  1844 incendiarism  throughout  England  reached  an unprecedented  scale"  and actually  attained  an  incidence  rate  of  twice  that  which  occurred during  the  Swing  period  (1990, 107).  According  to David Jones,  "arson  was the dominant  form of rural  protest  in East  Anglia  during  the  years  1842-51," reflecting  heightened  farm-labor  oppression and  increasing class  struggle  (1976, 6).  High  unemployment  in  Suffolk caused  a  peak year  for  arson  there  in  1844 (Charlesworth 1983,162);  and  in  Cambridgeshire, during the  early  1850s, Sir  James Caird  noted  that  "these incendiary  fires  are  said  to  be of almost nightly  occurrence," causing  farmers to make  certain  adaptations in their  harvesting methods: "The  corn ricks  are  built in different  parts  of the fields,  seldom contiguous,  so that  if one should  be fired  the  rest  may  have  some chance  to escape" (1967,467).  Townscapes  in  Cambridgeshire likewise  were  transformed: "The  scale  of incendiarism  in these  villages  during  the 1840s  altered  their  architecture since re-

placement  buildings  were  constructed  of brick  and  tile,  a  less risky  proposition  for insurance  companies"  (Archer  1990, 149).

Arson  was  also  charring the  landscape  of  Wales, often  due  to  "long-standing battles  over  common rights,  encroachments  and  sheep-walks" (Jones  1985,97).  Despite contrary  claims that "the  Welsh  did not resort  to incendiarism," Jones  recounted

sections.ALGERIA IN FLAMES:
Just  as British  fires  were  fading,  the mountains  of northern  Africa  experienced  the beginnings  of arson  as  a  weapon  of peasant  resistance. Arab  and  Berber  peoples  inhabiting  the forested  highlands  of what  was  to become  Algeria were  cultivators  and pastoralists  who worked  within the fire  ecology  of their  Mediterranean landscape. Late-summer  controlled  burning  was  a  traditional  method  of enhancing  forage  the following  season,  one that  opened  up  farmlands for  cereal  and  vegetable  crops.  This clearing  by fire  was  part  of a crop-livestock complex  with a three-year  fallow  (Prochaska  1986,  230). Although  rights  to use  cleared lands  were  hereditary, the forest  at large  was considered  a common resource.  After  the 1830 French  invasion,  colonial authorities  expropriated these  lands  and  began  to issue  concessions  during  the  1850S and  186os  that  stimulated  a  thriving  commercial  cork  industry. Forestry  officials  attempted  to administer  a  forest  code  imported  from  Europe that  strictly  curtailed traditional subsistence  activities,  including  the pasturing  of sheep and goats.  When petitions submitted  by peasant  groups  failed  to stop this onslaught  on indigenous rights,  incendiarism  flared.

Between  186o  and  19oo a  series  of conflagrations erupted  as  peasants  torched  the woods; particularly bad  years  were  1871,  1877,  and  1881. Pushed  aside  by settlement schemes and the demarcation  of state-controlled  forestlands,  herders  resorted  to burning  as  a  tool of resistance: "In  protest  they  fired  the  reserved forests" (Pyne  1997, 121).  Forest  arson  was the lead  weapon in "the  clash  between  two opposed  ways  of life,  between  two  political  economies"  (Prochaska 1986, 239). As  control  of  the  forest shifted  from  the subsistence-based peasantry  to the capitalists holding  concessions, peasants  were  forced  to enter  the cash  economy  and  become  forest  laborers.  Incendiarism  abated  somewhat,  though  it  never  ended  entirely, as  resistance to French  colonial domination  persisted  and  finally  climaxed  in the  Algerian  Revolution  of 1954, which Nico Kielstra  characterized as  a  "peasant war"  (1978) and during  which,  Eric Wolf noted, incidents  of arson  were  common in the Aures  Mountains  (1969, 236). Even  several  years  later,  in August  1956,  a  fire  in the  Bainem  State  Forest  outside  Algiers  "was believed  to  have  been  started by  nationalist  rebels" (New  York Times  1956).
sections.SOUTHERN WOODS BURNING:
In  the United  States,  incendiarism  occurs  most frequently in the South  (Forest  Service  1978;  Clark 1984),  with  Alabama and,  especially, Mississippi  and  Louisiana noted as  hot spots (Hansbrough  1961;  Dunkelberger and  Altobellis  1975) (Figure  3).  These and neighboring  states  contain  expansive  tracts  of planted  pines  that  are  only  now reaching  maturity  and that have  been fuel laden  for several  decades.  But,  as  Alvin Bertrand  and  Andrew  Baird  correctly pointed  out,  "there is  no  way  to  understand the incendiary  problem  in the  Southern  region  without  a  knowledge  of the  cultural  history of this part  of the nation"  (1975,  5).

In  the  South,  colonial  and  postcolonial  settlement  patterns  responded  to the already  established  presence  of large  clearings  "maintained as  such  by  recurrent fires" (Prunty  1965, 165). At  the  beginning  of the  nineteenth  century, settlers  in the  region quickly  adopted  the  aboriginal technique  of firing  the  landscape.  European  agricultural  traditions  also included  the use of fire  (Otto and  Anderson  1982).  Although Amerindian burning was common in all areas of the continent, Stephen Pyne pointed to the southern  frontier  as home to "a  blend of European  and Indian  fire practices" and stated  that  "more  than  any  other  region  of the U.S.,  this amalgamation persisted  in the South, giving it an incendiary  tradition  without parallel  in America"  (1982,  124).

Fred  Kniffen  believed  that  the initial  impetus  behind  southern  woods burning was  the free-range  cattle  complex,  which  developed  when  the  traditional  European right to pasture  stock on common lands met the abundant  forage  opportunities provided  within the  large  expanses  of open,  parklike pine forests  created  and  maintained by fire (1990). This subsistence  adaptation  was aided  by a haphazard,  often noncontiguous  land-granting  process  whereby  many  undeveloped  or  uncultivated blocks of land remained  interspersed  with newly cleared  farms  (Hilliard  1972, 9). Eventually, as southern  timber  resources  became  recognized  and  valued,  many  of these  parcels  came  under  corporate  or  absentee  ownership. The  cattle  owners,  however,  still  considered  it  within  their  rights  to use  these  lands  to graze  their  stock  and to enhance  forage  by the tradition  of annual  firing  (Bertrand and Baird  1975, 16).

The superimposition  of commercial  forestry  added  fuel  to the fires  of southern incendiarism.  Fire  protection  became  the  leading  management tenet  of  large  corporate  landowners,  as it had earlier  been adopted  by the federal  government  when it consolidated  the remaining  public  domain  into national  forests.  Traditional subsistence  strategies  of the  backwoods  farmer-stockman were  threatened. As  Pyne  put  it: "The  Indian  whose hunting  grounds  had  vanished  into farms  had  a  counterpart in the  agrarian southerner  whose  hunting  and  herding  lands  were  swallowed  by  industrial forests"  (1982,  154).  Retaliatory  fires  became a common practice  known as "burning  the  big  man"  (Kerr 1958,29),  although  Albert  Smith  suggested that  arson  in Reconstruction-era  Georgia  may  have  been "violent,  interracial protest,  a form of revenge  for the racism  and poverty  that defined  the region's race  relations" (1985, 528).  More  frequently, many  areas  of the  South  experienced "fires of a  vindictive  nature"  that  may  be  linked  to forfeiture  of tax-delinquent lands  and  the  eventual  creation of large  holdings,  both public  and  private  (Folweiler  and  Brown  1946,  40).

By  the  1930s incendiarism  was  so rampant  in the South  that  the U.S.  Forest  Service hired  teams  of sociologists  to "conduct  research  into the underlying  reasons" for the fires, focusing on "the sociocultural environment within which acts of woods-burning  take  place"  (Dunkelberger and  Altobellis 1975, 5). These  sociological investigations  were  revived  during  the 1970S and  revealed that  many  of the reasons for the high rate  of fire  setting  in the South  persisted.  Although,  in the outsider's view,  "the  benefits  are  mostly  imaginary," the apparent  cause  of most incendiarism remained  "traditional woodsburning  practices" (Randall  1963, 54).
