Finally,  we assumed that large  families  need more grain,  reducing  the amount of arable  land that  can  be committed  to other  ventures  and,  as  a  consequence,  deducting  from  the value of sales.

We divided the households  by county to determine  whether  results  would vary by location. They do, significantly: The model for Huai'an  achieved  a much better level  of explanatory  power  (adjusted  R2 =  0.71)  than  did  that  for  Huaiyin  (adjusted R = 0.38). For  the  five  independent  variables, across  the  two  locations,  only  one  variable,  ECONAREA, was significant  in both places  (even at p = .11, when the signs reverse).  Still,  two of five  hypothesized  variables are  significant  for  Huaiyin  (at .05 or better),  and three  of five  are  significant  for  Huai'an  (at .05  or better).

In  sum,  the  models  are  significant  and  stable,  although  the  explanatory power  of the Huaiyin  model is limited.  What  is most clear  is  that  although  these  two  counties are  adjacent,  Huaiyin  and  Huai'an  are  different  places-and that  their  farm  households  have  adopted  very  different  strategies for  generating income from  agriculture. The following scenario  emerges.

For  the Huaiyin sample,  the highest reported  sales  of off-farm  products  come from  households  that  grow  grain  but  use  their  surplus  for  feeder  operations  at  home

and  sell  no grain  to  the  state. This  is  the  way  to  live  in  a  rice-growing district  and  still make  some money:  One grows  grain  as  required, but one does  not sell  it-one  converts it to pork.  A further  measure  of Huaiyin's focus on livestock  is that the area sown to economic crops is actually  a drag  on maximum  sales  per household (the coefficient  for  ECONAREA in Huaiyin  is  negative). With  prices  for  quality  feed  at  levels  at  or  above  mean  prices  for  rice  and  wheat,  farmers gain  the  most  by  raising  livestock  and  feeding  them  surplus  grain,  even  though  rice  and  wheat-the  major  grains of these farms-are  extremely  inefficient  feedstuffs.  This is reasonable  from the household's  perspective  but a poor use of resources.

The results  for Huai'an  are  markedly  different,  for farmers  there  are  utilizing increasingly  unique income-generating  strategies;  and whereas  Huaiyin  farmers concentrate  on livestock,  those  in Huai'an  concentrate  on vegetables.  Huai'an  specializes  in selling  vegetables  to cities,  and the sale of livestock  is not a significant contributor  to the  gross  value  of sales.  Significant relationships  for  Huai'an  include total  crop  area,  area  sown in economic crops  (p = .11), distance  to fields,  and  size  of the household. The larger  area  sown to nongrain  crops  translates  to a  higher  gross value for  vegetables  sold by Huai'an  farmers.  Greater  sales  mean  higher  incomes.

Commercialization  of agriculture  has helped farmers  in Subei,  but their incomes lag when compared  with those of factory  workers  (Su and  Veeck  1995).  Reported  per  capita  incomes,  adjusted for  inflation,  for  the  Huaiyin  households  in the survey  rose  only  34 percent,  from  u.s.$187.oo  in  1987 to  U.S.$251.00 in  1996. In Huai'an,  beyond  the reach  of legislation  that  makes  grain  growing  mandatory, the increase  was  also  34  percent, but  the  mean  absolute  per  capita  income  was  25  percent greater there than in Huaiyin, because per capita income increased from u.s.$235.00 to U.S.$314.52.  This compares with an urban per capita income  in Jiangsu in 1987  of u.s.$350.OO,  which  increased to u.s.$625.54 in 1996 (ZTN  1988, 199;  1997,  300).
sections.FINDINGS:
In Jiangsu  a clear  distinction  exists  between  grain  economies and economies that produce other crops. Despite price adjustments  and subsidies,  grain production during  the reform  era  remains  a poor investment  for  household  labor  and  capital. Net income from the production  of wheat  has changed  only insignificantly  since 1987.  Returns  for rice are slightly  better,  but only because  price adjustments  are greater.

Although  we recognize  that  policies  surrounding  grain  production  are  fraught with a  peril  that  many  a  European Union or  American  trade  negotiator knows  all  too well,  we believe  that the other  positive  results  of China's market-reform  strategies deserve  greater  international  recognition.  Because  of the fixation  on grain-related issues,  this respect  has yet  to materialize.

If any  other  nation  were  to record  increases  in production  commensurate  with China's, the  pundits  would  be ecstatic.  Our  surveys  show  that  economic  conditions are  improving  on the  farms  of Huaiyin  and  Huai'an, an  area  once  renowned  only  for great  poverty.  Simply  put,  market  access  has  improved  remarkably, due in no small

measure  to sales  of vegetables  and  livestock.  A  great  variety  of products  from  Subei now flow quite freely  to Sunan  and  beyond,  providing  consumers  with better  diets and more choices. Still, oversupply  and insufficient  information about regional market  prices  have  limited the benefits  of nongrain  farm  production.

The  market  alone  cannot  solve  problems  of  low  returns for  meat,  grain,  and  produce:  Every  major  agricultural nation is experiencing  low prices  and related  problems in the new millennium.  Still,  our surveys  support  other  research  and  popular opinion which  maintain  that  the  "grain  problem" must  be  resolved through  a  mix  of policy adjustments  and economic incentives (Liu and Huang 1995;  China Daily 1996;  Huang  1998).  Most  Chinese  experts  suggest  that,  painful  though  the  process  be in the  short  run,  grain  markets must  be  reformed  and  allowed  to reach  some  equilibrium of price and supply.  Government  intervention  can cushion the adjustment. Considering  the agricultural policy  histories  of the  United  States  and  other  Western nations,  simply  rushing  headlong  to the market  may  well  cause  as  much  damage  in China  as  ignoring  the  problem.  Typically, the  fastest way  to fuel  inflation  and  unrest in China's  urban  areas,  and  to restrict  the  growth  of the  economy  at  large,  would  be to raise  the price  of food, particularly grain,  rapidly.

China's  leaders find themselves  in a dilemma, albeit a common one. Grainsecurity issues are  important to Beijing  and the urban  population of China,  but continued market  reform  of the agricultural sector  is of even  greater  concern.  The sheer  count of farmers  in China  makes  nationally  instigated  draconian  regulations affecting grain production genuine threats  to social stability.  Higher consumer prices  will fuel inflation and make  manufactured  goods more expensive  in global and domestic markets.  Continued low prices  will assure  long-term shortages  of grain  while other  agricultural activities  claim  ever-greater shares  of  land,  labor,  and capital.

If  the  agricultural reform  policies  that  are  being  revised  do not somehow  square the circle  and promote grain  production,  while also permitting  the production  of crops currently  under the "invisible  hand,"  national interests  will suffer.  On the other  hand,  times  change.  Farmers wish  for,  perhaps  now even  demand,  inclusion  in this debate.  The agricultural economy found in every  province,  every  county,  and perhaps even every  village is now often quite different  from that in neighboring places.  Agriculture in more  affluent  regions  has  grown  increasingly commercial  and diversified, reflecting  a  growing  responsiveness to  the  larger  economy  (Xu  1988; Fleisher and Liu 1992; Li R.  X. 1996;  Zhou 1996).  Poor  locations in central  or western China  still  depend  on grain  and  a  strictly  limited  number  of cash  crops.  This  makes much more complicated  the implementation  of nationwide  pricing,  distribution, and  environmental  protection  policies  sent  from  Beijing. If  effective  policies  cannot come from  the  top down,  from  where  do  they  issue? Are  the  provinces willing  to  take on the task?  Would concentrating  power  and policymaking  at the provincial  level help?

It  is  increasingly clear  that  grain  production  and  other  agricultural activities  are moving in different  directions  in response  to different  economic stimuli.  Although

this has raised  incomes,  in Jiangsu it has  also  introduced  inputs  with a direct  effect on the environment  and  health  of consumers.  Issues  of greatest  concern  in the flat alluvial  lands  of East  China  include  the  use  of field  plastics,  a  decline  in the  application of organic  manures,  and  the  greater amount  of pesticides  and  herbicides  associated with nongreenhouse  vegetable  and grain  production.  Furthermore, because most nitrogen,  phosphorous,  and  potassium  for  grain  production  now come from inorganic  fertilizer, health  problems  related  to field  runoff  and  local water  quality are  on the rise.

Market  and  government  must  work  together  to find  solutions  to  these  problems. Consumers  with choices  may  demand  pesticide-free  produce,  certified  meats,  and better-quality  products.  The "green  food"  movement  in Jiangsu  is a case  in point. Local  activism  will  alert  the  government  to  the  significance of these  issues  to  Jiangsu residents.  Farmers will  respond  when  consumers  pay,  or  if  the  government  provides financial  and  technical  support.  Still,  farmers will  continue  to  use  the  least  expensive pesticides  and herbicides-oil based and enduring-unless they are regulated  and offered  affordable  alternatives.

There  is an  irony  in the  timing  of our  research. When  we set out to conduct  the interviews  and surveys  in 1996,  China's  economy was booming. Over  and over  we asked experts, "How can the superheated  economy be slowed?"  As we conclude work on this article  in 2000, a recession  is hobbling  the nation's  general  economy, driving  large-scale layoffs  in Jiangsu's historic  heavy-industry cities  of Nanjing,  Xuzhou, Yangzhou,  and Nantong. Recession  threatens  erosion of the success  we saw during  our  stints  in  Huaiyin  and  Huai'an Counties.  Such  are  the  dangers of  the  marketplace.  The more integrated  these local economies become, the more they are affected  by macroeconomic  trends.  Industrial  cities,  in consort  with Shanghai  and the great  Sunan  cities  of Suzhou,  Wuxi,  and  Changzhou,  represent  the consumers who have  played  a critical  role  in transforming the rural  economy.  Distant  markets may  shine  with  the  beacon  of prosperity, but dependence  upon  that  beacon  can  put Jiangsu  farmers  and  the  villages  they  represent at  risk-an old  lesson,  always difficult to master.

records.title: Biodiversity and land-use change in the American Mountain West
records.abstract: Rural private lands in the Mountain West of the United States are undergoing a profound land-use conversion, from agriculture to low-density residential or exurban development, though little scientific study documents the ecological consequences of this change. Nongovernmental conservation organizations are working with ranchers to keep rangeland out of development and in ranching, ostensibly because these organizations believe that biodiversity is better protected on ranches than on exurban developments. We compared plant and wildlife communities across the principal rural land uses in the Mountain West: protection, livestock ranching, and exurban development. Native plant and faunal biodiversity was better maintained on ranches and protected areas than on exurban developments. Exurban developments favored species that were nonnative or adapted to human-altered environments. The continued conversion of ranches to exurban development suggests a long-term alteration of the region's natural heritage.

sections.BIODIVERSITY AND LAND-USE CHANGE IN:
JEREMY  D. MAESTAS,  RICHARD L. KNIGHT,  and WENDELL  C. GILGERT

ABSTRACT.  Rural  private  lands  in the Mountain  West  of the United  States  are  undergoing  a profound  land-use  conversion,  from  agriculture to  low-density  residential  or exurban  development,  though  little  scientific  study  documents  the  ecological  consequences of this  change. Nongovernmental  conservation  organizations  are  working  with ranchers  to  keep  rangeland out of  development  and in  ranching, ostensibly  because these  organizations  believe that biodiversity  is better  protected  on ranches  than on exurban  developments.  We  compared plant  and wildlife communities  across  the  principal  rural  land uses in the Mountain  West: protection, livestock ranching, and  exurban development.  Native  plant  and  faunal biodiversity was  better  maintained on ranches  and  protected areas  than  on exurban developments. Exurban developments  favored  species  that were nonnative or  adapted  to human-altered  environments. The continued conversion  of ranches  to exurban  development  suggests  a  long-term alteration  of the  region's natural  heritage.  Keywords: biodiversity, exurban  development, land use,  ranching.

Conservationists have an admirable  history  of  documenting the  impacts  of  human  land  uses  on  biodiversity  to  better  inform  resource-management decisions. Considering  all  that, the state of our current  knowledge  about land-use  changes  in the Mountain  West of the United  States is less than  satisfactory.  Across the  region, we work to diminish  extractive and  commodity-based industries,  such as water development,  logging,  mining,  and livestock  grazing,  but have  largely  failed to  recognize the  ecological  consequences  of our own  actions,  especially  where we choose  to live and  play.  While we devote  much  of our attention  to the traditional  consumptive land  uses  that  characterized the "Old West,"  other  threats to  biodiversity  become more  pervasive  each  year  with the  emergence  of a "New West."  Urban  sprawl and outdoor  recreation,  for  example,  are the second  and fourth  leading  causes  of the decline in  federally  listed threatened and  endangered species (Czech, Krausman, and Devers 2000).

The character of the New West is  being shaped by  a flood of  immigrants  seeking to  enjoy  the  natural amenities  and  recreational  opportunities of  a  region  rich  in

*fi MR.  MAESTAS is a  graduate student  in wildlife  biology  at Colorado  State  University, Fort  Collins, Colorado  80523-1474,  where DR.  KNIGHT is a  professor  of conservation  biology  and where MR.  GILGERT is a  faculty  affiliate  from the USDA-NRCS Wildlife  Habitat  Management  Institute.

public  lands  (Power 1996;  Masnick  2001).  Importantly,  however,  only  half  of  the West  is  public  lands;  the most  productive lands  in the  region  are  in  private  ownership (Scott  and others 2001). This is critical,  because  the most  profound  land-use change  in the New  West  is the  conversion  of  private lands  presently in  ranching  and farming  to rural  residential, or  exurban, developments  (Knight  2002). Unfortunately, conservationists  have  given  scant  attention  to  studying  the  ecological  implications of this western  land-use  conversion.

Addressed  here  are  some  of the  ecological issues  associated with  land-use  change in the Mountain West. For readers  who are unfamiliar  with the  region's  current status,  we  provide  a brief review of the  changes  that are  occurring  with human population,  dominant  land  uses,  and  growth  patterns. We  then examine  an  emerging strategy  that is  being implemented  to  protect  biodiversity  from these  growth pressures.  Testing  the unstated  assumptions  of this new conservation  strategy, we present  the results  of a  comparison  of  biodiversity on the three  principal  land  uses beyond incorporated  city  limits in the Mountain  West:  protected  areas  (areas  protected  from  residential development),  livestock  ranches, and  exurban  developments. We conclude  by considering  the  implications  of our  findings  for conservation.
sections.EXURBANIZATION OF THE MOUNTAIN WEST:
The  Mountain  West  of the United  States  is  experiencing a  human  population  boom that  rivals  any  in its  history.  Of the  eight  states  that  make  up  this  region-Arizona, Colorado,  Idaho,  Montana,  Nevada,  New  Mexico,  Utah,  and  Wyoming-five  are  the fastest growing  in the  country  (Figure  i). Metropolitan areas  and  their  suburbs  have accommodated  much of this  in-migration,  but rural  areas  are  growing  at a faster rate  (Heimlich  and  Anderson  2001).  Driven  by  a mixture  of economic and  qualityof-life  features,  people  are  increasingly drawn  to the rural  Mountain  West  (Power 1996).  Unlike  previous  booms driven  by  resource  extraction  and  commodity production,  the  present  period  of  growth  is fueled  by  the  expansion  of service,  recreation,  and information  industries  and is marked  by  the conversion  of  private  land use from  agriculture to exurban  development  (Riebsame,  Gosnell,  and Theobald 1996;  Sullins and others  2002).

As a  result,  three  of the  principal land  uses  in the rural  Mountain  West  today  are protection,  livestock  ranching,  and exurban  development.  Exurban  development refers  to  low-density  residential development  that  occurs  beyond  incorporated  city limits  (Nelson  and Dueker  1990;  Knight  1999).  The main  human  use in  protected areas  is  outdoor  recreation and  the  protection of  perceived natural values;  on ranches it is livestock  production;  in exurban  developments  it is human residence.  The amount of land in  protection  is  relatively  static,  with little added  annually.  The amount of land in  ranching  and exurban  development,  however,  is in flux:  Many ranches  are  being  subdivided  into  exurban  developments. In  Colorado,  for  example, 110o,ooo hectares  of  agricultural land  were  converted  to commercial  and  residential development  every  year  between  1992 and  1997  (Obermann,  Carlson, and  Batchelder 2000).

The extent of land-use  change  due to  population  growth  in rural areas of the Mountain  West is  greater  than that in urban areas because  of the  dispersed  nature of  exurban  development  (Theobald  2000; Sullins and others  2002). Instead of focusing growth  within  incorporated  city limits,  exurban  growth  exists as  pockets  of residential  development  embedded  in a matrix of  agricultural  and  protected  lands. Nearly  80  percent  of the land used for houses  constructed between  1994  and  1997  in the  United  States was  in  nonmetropolitan areas  (Heimlich  and Anderson  2001). Sites  adjacent  to  public  lands are  particularly  attractive for  development  (Riebsame, Gosnell,  and Theobald  1996;  Swanson  2001).  Also,  exurban  developments require  more land than do urban and suburban  developments  because each house is situated on a large  lot  (typically 4-16 hectares). Fifty-seven percent  of the houses built between  1994 and 1997 were on  lots  at least  4  hectares in  size  (Heimlich  and Anderson  2001). In general,  exurban  developments  increase the influences  associated with human  residences  at two  spatial  scales:  site,  with  highly  dispersed  housing;  and  landscape, through  the  placement  of  developments  in rural areas  (Duerksen  and others  2000).

In contrast to the  ecological consequences  of urban and suburban  development, the  effects  of  exurban  development are not  well  studied.  Many  researchers have documented  changes  in wildlife  communities in  and  around  metropolitan areas (Emlen 1974;  Beissinger  and Osborne  1982; Mills,  Dunning,  and Bates 1989;  Engels

and Sexton  1994;  Blair  1996;  Germaine  and others  1998; Bock, Bock,  and Bennett 1999;  Crooks and Soule  1999).  Far fewer studies have examined  biodiversity  associated with exurban  developments,  and no studies have  compared  biodiversity  on exurban  developments  with that on  ranches and  protected  areas  (Vogel 1989; Harrison  1997, 1998;  Odell  and  Knight  2001). Although  little  is known  about  the conversion  of ranchland  to exurban  development,  conservationists  have assumed that  it  results  in a  simplification of  biodiversity, favoring  generalist species  that  thrive in association  with humans over  those that are  more sensitive  (Knight  and Clark 1998;  Knight  2002; Knight  and others  forthcoming).

In  fact,  wildlife  habitat  is affected  both  directly and  indirectly  by  the conversion of western  ecosystems  to exurban  development  (Knight  and Clark  1998).  Soil and vegetation are  directly disturbed  and  lost  in  the  construction of  houses,  roads,  fences, and communication lines. Habitat  quality  is  degraded  by  a  proliferation  of nonnative  plants  and  the  presence  of  humans,  their  automobiles,  and  their  pets (Mills, Dunning,  and Bates  1989;  Knight  and Clark  1998;  Miller,  Knight,  and  Miller 2001). These  changes  result  in elevated mortality  rates,  as  well  as  habitat  loss and  degradation.
sections.CONSERVATION RESPONSE:
Concern  about  the conversion  of the Mountain  West's natural  heritage from  a  mixture  of  generalist and  specialist  species  to a narrower suite  of  human-adapted  species has  generated  a new  response  to  biodiversity  protection among nongovernmental conservation  organizations (NGOS). The traditional  response  to  protect biodiversity from  anthropogenic  degradation has  been to  purchase land  and  designate  it as  a  protected  area.  The  emerging  response  is to work  with ranchers  to  protect  biodiversity while  keeping  the  land  in  private  ownership  and  as  a  working  ranch (Alexander  and  Propst  2002). Typically, development  rights  on the ranches  are  acquired  through  purchased conservation  easements  while  ranchers  continue  to raise livestock.  This  approach  has become  increasingly  popular,  especially  among  NGOS such  as  The  Nature  Conservancy and the  Rocky  Mountain  Elk  Foundation  (Weeks 2002). In  Colorado, about  35,000  hectares of  private land  have  been  protected  through conservation  easements  by  The Nature  Conservancy  and  24,000 hectares  by  the Rocky  Mountain  Elk Foundation (GCOFR  2000). This  strategy  has  increased  the number  of land  trusts  that  seek  to  protect  private land  in  agriculture from  development.  By  2000,  more than 1,200 land trusts in the United States  had  protected roughly 1,051,000 hectares  through  conservation  easements  (LTA 2001).

This  emerging  response  to  biodiversity  protection  has some untested  assumptions, however.  It assumes  that  biodiversity  on ranches  is no different  from that found on  protected  areas,  or at least that  biodiversity  is better  served  on ranches than on exurban  developments.  NGOs are  taking  this mode of action to  protect biodiversity  with  virtually  no scientific  evidence  to  support  their  approach.  They continue with this  strategy  even  though many  environmentalists argue  that livestock  ranching  is  perhaps  the most detrimental  land use in the West  (Fleischner

1994;  Wuerthner  1994;  Donahue  1999). We tested the  assumptions  of the  emerging strategy  by comparing songbird,  mammalian  carnivore,  and  plant  communities across  the  gradient of  intensifying rural  land  uses  of  protection,  livestock  ranching, and exurban  development.
sections.STUDY AREA AND SITE SELECTION:
We conducted  our  study  from  May through  August  during  2000  and 2001 in the foothills  along  the  Front Range  of the  Rocky Mountains  in  northern  Larimer County, Colorado  (40050'  N, 105°15' W).  The  study  area  is  approximately 40  kilometers northwest  of Fort  Collins, the  nearest metropolitan area.  The  land-use  matrix  of the  region is a  blend of  private  ranchland, public  protected  areas,  and exurban  developments. The  vegetation is  a  mosaic  of  shrubsteppe and  mixed-grass prairie. Dominant  grasses include needle-and-thread  (Stipa  comata  Trin.  &  Rupr.  var.  comata),  blue  grama (Bouteloua  gracilis  [Kunth]  Lag.  var.  gracilis), western  wheatgrass  (Elymus  smithii [Rydb.]  Gould),  and  cheatgrass  (Bromus  tectorum  L.).  Shrubs  include mountain mahogany (Cercocarpus montanus  Raf.  var.  montanus),  skunkbrush  sumac  (Rhus trilobata Nutt.  var.  trilobata), and  bitterbrush (Purshia tridentata [Pursh]  DC.).  Common forbs include  fringed sage (Artemesia  frigida Willd.)  and  hairy goldaster (Heterotheca villosa  [Pursh]  Shinners  var.  villosa).  Average  annual  precipitation ranges  from  33  to  46 centimeters,  with  75  percent  of it  falling  between  April  and September  (Moreland  1980).

The  study  was  restricted to sites  with similar  physical  characteristics, including the  same  shrubsteppe  plant  community, with  elevations  between  1,740  to  2,200 meters,  and similar  soil  types  to reduce  natural variability  among  sites.  Study  sites had to  comprise  at least  1,ooo  hectares  in order  to minimize the influence  of surrounding  land uses.  We  used  1:24,000  orthophoto-quadrangle maps  and  plat  maps from the Larimer County  Assessor's Office  to determine  potential  sites.
sections.STUDY DESIGN AND DATA COLLECTION: We  compared  songbird,  mammalian  carnivore, and  plant  communities  across  three land uses:  public protected  areas  (Colorado  Division of Wildlife's  State  Wildlife Areas)  whose  principal use  was  outdoor  recreation and  wildlife  protection  (no grazing, logging, mining,  or water  development);  private-land  livestock  ranches  with cattle;  and  exurban  developments  with one house  per  14-20 hectares.  We  randomly selected  ninety-three points  across the three land uses to  survey songbirds  and mammalian  carnivores  and  sixty-nine  points  to  sample  the  plant community.1 At each  point  we  sampled  communities  using  75-meter  fixed-radius point  counts for songbirds,2  scent stations for mammalian  carnivores,3  and 20-by-50-centimeter quadrats  for  plants.4
sections.FINDINGS:

in exurban  developments.  Plant communities on ranches,  however,  differed  from those in  protected  areas  and exurban  developments.

sections.IMPLICATIONS FOR CONSERVATION:
Our results  support  the  emerging  strategy for  biodiversity  protection  being  implemented  by  environmental  NGOS.  Ranches  in our  study  supported  a more desirable biodiversity than  did  exurban  developments. This  is  evident  for  three  reasons.  First, ranches  were  virtually  the same as  protected  areas  in terms of  populations  of human-adapted  wildlife  species.  Second,  ranches  had  enhanced  populations  of native wildlife  species  of  conservation  concern  compared  with exurban  developments. Third,  plant  communities  on ranches  had  more  native  and  fewer  nonnative  species than did exurban  developments.

A more  ambiguous  relationship exists  between  ranches  and  protected areas.  The assumption  that these two land uses  support  similar  biodiversity  is  only partially borne out  by  our observations.  Ranches  and  protected  areas  supported  similarly low  populations  of  human-adapted wildlife  species  but  produced  variable  populations of other  species.  Also,  protected  areas  had a  higher  prevalence  of nonnative plant  species  and  fewer  native  plant  species  than did ranches.

A  generalization from our  study  is that there  is an increase  in  human-adapted wildlife  and  nonnative  plant  species  with  exurban  development. Interactions  among native,  nonnative,  and  human-adapted  species  could result  in  simplification  of the Mountain  West's  natural  heritage,  favoring  species  whose  evolutionary  life histories  allow  them  to exist  with  humans.  This  change has  negative  implications  for  the maintenance  of  biodiversity  at both the site scale  and the  landscape  scale,  and its consequences  are  increased  with  increasing  development  (Knight  2002).

Elevated  populations  of  human-adapted  songbirds  may  be  occurring  to the detriment  of other  species  (Marzluff, Gehlbach,  and Manuwal  1998).  For  instance, nest  predators  such as the black-billed  magpie (Pica  hudsonia)  may  lower the reproductive  success  of other birds in an area.  The blue  jay (Cyanocitta cristata),  a similar  nest  predator, has  been shown to increase  with urbanization  and  to  play  an important  role in the decline of an  endangered  bird,  the  golden-cheeked  warbler (Dendroica  chrysoparia) (Engels  and Sexton  1994).  The nonnative  European  starling (Sturnus  vulgaris)  competes  aggressively with native  birds  for  nesting  cavities. In one area  in  Nevada,  starlings succeeded  in  excluding  native  birds  from  nest sites for  five  years  (Weitzel  1988). Eric  Odell  and  Richard Knight,  who studied  songbirds in exurban  developments and  undeveloped  areas, found  that  exurban  developments supported  the  greatest densities  of black-billed magpies  and  European  starlings  and the lowest densities of other  songbirds,  which  may  be attributed  to interactions between  these  species  (2001).

House cats  and  domestic  dogs  are  subsidized  predators that  have  been  shown  to extend  the  realm  of human  influence  and  have  substantial impacts  on wildlife  populations  (Churcher  and Lawton  1987;  Miller,  Knight,  and Miller  2001).  These freeranging  pets  can occur at elevated  densities,  as seen in our  study,  because  they  are supplementally  fed and do not  depend  on densities  of native  prey species.  House cats have been  implicated  in the decline and extinction of  scrub-breeding  songbirds  in two studies  in California  (Hawkins  1998;  Crooks  and Soule  1999).  Further-

more,  Kevin  Crooks  and Michael  Soule found that  songbirds  persisted  in  patches with  coyotes because  these  native  predators reduced  the  number  of house  cats  (1999). Coyotes  were detected  less  frequently  in exurban  developments  than in the other land  uses  in our  study, which could  result  in  unusually  high songbird  mortality  owing  to domestic  cats.  Domestic  dogs  are  known  to harass  and  kill  wildlife,  but their impacts  are  less well studied.  Research has shown that  they  can extend  the zone of human influence  and contribute  to the annual  mortality  of some  species (Ballard and others  1999; Miller,  Knight,  and  Miller  2001).  Domestic dogs  and  house  cats have  been documented  to be more  prevalent  in exurban  developments,  especially near  houses,  possibly  at  the  expense  of other  native  predators, which  were  less  abundant  in exurban  developments  than  in  undeveloped  areas  (Odell  and  Knight  2001).

Nonnative  plants  can  change community dynamics  by disrupting  ecosystem processes  and  degrading  the  quality  of wildlife  habitat  (Masters  and  Sheley  2001). For  instance,  the  proliferation of  cheatgrass in the Mountain  West  has altered  historic  fire  regimes,  favoring  nonnative,  annual  grasslands over  native,  perennial  species. This invasive  plant  has  displaced  native  plants  and altered  the occurrence  of shrub-obligate  songbirds  that utilize these  ecosystems  (Rotenberry  1998).  In our study,  eight  of the  twenty-three  nonnative  plant species  documented in exurban developments  were  found  solely  within that  land  use.  Two  of these  species,  spotted knapweed  (Centaurea maculosa Lam.)  and  leafy  spurge  (Euphorbia esula  L. var.  esula), are  noxious  weeds  that  have  been  shown  to lower  the  value  of  rangeland  ecosystems for  ungulates  such as deer  (Odocoileus spp.)  and elk (Cervus  elaphus)  (Trammell and Butler  1995;  Thompson  1996).

The results  of altered  biotic communities in exurban  developments  could be influential  at  two  spatial scales  (Duerksen  and  others  2000). At  the site  scale,  potential  interactions among  wildlife  species  suggest  that  exurban  developments  may  be functioning  as  ecological  traps:  areas  where  species  assess  the land to be suitable habitat  but then suffer reduced survival  and  reproduction  when  they  live there (Pulliam  1996;  Donovan and  Thompson  2001). Also at this  level,  nonnative  plants displace  native  plants,  thereby  altering  interspecific dynamics  and  reducing  habitat quality  for  wildlife  that  do best  in native  plant  communities.  At  the  landscape  scale, exurban  developments  could be  serving  as sources  that  produce  an excess  of human-adapted  wildlife  species  and  nonnative  plants.  Because  exurban  developments are  embedded  in rural  areas,  often  adjacent to  public  lands,  they  may  be  providing individuals  and  propagules  that  spill  over into  surrounding  lands.  Therefore,  the effects  of exurban  development  are  felt  not  just  within its  boundaries  but well  into other areas  (Buechner  and  Sauvajot 1996;  Theobald, Miller,  and Hobbs  1997;  Knight and Clark  1998).

If exurban  developments  are  sources  of undesirable species,  then the  emerging strategy  to  protect  biodiversity  by working  with ranchers  is correct.  Ranchers  and farmers  own much of the land  being  converted  to exurban  development  in the Mountain  West  (Theobald  2000). Our  study  found that  biodiversity was at least  as well served  on ranches  as  it was  on  protected  areas.  More  support  for  the new con-

servation  strategy is  provided  by  a recent  study  which  pointed  out that  most of our protected  areas lie  on the  least  productive  soils  and  at  the  highest  elevations,  whereas most  private lands  occur  in the  most  productive, low-elevation  sites  (Scott  and  others  2001). Our  results,  combined  with this  information,  suggest  that  we will not be able  to sustain  native  biodiversity in the Mountain  West  by relying  merely  on  protected  areas. Future  conservation  efforts  to  protect  this  region's natural  heritage will require  closer  attention  to the role  of  private  lands  (Knight  1999).
sections.CONSIDERATIONS FOR LAND-USE DECISION M:
Inferences  from our  study  should be viewed as  speculative, but if further  studies support  our  findings, land-use  planners  need  to be aware  of the  ecological  effects  of exurban  developments across  the  Mountain  West.  The  Ecological Society  of  America recently  published  a  report  that  provided  ecological  principles  and  guidelines  for land-use  decisions  (Dale  and others  2000). Christopher Duerksen  and others  have written  a  useful  handbook  that  gives  suggestions  for  reducing human  impacts  associated with  housing  developments (2000). Decision  makers concerned  about  the sustainability of land  uses  and  the  maintenance  of  biodiversity should  consult  these documents and others  and  encourage  more  informed  conversations  about  the implications  of land-use decisions.  We  suggest  three  additional  points,  derived  from an  ecological  perspective, to consider  when  making  land-use  decisions  in the rural Mountain  West:

1.  The  location  of development is  ecologically relevant.  Low-elevation  lands  support  a  disproportionate  amount of  biodiversity  and can be the most  ecologically sensitive  (Romme  1997).  Additionally, the effects  of  development  extend  beyond  its boundaries  and can be  expected  to influence  surrounding  lands.  Strategic  placement of exurban  developments within  a  rural landscape  is  critical (Knight  and  Clark 1998).
2.  Low-density residential developments influence biotic  communities. Even  at  densities of one house  per  14-20 hectares,  the effects  of human residences  are  seen. It cannot be assumed  that,  because  most of the land within exurban  developments remains  undeveloped,  it is suitable  for all  species  that  would occur  there  if houses were  not  present. And,  of  course,  it is  not  just  houses  that  come  with  exurban  development-some  homeowners  load  up  their  unbuilt  acreage with  4H  livestock, horses, or other  stock,  which  greatly  extend  the  humanizing  effects  on a site. In  doing  so, exurban  development  patterns  spread  change  associated  with  human  developments farther  across  the  landscape  than  would more  concentrated development  densities, such as  those in urban  and  suburban  areas.  Laws  that  exclude  certain  development densities  from  the  county  review  process  should  be reevaluated. For  example,  Colorado  law  allows  subdivisions  of one house  per  14  hectares  or  greater to avoid  county review,  thereby  encouraging  this  density  of  development  (Riebsame,  Gosnell,  and Theobald  1996;  Romme  1997).  Cluster  developments  are  an alternative  settlement pattern  that involves  concentrating  houses and  leaving  the remainder  of the  purchased land  undeveloped (Theobald,  Miller,  and Hobbs  1997;  Odell and  Knight

- 2001). However, little is known  about the site- and  landscape-scale  effects of cluster development,  so caution  should  be used in  promoting  this  approach.
3.  Ranches are  important  in  biodiversity  protection.  Because  private  lands are often the most  productive,  lowest-elevation  sites,  they play  a  disproportionate  role in maintaining  biodiversity  that is not  found  in  protected  areas,  which  are  mostly  in the  least  productive,  high-elevation sites  (Scott  and  others  2001). Ranches in  our study  area  were as  good  as or better than  comparable protected  areas at  conserving biodiversity.

Conversion  of  ranchland  to  exurban  development should  be  monitored,  because  it will  likely  result in  a  simplification of  our  natural  heritage  and  an  everincreasing  number  of  species  with  declining  populations.
sections.NOTES:
1. For  the  songbird  and mammalian  carnivore  communities,  we  sampled  thirty-three  points  in exurban  developments,  thirty  on ranches,  and  thirty  in  protected  areas.  For  the  plant  community,  we sampled  twenty-three  points  in each  land use. Points  were  restricted  to areas  that met the  following criteria: at least  75  meters  from  riparian  areas; slope  of  35  percent  or  less;  at least  75  meters  from  the edge  of the land  use;  at least  20 meters  from  built structures  and  roads;  and at least  300  meters  from the next-nearest  point.
2. We  recorded  the  species  of  songbirds we detected  visually  or  aurally and  the  distance, in  meters, to those detections  at each  point.  Point  counts  were  eight  minutes  long,  with an initial  thirty-second quiet  period,  and  were  conducted  in a three-hour  period  after  sunrise.  Each  point  was  sampled  twice between  15  May  and  15  June 2000 and twice between  17  May  and  14  June 2001, which  coincides  with the breeding  season  for  most  songbirds in our  study  area.  The  computer  program  DISTANCE  3.5  (Thomas and others  1998)  was  used  to  generate  density  estimates.  To  test  for  statistical  differences between  land uses,  we  did  pairwise  comparisons of densities  using  an  approximate z-test.  An  c  = o.1o  was  set  a  priori to minimize  the  probability of  committing  a  Type  II  error, but differences were  ultimately  considered statistically significant  at  a'  =  0.03,  which  is Bonferroni adjusted  for  multiple  comparisons.
3.  The  presence  of medium-sized  mammalian  carnivores was  recorded  at  scent  stations  surveyed between  17  May  and 12  July  2000  and  23  May  and 16  August  2001.  Each scent station  was established  by clearing  vegetation,  rocks,  and  any  other debris  from a 1-meter-diameter circle  of  ground (Linhart and Knowlton  1975).  Bait  was  placed  in the center  of the station for four consecutive  days  to attract carnivores. Stations  were  examined  daily  for the  presence  of carnivore tracks.  We  tested  for  statistical differences  in  presence  and absence  proportions  of carnivores  at each station across  land uses  using Fisher's Exact  Test (PROC FREQ, SAS Institute  1999).  If the overall  test was  statistically significant,  we did  follow-up paired  comparisons  of  proportions,  again using  Fisher's Exact  Test.  Differences  were considered  statistically significant  at o  = o.1o.
4.  Thirty-meter transects  were  established  in the  four  cardinal directions  at  each  sampling  point. Sampling  occurred  within  20-by-5o-centimeter quadrats  placed  on the left side of each  transect  at  lo, 20,  and  30  meters  from  the  point,  with the 20-centimeter edge  abutting the transect.  Canopy  coverage (cover)  of individual  plant species,  as well as  percentages of rock,  litter,  and bare  ground,  were  estimated to the nearest  percentage  point.  One trained  botanist  made all cover  estimates,  while another observer  recorded  the data.  Sampling took  place  between  26  June  and 18  July  2001, which is  approximately  peak  biomass in our  study  area.  Fewer  than 1  percent  of  species  encountered  could not be identified  and  were  categorized as unknown.  At each  sampling  point  we calculated  a mean  value  for plant  cover  and  for  species  richness  to use  in  analysis. We used  one-way  analysis of variance  to test  for statistical  differences in cover  and  species  richness  across  land uses  (PROC GLM,  SAS Institute  1999).  If the overall  F-test  was  significant,  we used the Least  Significant  Difference  method to  compare  individual means. To meet  assumptions  of  normality  and  homogeneity  of variances,  data  were  squareroot  transformed for  analysis, but  results  are  presented in  the  original scale.  Differences were  considered statistically  significant  at o  =  o.1o.

sections.JEFFREY S. SMITH:
ABSTRACT. Continued  rural-to-urban  migration  has  helped  motivate  cultural  geographers, long suspected  of  having  a rural  bias,  to include urban areas  in their  purview.  Patterns  of gender,  class,  ethnicity, and commercialization  have  proved  to be fertile  subjects  for  research, but the elastic  links  between rural  and urban  places  are  not  yet  well understood.  Hispanos, despite  intense  feelings  of  loyalty  to their  rural villages,  moved en masse  to cities  in the  1940s. By  the  1950s  a  majority  of  Hispanos  were  living  in  regional  urban  centers  of the  upper  Rio Grande  country,  where  wages  were  higher  and  employment  was secure.  This  Hispano experience  is a crucible  for  examining  how urbanites' attachment  to rural  places  is manifested  in various cultural  expressions  brought  from  country  to  city: painted  murals,  burial  preferences, popular music, and  irrigation  ditches.  Understanding  threads of rural  culture that have  been  incorporated  into the urban  fabric  in turn leads  to clearer  comprehension  of the emotional attachment  that urbanites  have for rural  areas  and a better  appreciation  of the complexity  of the urban  cultural  environment.  Keywords: Colorado, Hispanos,  New Mexico, rural villages, urban place attachment.

Since  the end of World  War  II,  American  cities have  attracted  ever  greater  numbers  of new residents  in search  of diverse  employment  opportunities  and  amenityrich  environments.'  Since  the  early  198os, Atlanta,  Denver,  Houston,  Las  Vegas, Salt Lake  City,  and Phoenix have  consistently  topped  the list of the  fastest-growing urban centers  in the United  States.  With  surrounding  lands  being gobbled  up  at a rate of more  than  an  acre  an  hour,  rapid  urbanization  is  coming  at  a  heavy  environmental  and  social  price  (Stoel  1999; Theobald  2001).  As recent  news headlines  assert,  for many people  cities have become a  stress-inducing,  inhospitable,  and  impersonal environment with  polluted air,  rampant  road  rage,  heinous hate crimes, sprawl, and traffic  congestion (Muir 1999).  Cities are  popularly  perceived  as the root of many  a social ill.  Conversely, rural  areas  are  regarded as warm and  friendly  places where  one can  escape  the urban  jungle  and find  peace,  solace,  and comfort  (de  Wit 1997;  Jakle  1999).  As sanctuaries  that  possess  restorative powers,  rural  places  have become an  idyllic  retreat  from the  "increasingly urbanized and  fast-paced  world beyond"  (Wyckoff  and Dilsaver  1995,  4).

One  way  urbanites  deal  with the  "evils" of  living  in urban  centers  is  by incorporating  nonurban  practices into their  daily lives.  Just  as  the  romanticized  country  life centers  on  reclaiming the  purported  serenity  of nature,  rural  small-town  places  can offer a  nurturing,  extended-family  atmosphere  where residents  personalize  their relationships and  forge  strong  ties  to  place  (Jakle 1999).  Living  in a  city  can  be more tolerable  when one is surrounded  by  reminders  of the  presumably  peaceful,  caring, wholesome virtues  of a rural  lifestyle  (Little  1999).  A link  between  rural  and urban

places  is evident, then, in  my exploration  of rural  place  identification  among  urban-dwelling  Hispanos  in  Albuquerque,  Espafiola, and Santa  Fe,  New Mexico,  and in Pueblo,  Colorado.2
sections.LANDSCAPE ANALYSIS MOVES TO THE CITY:
American  cultural  geographers are  renowned  for their  meticulous examinations  of the built  environment (Wagner  and Mikesell  1962;  Norton  1989;  Foote  and others 1994;  Myers  and others  forthcoming).  For  decades  geographers with a cultural  focus have also  interpreted  patterns  of  ordinary  cultural  landscapes  (Meinig 1979a; Groth and Bressi  1997),  including  the work of such well-known scholars  as Peirce Lewis  (1979), Donald  Meinig  (1979b), J.  B.  Jackson  (1984, 1994),  Allen  Noble (1992), Wilbur  Zelinsky  (1992), and  Terry Jordan, Jon  Kilpinen, and  Charles  Gritzner  (1997). The  majority  of these "traditional" pieces  have focused on the attributes  of rural, folk,  or  preindustrial societies.  As  James  Duncan  (1990)  and others  have  acknowledged,  the  methodologies  and  corpus  of  knowledge  advanced  by  this  approach  to cultural  geographical research  have  provided  a solid foundation and a tested  set of axioms on which the future  of the  subdiscipline  can be built.

Increasing  urbanization,  however,  combined with a call for the  application  of more  socially  grounded  and  theoretically based  investigations, is  precipitating a  shift in the research agenda  of  today's  largely "new"  cultural  geographers  (Cosgrove  and Daniels  1988;  Jackson 1989;  Cosgrove 1993,  1994;  Duncan  and  Ley 1993;  Holdsworth 1993; Duncan  1994;  Mitchell  1994).  Social  interaction  in urban  and industrial  places helps  drive  the  research of some  present-day cultural geographers  (Ley  1996;  Hayden 1997; Wheeler  1998; Peach  2002).  Furthermore, the  1990os witnessed  a  growing  number of scholars  who  explored  the  complexity  of urban centers  (Muir 1999;  Myers and others  forthcoming), especially  those who  sought  to understand  the role of landscape  in the  development  of culture  (Mitchell  1994; Wheeler  1998).  Interpreting  urban  patterns  of  ethnicity (Arreola  1994;  Ruddick  1996;  Wood 1997;  Li  1998), gender  relations  (Hayden  1981;  Watson  1986; Spain 1992;  Fincher and  Jacobs 1998), employment  and class  (Mitchell  1993; Blake  and  Arreola  1996;  Bondi  1998;  Hiebert 1999),  social and  political  economy (Harvey  1989;  Zukin  1995; Mitchell  1996;  Warren  1996;  Kloosterman, Van  der  Leun,  and  Rath  1999),  and  development,  consumption, and commercialization  (Kenny  1995; Smith  1996)  is  proving  to be a rich area for research. Of  growing  interest,  especially  among  the  postmodern  and  poststructuralist  geographers, is  analysis of  social-spatial contestations  in urban  settings  (Mills 1993).  The  amalgamation  of  contemporary  cultural  geographical  studies affirms that  values,  ideologies,  and  identity  are  all  meaningfully  represented in the  socially constructed  landscape.  Unfortunately, as the laments of a chorus of scholars  indicate, we have done  little  more  than  scratch the  surface in our  attempt  to  comprehend the  complexity  of urban culture  (Parsons 1994;  Wheeler  1998;  Mitchell  1999).

As  increasing  numbers  of  cultural  geographers  reposition their  research  endeavors and move from examinations  of rural locations  to cities, a  gap is opening  in the  body  of  literature.  The  ongoing  blurring  of  rural and  urban  culture  requires

that more work  be done at their interface  so we can more  fully appreciate the link between  rural  and urban  places  (Rigg  1998).  A few  years  ago  Urban  Geography Editor  James  Wheeler  issued  a call  for  manuscripts  that focus on the interconnections between rural  and urban  places (1998).  His words reflect  the  growing  realization that  only through  such  scholarly  endeavors  will we  improve  our  understanding of how urban cultural  landscapes  are  constructed.  Others  agree:  "A  more substantive understanding  of  landscape  ...  cannot  focus on the  country  or on the  city,  but must incorporate  the mutual definition and relations of both"  (Olwig 1996, 645).  The discord  between  "traditional"-largely  rural-and  "new"-predominantly  urbancultural  geographical  approaches  only  serves  to limit scholars'  scope  of research. An effective  way  of  decoding  the hidden  meanings  within the  complexity  of urban centers  is to examine  more  closely  the various  interlinkages between rural  and urban  places.  "As  a cultural  construct,  the  meaning  of the  city  can be  deciphered  by closely examining  its  complex relationship  with the culture  of which it is a  part" (Domosh  1992, 475).  A clearer  appreciation  of  links between  rural and urban  culture  will better  inform us about the urban  experience.
sections.PLACE ATTACHMENT:
Even  through  the late  1970s  cultural  geographers  devoted  relatively little research energy  to  understanding  how  place knowledge  is  organized  or to  capturing  the emotions  that  people  develop  about  places  (Wright 1947;  Tuan  1977;  Sopher 1979). Yi-Fu  Tuan  stepped  up  to the  plate,  publishing  two treatises  in which he  explored attachment  to  place.  He introduced  the  concept  of  "geopiety," the intersection  of devotion  to  place  and  one's  native  land  or  country  (1976). This  helped  readers  grasp a reverence  for home. Then, in  Space  and  Place,  Tuan  explained  the  concept  of a homeland as  "an  archive  of fond memories  and  splendid  achievements  that  inspire the  present;  place  is  permanent  and hence  reassuring to  man,"  and "the  more ties there are  [to  a  place],  the  stronger  is the emotional  bond"  (1977,  154,  158).

These two works broke new  ground  in  comprehending  how  deep  emotional attachments  to  place  develop.  Since  then,  however,  interest  among  cultural  geographers  in  people's  strong  attachment  to  place  has  been intermittent.  One  example  of research  in the Tuanian  mode is Ben  Marsh's acclaimed  work on anthracite  mining towns in northeastern  Pennsylvania  (1987).  Marsh  explains  that,  despite  endemic poverty  and economic  collapse,  residents  refused  to leave  their  home communities because  of their intense  bonds with the  place  and their  sense of rootedness.

By  the  mid-199os  the  body  of  geographical  literature  on emotional attachment to  place  had  advanced  considerably. After  monographs  by  Alvar  Carlson  (199o)  and Richard Nostrand  (1992)  and  a session  at the  1991 meeting of  the  Association of American  Geographers,  a special  issue  of  the  Journal of  Cultural  Geography,  later reworked into book  form, was devoted  to the  concept  of homeland.  Guest editors Richard Nostrand  and Lawrence Estaville Jr.  found  scholars who  could  persuasively argue for the  emerging  homeland  concept  and  discuss  their  research as examples (1993,  2001). Although  some  culture  groups  bond  with  a  place  more  readily than do

others, consensus  among  the  contributing authors  is that the  most  important ingredient  in  the  development of  a  homeland is  deep  emotional attachment  to  a place  (Arreola 2001; Conzen  2001; Jett 2001;  Jordan-Bychkov  2001; Nostrand  and Estaville  2001;  Schnell  2001).

The homeland  concept  is  significantly  improving  our  appreciation  of the  deepseated  feelings people  have for a  place.  Even  though  Nostrand  and Estaville's  anthology  is a  significant  addition  to homeland  literature  (2001), additional  geographical accounts  are needed.  As Richard Muir  concludes,  "Often the  significance  of  place and the  meanings  associated  with  [that place]  lie at the core of a  person's identity," yet  "much  concerning  the  relationship  between  people  and  places  remains  poorly understood"  (1999, 274).

Dolores  Hayden recognizes  that scholars from various  cognate  fields are also examining  place  attachment.  "[E]nvironmental  psychologists ... define  place  attachment  as a  psychological  process  ..,  .and suggest  that  place  attachment  can  develop social,  material and  ideological  dimensions,  as individuals create  ties to kin and  neighbors,... and  participate  in  public  life as residents of a  particular community"  (1997, 112).  Place attachment has also been  incorporated  into the research  agendas  of  many sociologists  as  they try  to  explain  the  power  of human connections  to  places  that  may no  longer  exist;  for  example,  to  neighborhoods that have been  obliterated  by  urban renewal  (Hayden 1997).  Some  scholars have even  argued  that more research should be conducted  on the need to  belong  to a  particular place  from a  biologically  based perspective  as it  incorporates  the  concept  of  territoriality  (Muir 1999).

Cultural  geographers  obviously have  no  monopoly on  the  study  of  place  attachment,  but we should  be  capitalizing  on  our  unique  perspective  on  landscape analysis  to further understand the  deep-seated  ties  people  have for  particular places. "When  [people's]  experience of  other  places  suggests  that  some  familiar  things at home  may  be  distinctive,  these  become symbols  of home"  (Sopher  1979, 137). Cultural  geographers are best  qualified to  read  the  "symbols of  home,"  especially  as  they  are manifested in  ordinary  landscapes. Few  geographical  studies have  provided evidence  of  the  extent  to  which  urban  residents  bond  with  rural places.  More  geographers  need  to  analyze  the urban  landscape  for the  strong  emotional attachment  city  dwellers have for rural areas.  Using  the  Hispano  urban  experience,  this  study  reveals some  of  the  symbols of  the  interplay  between  rural and urban  places  and will,  I  hope,  further our  comprehension of the  complexity  of the urban structure.
sections.HISPANOS OF THE UPPER RIO GRANDE:
Early  New Mexico scholars  quickly  concluded  that, for  Hispanos,  the  community in which  they were born and raised is the most  meaningful  aspect of their lives. In 1954 John Burma  wrote  that  it  is  impossible  to  overemphasize  the  importance of  the home  village  to  Hispanos.  He stressed that individuals  are identified  first and foremost  with  their  community of  birth,  and  loyalty  to  that  community reaches a degree unknown  in most of the rest of the United  States. Little has changed: The home

community  is still  central  in the  lives  of  Hispanos  (Martin  2000).  As  Nostrand  concluded  in  1992,  no other  place  is as  meaningful  to them as  their  native  village.  Two popular  New Mexico  publications  have  further  captured  the essence  of  allegiance to  place.  The  September  1997  issue of New  Mexico  Magazine featured  an article  on La  Querencia  (which  was  roughly  translated  as "the  place  of  your  heart's  desire")

FIG. 1--Hispano  place-names  referred  to in the text.

<!-- image -->

(Fauntleroy 1997). For  Hispanos, in a  term  borrowed  from  bullfighting, the  querencia is the  village  in which  they  were  born and raised,  the  place  where  they  feel completely  at  home and  know  they  belong.  A second  publication, La  Herencia  del  Norte, has  periodically featured  letters  to the  editor  under  the  subtitle  "Hogar  dulce  Hogar" (Home  Sweet  Home).  Contributors explain  what  makes  living  in their  New  Mexico village  special  to them.  Because  of the  unequaled  bonds that  many  of them  express

for their  rural  villages  in northern  New Mexico and southern  Colorado,  Hispanos make an ideal culture  group  for  examining  the ties urban  residents  have for rural places.

Before  the  1940s  Hispanos  were  principally subsistence  farmers  and  ranchers. As Sarah  Deutsch  documented,  even  though  numerous  Hispano  men took  jobs  as  itinerant  laborers  in the  potato  and  sugar-beet industries  of northern  and  central  Colorado,  they always returned  home to their  small  village  (1987). In  the  1940s,  however, despite  deep  attachment to  home,  Hispano  families began  moving  to  regional  urban centers  that  offered  higher-paying jobs.  By  the  mid-195os a  majority  of all  Hispanos were  living  in the urbanized  areas  of  Albuquerque, Phoenix, Denver,  and,  closer  to home, Pueblo, Espaflola,  and Santa Fe  (Nostrand 1992).  Because of  the  feelings Hispanos  have  for  family  and  village  roots,  many  former  residents  continue  to own rural  property, to which  they  return  on weekends,  holidays,  and  vacations  (Carlson 1990; Smith  1997;  Martin  2000). Furthermore, aspects  of  Hispanos' lives  that  remind them of the rural  village  ideal  have  become  particularly meaningful.

To  explore  the  ways  in which  Hispanos  have  incorporated  their  extraordinarily deep  emotional attachment  for rural  areas  into their  city  lives,  I amassed  evidence during  seven  years  of fieldwork  and informal  interviews  throughout  the rural  villages  and urban  centers  of New Mexico  and southern  Colorado.  In  the summers  of 1998  and  1999  and the fall  of  2000 I  systematically analyzed  the  landscape  in Albuquerque,  Espahfiola, Santa  Fe,  and Pueblo  (Figure  1).  In addition  to commercial  districts,  my  field observations  of  public space-places  where  the  landscape  has been influenced  by  a  community  of  people-focused on  Zip-code  areas  in which, according  to the  1990  U.S.  census,  a  plurality  of residents  were  Hispanos.3  The accuracy  of  my  personal  observations was  verified through  numerous  informal  interviews with  key  informants,  including  housewives,  retired  couples,  employed  and unemployed  or disabled  residents,  business owners and directors,  business  employees (both  male and  female),  scholars  from local  colleges  and  universities,  and  government officials.  Extensive  daily  notes, photographs,  and sketches  documented  my findings  and  allowed  me to  synthesize and  distill  the  information  I  gathered. I  found four  areas  that  show  urban  Hispanos'  strong  ties  to rural  areas: murals,  mortuaries, music,  and  acequias  (irrigation  ditches).
sections.MURALS:
From  the  preservation of historic  buildings  to the creation  and  designation  of  public  landmarks and  memorials,  people  mark  their  heritage in a  variety of  ways.  Highly visible  features,  such  as  Mount  Rushmore,  the monuments  in  Washington,  D.C.,  or, tragically, the World  Trade  Center  towers,  hold  public significance  and serve  to enhance  people's  sense  of  place  (Tuan 1977; Foote,  T6th,  and  Arvay 2ooo;  Godfrey 2002). On  a less  grandiose  scale,  ethnic  groups  personalize  their  landscapes,  emphasizing unique  traits and elaborating their shared identity  (Ford and Griffin 1981). Features  on  the  landscape  consolidate shared  meanings and  build  community (Duncan  and  Ley 1993).

The creation  of  public  murals  is a common method  whereby  Hispanic  populations enhance their  community identity.  These  expressions  of vernacular  art not only promote  community pride,  cooperation,  and  stability  but also  signal  the  presence  of a  particular ethnic  substrate within the  larger urban  center  (Ford  and  Griffin 1981; Hayden  1997). After  an  extensive  examination  of murals  in San  Antonio,  Texas, Daniel Arreola  concluded that  painted  murals are a visual  landscape  artifact  that supplements  oral  tradition:  " [B]y  re-creating and  projecting  images  of well-known ... personalities  as well as historic events ... murals serve as mnemonic devices" (1984,  414-417). As Arreola  explains,  in the absence  of written  records,  murals  that adorn  public space  are  an  enculturating  medium that  strengthens  group memory.

Hispanos  of the  upper  Rio Grande  region recognize  that  public  murals have long  been a  popular  form of cultural  expression  among rural-dwelling  residents. Many  rural  Hispano  communities contain artistic  renditions  that adorn  the landscape  of both  private  dwellings  and  public space.  Similar  idealized  scenes  now  appear  in urban  centers  with a  large  Hispano  population.

In San  Luis,  Colorado,  for  example,  a  mural  painted  by  the  well-known  regional artist  and  sculptor  Carlos  Sandoval  graces  a wall  in the heart  of the small  community (Figure  2).  The mural  depicts regional  cultural  traditions,  Hispano farming life,  and a bountiful  goodness  of the earth.  Crowning  the mural are  the crucified Christ  and four  Spanish  conquistadores  in full armor.  This section is  particularly laden with cultural  meaning,  not  just  for  religion  but because  the  conquistadores signify  the  important  distinction  Hispanos  make  between  themselves  and all other people  of  Hispanic origin  in the United States.  Equally  impressive  is a mural in remote Truchas,  New Mexico,  that carries  viewers from the  top  of the  Sangre  de Cristo Mountains-the  principal  mountain chain of New Mexico and southern Colorado  along  the Rio  Grande-down the  valley  to the  religious  mecca  of  Chimay6 (Figure  3).  Embedded  in the scene are  locally  prominent  physical  and cultural  features.  Another  mural,  in San  Miguel,  New  Mexico,  honors the local  Catholic  church and the  important  role it has  played  in residents' lives  by portraying  major  figures and events in the life of the church  and the  community (Figure  4).  For  the ruraldwelling  Hispanos  who live  in communities  such  as  these,  murals  consolidate  shared meanings  by reminding  them of the richness  of their lives  and their  cultural  traditions.

In the Atrisco  suburb  on  Albuquerque's west side,  murals  serve  a similar  purpose.  A  enduring  and common mural  theme,  even in this  metropolis  of more than half a million  people,  is the rural  village  ideal.  Residents  of the Alamosa  neighborhood of Atrisco  were  having  a  particularly difficult  time  fighting  gang  activity  and graffiti.  One resident,  who  prefers  to remain  anonymous, explained  to me that the community  responded  by bonding  together  to  promote  a cleaner, safer environment.  Even more  significant,  neighborhood children  and adults painted  murals on perimeter  walls  depicting  positive  aspects  of their lives, around which  other members of  the  community could  rally. Although  many  of  the  murals  have a  religious connotation, one  noteworthy  panel  depicts  a small  village  at the base  of what  are

FIG. 2-Carlos  Sandoval's color mural  in San  Luis,  Colorado,  depicts  various  aspects  of life in the rural  community;  in the middle  top panel  are  the crucified  Christ  and four  Spanish  conquistadores. (Photograph  by  the author,  September  2000)

<!-- image -->

unquestionably  the  Sangre de Cristo  Mountains  (Figure  5).  Brought  into the  city  is the home  village,  a not  entirely  abstract  ideal  in which residents  can find  comfort and  security.

A second mural  in Atrisco  features  a  bucolic  scene  from  the forlorn  Santa  Clara Cemetery.  Completed  in  1999  by Leopoldo  Romero,  the  painted  mural  depicts  an idealized  view of a small town with two  prominent  churches  and  adjoining  cemeteries  (Figure  6).  The ideal reconnects  to a lost or distant  past  and  suggests  that eternal peace  and  happiness are  achieved only  when  one's  final resting  place  is  among the rustic  hills  of home.  Equally telling  is  how  the  mural  has  been  treated: By  the  fall of 2000 some sections of it had been scaled  off,  and  graffiti  had been added.  The idealized  rural  scene,  however,  had been left unblemished.
sections.MORTUARIES:
To be buried behind a  cemetery  wall similar  to one  they  remember  in the small village  where  they  were  born is  simply  not  enough  for some  Hispanos:  They  want to be interred  at  the  actual  site  of their  family's roots.  Among  the  greatest  challenges in  identifying ties  between  rural  communities  and  urban  centers  is  overcoming links that tend to be  profoundly  personal  and therefore  all but invisible.  So it is with burial  practices  of  family  members.  As cultural  spores,  cemeteries  are  a  landscape artifact  that houses a wealth of information.  Physical  anthropologists  long  have

FIG. 3-A  view of the  Sangre  de Cristo  Mountains  from  Truchas, New Mexico,  and the  rolling  hills in the  vicinity  of  Chimay6,  as  portrayed  in a color mural in Truchas.  (Photograph  by  the author, September  2000)

<!-- image -->

FIG. 4-The  center  of this color  mural  in San  Miguel,  New  Mexico,  shows  the  community's Catholic church.  On the left  is  the crucified  Christ  at  night;  on the  right  is  the  Virgen  de  Guadalupe in  daylight. (Photograph  by  the author,  September  1997)

<!-- image -->

FIG.  5-A  color mural on the  perimeter  wall of the Alamosa  neighborhood  in  Albuquerque,  New Mexico,  depicts  a small  village  at  the base  of the  Sangre  de Cristo  Mountains,  next to the Rio Grande. (Photograph  by  the author,  September  2000)

<!-- image -->

known that  burial  grounds  are  indispensable as a tool for  uncovering  the secrets  of a local  culture.  Unfortunately, cemeteries  reveal  little  about  the last  known  place  of residence  of the deceased;  such information  goes largely  unreported  on  cemetery headstones.

Graham  Rowles  and Malcolm  Comeaux  assert  that  "post-death  migration"  or long-distance  shipment  of human  remains,  is  strongly  correlated with  people's  attachment  to  place  (1987). Their  evidence  shows  that,  cross-culturally, people aspire to be laid  to rest  in a  place  for  which  they  hold a  particular affinity. Often  they  call that  place  "home." For  some  people,  home is their  place  of  birth;  for  others,  a  place where  significant  events  unfolded  during  their  lifetime.  For  most  Hispanos,  home is  unquestionably the  village  of their  family's roots.  With  few  alternatives available, I used data  from  interviews  with  mortuary  directors  to track  final  journeys.

In  the  commercial  districts  of the cities  I  examined,  numerous  mortuaries  serve local  needs.  The  funeral  homes,  however, tend  to be  commercially  segregated, based on  ethnicity.  In  Espafiola, for  example,  the Block-Salazar Mortuary  provides  most of the  burial  services  for  local  Hispanics.  According  to monument consultant  Alicia Duran,  slightly  more than 20  percent  of Block-Salazar's business  relates  to  people who want  to be interred  in their  hometown  cemetery  (1999).  In  these  situations,  the mortuary  typically  arranges two services: one at  the  mortuary for  family  and  friends

FIG.  6-Santa Clara  Cemetery, in the  Atrisco  suburb  on the  west  side  of  Albuquerque, a color  mural on the  perimeter  wall,  painted  by Leopoldo  Romero  in  1999,  that  portrays rural  houses  and  two community  churches  with headstones  surrounding  them.  (Photograph  by  the author,  September  2000)

<!-- image -->

who live  in  the  Espafiola-Santa Fe  area, and  a  second,  graveside, service  in the  smalltown  cemetery.  Duran  explained  that most of their out-of-town business  is in the small  villages  of northern  New Mexico  and southern  Colorado.

In  Pueblo, Colorado,  of the twelve mortuaries  that offer burial services,  the Romero  Family  Funeral  Home is the  recognized  leader  in service  to the local Hispanic  population.  Director  Larry Romero  informed  me that  nearly  15  percent  of the services conducted at his  mortuary  are for families whose relative  wished to be buried  in their  hometown  cemetery  (1999).  For  the Romero  Family  Funeral  Home, the  majority  of their  nonlocal burials  serve  Hispanos  who lived  in Colorado's  San Luis  Valley, a rural  Hispano stronghold  (Smith  1999).
sections.FOLK MUSIC:
From  highbrow  classical  to the  pulsating  rhythms  of  rap  and  bebop,  music  is one of the  purest  forms of cultural  expression. Music  plays  an  integral  part  in  expressing tastes,  preferences, fears, and  fantasies. It  serves as  an  effective means  by  which  memories of a  place  are  recalled.  Since  the  1970s  a  growing  number of cultural  geographers  have  interpreted  the  geography  of  music. As illustrated  by  the  carefully composed  overviews  by Lily  Kong  and  by  Peter  Nash  and  George  Carney, as  well as a  special  issue  of the  Journal  of  Cultural  Geography, music research  has become extensive and varied  (Kong  1995;  Nash and  Carney  1996;  Carney  1998).  One of the

more  popular themes  has  been  the  interpretation of  place  identity in  music,  mostly in either rock  and  roll  or  country music  (Curtis and  Rose  1983;  Carney 1990o, 1998; Kong  1995). For  example, Louis  Woods  and  Charles Gritzner's content  analysis of country music  concludes that  a  portion of the  genre  portrays nostalgia and  yearning  for  a  simpler way  of life  (1990).  People's disenchantment with urban  living, especially among  uprooted migrants, leads  to  homesickness for  the  rural landscape and  an  agrarian lifestyle. Woods  and Gritzner conclude  that  country music  is a symbolic reminder and  expression of desire for  a  past time  and  a  distant place.

For  many ethnic  groups music  is  a  vital  source  of  subcultural identity. Unfortunately, place-specific analysis of ethnic  music  has  been  largely ignored  by  geographers  (Curtis and  Rose  1983). As  Carney laments, "[our]  geographic knowledge of ethnic  music  is  practically nil  despite the  fact  that  anthropologists, folklorists, and ethnomusicologists have  for  years studied variations in  both  rural and  urban  contexts." "Where," he wonders, "are  the  geographical studies  on the rich  and  variegated music  traditions of the  Hispanic Southwest, French of southern  Louisiana?" (1998,  5).  Still  more  surprising is  that  geographers have  all  but  overlooked how  ethnic music  perpetuates social  identity, strengthens a  group's perception of  space, and  helps  maintain cultural or  ethnic  ties  to a  place  (Kong 1995).

In  traditional rural Hispano  communities, music  accompanies a  large part  of village life.  From  the  melodious hymns  of church, to the  ballads sung  during holidays and  family celebrations, to  the  Penitente chants, music  adds  flavor to  Hispano culture. It  is  at  community celebrations, however, that  music  strikes a  special chord. According to  the  local  writer Nasario Garcia, feast-day celebrations, with  their  music and  dancing, are  especially important events  in the life of the rural  Hispano community (1999). Historically  each  village typically supported  three or four musical  groups  that  played at  these  special social  events.  Some  of the  more  talented  groups  gained  a  regional  reputation and were  paid  to travel  to  nearby villages to  play.  Today the tradition of small  bands  and  musical groups  in rural Hispano villages continues.

Described as  a  blend  of  Spanish guitar and  German polka  music, Hispano  songs have  a  clarity and  heartfelt tone  that  distinguishes them  from  other  Latin American music,  including  Tejano music  (Welsh  1999).  A more  defining  characteristic of Hispano music  is that  most  songs  are  corridos (musical folk  tales).  Many  Hispano corridos can  be traced to medieval Andalusian verses  and  ballads brought over  by colonial  Spaniards (Herrera-Sobek 1993). Corridos have  always been  a traditional Hispano  way  of  expressing feelings and  an  important way  of  disseminating newsworthy information (Lopez  1999; Chivez-Bent and  Sanchez 2000). Today some  of the  most  popular Hispano  corridos are  tales  about  life  in rural  New  Mexican villages.

When the famed Hispanic  songwriter Micky Cruz left New York  City after high school,  he  began  his career by playing  for audiences  throughout  New  Mexico.  Before he played for Bo-Diddley  or founded  Cruzin Records, Micky recounts, Hispano audiences asked him to quit playing those other songs  and play the traditional  songs

everyone  loved  (Lopez 1999).  "So  [he]  went to a record store and  bought  some  tapes to learn traditional  songs  from New Mexico  so  [he]  could  keep  his  job" (p. 45).

Urban-dwelling  Hispanos  continue  to  yearn  for traditional  corridos  that  are rooted in the rural areas.  As one  of more than  sixty  radio stations  in the  Albuquerque  and  Santa Fe  listening  area, public  radio  station  KANW has  helped  meet  that demand  with  its New  Mexico  Spanish  music  format.  The  station  plays songs  that are  representative  of the music  traditionally  found  in the  villages  of northern  New Mexico.  According  to  Program  Director  George  Welsh  Jr.,  all of the  Hispano  music aired on  KANW is written  and  performed  by  local  New  Mexico  artists  (1999).  The station's  policy  is that  any recording  sent in will be  played  on the air at least once,  no matter the level of  talent. Welsh indicates  that  many  of  today's  older  New  Mexico residents  enjoy  singing,  playing,  and  listening  to  the  traditional  songs  they  heard their  parents  and  grandparents sing  as  they  were  growing  up.

Since the introduction  of its current format in  1973,  the station  has  enjoyed  tremendous  success.  Intermixed  with  news  and  personal  dedications,  the  time  slot between  5:00 A.M.  and  3:00  P.M.  each  Saturday  has the  highest  overall  ratings  in the listening  area;  no  time  slot  captures  a  larger  share of listeners  in the  Albuquerque and Santa Fe  metropolitan  areas. Like other  public  radio  stations,  KANW conducts semiannual  fund-raising  campaigns.  Because of its  overwhelming  popularity,  however,  it  has  been  able  to  scale  back  the  semiannual  fund-raisers  and  supplement them with a  single campaign  held one  Saturday  each  year.  In  eight  hours the station is able to raise more  money  than it does  during  the other two  campaigns  combined (Welsh 1999).

Another  source of revenue for the station  is its sales of cassette  tapes  and compact  discs of the more  popular  New Mexico  Spanish songs.  Filled with sixteen  songs, volume  1  sold more than io,ooo  copies  between  1997  and  1999.  In the sixteen months after volume  2 was released it sold well  over  8,000  copies.  By  2002 the  station  was offering  its  eleventh  volume  and  had  lost  count  of  total  sales. A  wide variety of songs  make  the  cut,  but  those  about  local  New  Mexico  villages are some  of  the most popular. For  example, Paul  Pifio sings about  "Las Estrellas  de  Nuevo Mexico,"  Steve  Ortiz  has  a  song  titled  "Que  Viva  New  Mexico,"  and  one  of  Roberto  Griego's  most  recognized songs  is "Arriba Nuevo Mexico."  The  popularity  of  these  artists  is due  in  large part  to  the  fact that  they  sing  about  small  New Mexico  towns  with  which  listeners  are  intimately familiar. Welsh  says  that  people simply  cannot  hear these  songs  enough;  they  constantly call  in  to  request  them (1999).

In an  attempt  to further  capitalize  on the  appeal  that  Hispano  small towns  have for  listeners,  in  1998  KANW erected  a  relay  tower  in  the  far northern  New  Mexico village  of  Questa.  Located 150 miles  north  of  Albuquerque,  Questa's  200ooo population  was about  1,8oo00. By adding  to  its extensive  network  of  relay towers,  KANW  is able to  effectively  link  rural and  urban residents  throughout the  northern  part  of the state. More  important,  during  Questa's annual  feast-day  celebration  KANW has aired a "live remote" from  the  town.  All  of  the  day's events  are broadcast  to  the

Painted  by  Frederico Vigil  in  1989,  the scene includes  a  community  acequia,  a butterfly, a  hummingbird,  a man  catching  fish,  women  dancing,  and two men  irrigating a  field;  in the center  is an  overflowing basket  of fruits  and  vegetables.
